Jama said Isiolo International Airport, which was constructed during the administration of President Kibaki to help in the export of miraa and horticultural goods from the Mt Kenya region and livestock products, mainly meat and hides, lies idle because the expansion of the runway from 1.5 metres to 3 metres had not been done.

In response, Gachagua said the airport was meant to create employment and wealth, but the Kenya Kwanza administration had instead left it in ruin deliberately, claiming the move was aimed at sabotaging the economy of Mt Kenya and pastoralists’ economies.

“What was the good about destroying the Imenti forest to construct an airstrip for an individual while there is an international airport meant partly to serve the entire region just a few kilometres from Meru town?” Asked the DCP leader.

World.title: Relief for schools as government releases Sh18.5b capitation
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Education CS Julius Ogamba. [File, Standard]

The government has released Sh18.5 billion in capitation to support operations in public basic education institutions during the third term of 2026, as schools reopened across the country on Monday.

Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba said the funds have already been released and will support learners in pre-primary, primary, junior and senior schools.

The allocation is intended to facilitate smooth school operations and ensure learning activities continue without disruption.

The Sh18.5 billion has been distributed across three major capitation programmes, with Free Day Secondary Education (FDSE) allocated Sh10.963 billion, accounting for the biggest portion of the Term Three capitation.

The money will support operations in public day and secondary schools and comes as institutions prepare learners for a busy academic term.

Free Day Junior School Education has received Sh6.1 billion, to support learners in the second tier of basic education and help institutions meet operational requirements as the Competency-Based Education system continues to expand.

Meanwhile, Free Primary Education has been allocated Sh1.4 billion to support learning in public primary schools.

The funds come as a relief to school heads who had raised concerns on the insufficient funds disbursed to schools this year.

However, Ogamba said the disbursement demonstrates the Government's commitment to ensuring that learners have access to free and compulsory basic education as provided for under Article 53(1)(b) of the Constitution.

“The Government affirms its commitment to fulfil its duty to learners and educational institutions,” said the CS.

Ogamba also warned school heads and principals against misuse of the funds, directing them to ensure the money is spent prudently and for the benefit of learners.

School administrators have further been cautioned against imposing unauthorised levies on parents and learners.

Ogamba said the Ministry would take firm action against institutions found to have misappropriated public resources or imposed illegal charges.

“We will deal firmly with any verified cases of misappropriation of resources and the imposition of unauthorised levies,” he said.

The warning comes as schools reopen for the third term, a period that is expected to be particularly demanding for institutions and learners because of the academic activities and assessments scheduled for the school calendar.

The Ministry has maintained that capitation is meant to ease the financial burden on families and enable schools to provide essential services without passing prohibited costs to parents.

Ogamba reiterated that school administrators must remain accountable for the public funds entrusted to them, warning that verified cases of misuse will attract action from the Ministry.

The Government has also reaffirmed that every child is entitled to free and compulsory basic education, placing the responsibility on education officials and school managers to ensure capitation achieves its intended purpose.

World.title: Ndindi Nyoro begins nationwide political mobilisation ahead of 2027
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro after attending service at Gathuki-ini ACK Church on August 23, 2026. [Boniface Gikandi, Standard]

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro has said he will take his campaign for national transformation across Kenya as he positions himself for the 2027 presidential race.

Ndindi said he was interested in leadership committed to addressing concerns in education, health, youth and unemployment, among other needs.

Nyoro, who is the People’s Party of Kenya leader, spoke at St Michael Gathuki-ini ACK Church in Kiharu on Sunday, where he called for respect and political maturity.

Addressing residents in Kiria-ini (Mathioya) and Gakira (Kangema), he urged politicians to engage in a responsible manner.

“I trust in God that after next year Kenya will be able to have leadership that will be responsible for improving citizens' standards of living,” he said.

He regretted that hundreds of university graduates in the area were yet to secure employment.

“I plead with Kenyans to support my course that is geared to transform the nation and ensure equality and transparency,” said the PPK leader.

Nyoro said that after engaging Murang'a residents, he will take his transformation campaigns to all parts of the country.

Speaking at Kiria-ini market, he said he would engage the people to seek their blessings.

“All along had been feeling the urge to lead the country, thus the need to come out in the open and fight for position,” he said.

On Monday, the MP announced his exit from the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA), declaring that he will join the opposition ahead of the 2027 General Election.

Nyoro, an economist serving his second term as Kiharu MP, said he will work with opposition leaders to push for what he termed real change in Kenya.

The legislator said all opposition presidential aspirants are welcome at rallies organised by the PPK.

His move marks a significant political shift as parties and leaders begin positioning themselves ahead of the 2027 polls.

World.title: City Hall in rush to expand drainage system ahead of El Nino
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja during an inspection tour of the ongoing drainage system expansion. [GPS]

Nairobi County has embarked on drainage expansion works aimed at mitigating floodwaters ahead of El Nino rains.

Governor Johnson Sakaja, while calling on city residents to remain alert and proactive, said City Hall has intensified preparations and accelerated identification of hotspots.

The governor on Friday said his administration is taking early and coordinated action to minimise the impact of heavy rains, urging residents to stay calm, pay attention to official information and follow guidance from the multi-agency team established to coordinate the city’s preparedness and emergency response.

“We are working proactively to address the challenges of flooding before El Nino hits the ground. We urge our people not to panic but to be alert and get information from our multi-agency team,” said Sakaja.

The Governor spoke during an inspection tour of several flood-prone areas in Nairobi, including the Mombasa Road-Bunyala Junction corridor and Globe Roundabout, which experienced significant flooding during previous heavy rains.

Sakaja said drainage works are already underway in the affected areas, with teams working to open up and deepen drainage channels, clear obstructions, and improve storm-water flow to prevent a repeat of the flooding witnessed previously.

His remarks come as weatherman warned of increased rainfall in the coming months, with Nairobi among the urban areas requiring heightened preparedness because of its exposure to flooding and the impact of heavy rainfall on roads, settlements and other critical infrastructure.

Sakaja said the county has so far brought together the disaster management teams, Kenya Red Cross, Kenya Urban Roads Authority (KURA) and Kenya National Highways Authority (KeNHA) under a coordinated programme worth Sh2.4 billion to strengthen Nairobi’s flood resilience.

Of the amount, Sh2 billion has been set aside for drainage and flood-mitigation works targeting 19 roads in flood-prone areas.

The projects are at an advanced stage, with tenders awarded and contractors expected to commence implementation after completion of the necessary processes.

Sakaja reiterated that the programme will complement ongoing county interventions under the Nairobi Regeneration Programme, which includes the rehabilitation and upgrading of critical infrastructure across the city.

“The Sh2 billion will support a comprehensive drainage overhaul that complements the ongoing Nairobi Regeneration Programme. Our goal is to permanently address the flooding challenges that have affected the city for many years,” Sakaja said.

He said the focus is not only on responding to floods after they occur, but on addressing the infrastructure weaknesses that have historically made Nairobi vulnerable to flooding.

To strengthen preparedness, the county has established five specialised sub-committees under the multi-agency framework.

The committees include Infrastructure and Drainage; Emergency Response and Evacuation; Shelter and Relief; Security and Traffic and Communication.

While the Infrastructure and Drainage committee will coordinate the clearing and improvement of drainage systems, rivers and other critical infrastructure, the Emergency Response and Evacuation committee will oversee rapid response, rescue and evacuation operations whenever emergencies occur.

The Shelter and Relief committee will prepare safe shelters and coordinate the provision of food, water, medical assistance and other essential support to affected residents.

The Security and Traffic committee will coordinate security, traffic management and emergency access, while the Communication committee will strengthen early-warning systems, public alerts and timely dissemination of information.

Sakaja said the county is also mobilising personnel, equipment and other resources to clear blocked drains, remove silt and waste and strengthen emergency response systems in areas identified as vulnerable.

He urged residents and their associations, businesses and other stakeholders to play an active role in flood preparedness by keeping drainage areas clear and paying attention to official warnings.

The county chief said residents in high-risk areas will be provided with timely information on emerging weather conditions and the actions they should take when heavy rains occur.

“We don’t want people to panic. We want people to be proactive, to listen to information and to work with us. The multi-agency team is in place, and we are preparing before the rains intensify,” Sakaja said.

According to him, the multi-agency approach will also help eliminate jurisdictional gaps by bringing together national and county agencies to operate as one coordinated team.

He said the combination of drainage upgrades, emergency preparedness, early-warning systems and coordinated response would strengthen Nairobi’s resilience and reduce disruption caused by heavy rains.

The multi-agency team is expected to meet next week to review progress, coordinate ongoing works and further push the city’s El Niño preparedness agenda.

World.title: Six months into the Iran war, Iranian Americans remain divided over what comes next
World.content:
Los Angeles —

Six months since the United States and Israel launched the first strikes on Iran, the physical, financial and emotional impacts of the war have reverberated from Tehran across the world, including to the vast Iranian community in the US, which has been divided with varying opinions on how the war started and what is has – or hasn’t – accomplished.

The Iranian diaspora spans multiple generations and waves of exile, from those who left after the 1979 revolution to more recent arrivals who fled crackdowns and protest movements. Those experiences helped shape sharply different reactions to the conflict. Some Iranian Americans, particularly among anti-regime activists, welcomed US and Israeli strikes and saw them as a potential path toward ending the Islamic Republic’s rule.

Others feared the human cost of military escalation and warned that civilian suffering and regional instability could outweigh any political gains. The divide reflects not only differing political views, but competing experiences of exile, repression and what many believed the future of Iran should look like.

At the start of the war, CNN spoke with Arezo Rashidian, a longtime monarchist activist aligned with Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s last shah who helped organize protests in the Los Angeles area. At the time, Rashidian welcomed military action against the Islamic Republic and told CNN she hoped the United States and Israel would conduct “targeted attacks on bases to bring down that regime.”

Six months later, Rashidian says that optimism has largely given way to disappointment among many anti-regime activists.

“We really wanted regime change … it’s been six months now, and it didn’t get to that point,” she said, describing a mood of frustration and uncertainty.

Rashidian said her family members and contacts inside Iran have described what they see as a renewed climate of fear in the months since the height of the fighting.

People wave US and pre-revolutionary Iranian flags as they protest the Iranian regime outside of Los Angeles Stadium in Inglewood, California, on June 7, ahead of the start of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Sarah LaiAFP/Getty Images

According to Rashidian, people are increasingly reluctant to discuss politics or their involvement in January’s protests, fearing surveillance and retaliation. “Now that the war is a little bit quieter, now the secret police are starting to mobilize,” she said.

Her comments come as CNN has reported on a renewed focus on enforcing Iran’s mandatory hijab laws, with videos showing women being publicly admonished over their clothing and businesses facing scrutiny for alleged dress-code violations.

Rashidian also described accounts of arrests, executions and broader security crackdowns – claims CNN cannot independently verify.

Despite her disappointment, Rashidian said she continues to support tougher sanctions against Tehran, which she hopes will “tighten the rope” around the regime.

This week, Washington threatened further measures, which Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said will target a complex network built by Iran that allows its entities to evade the wide-ranging sanctions.

But the much-anticipated announcement of Trump’s “economic D-Day” measures left many underwhelmed, after Washington decided to hold off on imposing major new measures, instead focusing largely on expanding and stepping up enforcement of existing sanctions.

Iran has said it can inflict reciprocal pain, warning of expanded strikes on regional oil producers and European countries, and even teasing the weaponization of its nuclear program.

The Minab school which was damaged by a strike on February 28, in Minab, Iran, August 27. Majid Asgaripour/Wana News Agency/Reuters

For Aria Rostami, a 38-year-old Iranian American museum professional in New York who grew up in Southern California’s Iranian community, the past six months have fundamentally changed the way he relates to other Iranian Americans, being at odds with how enthusiastically some embraced the military intervention.

“I was really disheartened by the community when they were on the streets cheering the war,” he told CNN.

The conflict, Rostami said, exposed divisions within the diaspora that have left him questioning assumptions he once took for granted. “There was a time where if I met somebody who was Iranian, or I’d hear people speaking Persian on the street, I had a specific feeling about it,” he said. “Now it’s changed to suspicion or an uncertainty. I don’t know where their politics are. I don’t know what they believe.”

Before the conflict, he said, supporters of intervention often argued that “Iran is different” — call it Iranian exceptionalism.

Personally, he says, he never accepted that premise. “Why would you want the United States to be involved in a war or have any military action in Iran, given what we’ve seen in the last 20 years with Iraq, with Afghanistan, with Libya?”

While Rostami acknowledges many supporters of the war are now disappointed, he believes they were sold false expectations about what military intervention could accomplish.

“People are being lied to, manipulated, played for a fool,” he said.

Still, he rejects a simplistic caricature of those who backed the war. “There’s real pain there,” he said. “I do think people have been taken advantage of and manipulated.”

World.title: A power struggle in Iran could decide when Trump’s war ends
World.content:
More than four decades ago, after months of setbacks in the war against Saddam Hussein’s Iraq, thousands of young Iranian troops launched a surprise offensive that turned the tide.

But rather than consolidate victory, the then-supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, wanted more: To topple the Iraqi dictator, who was drawing increasing support from Washington, and demonstrate to future enemies that war with Iran will exact a heavy cost.

The Iraq conflict was pivotal moment in shaping the modern Iranian state. Khomeini’s decision turned it into a six-year war of attrition that killed hundreds of thousands, one of the bloodiest conflicts in the region’s modern history. And now, years on, the question of whether to press on or cut a deal is once again facing Iran.

The revolutionaries who led the offensive dominate the seats of power in Tehran. To them, the current US-Israeli war, like the conflict with Iraq, was an imposed war whose outcome would not be determined by which side was most powerful – but which one would endure. On the other side, a more moderate camp senses a chance to consolidate Iran’s gains in talks that have made little progress.

After six months of war, the deadlock has left the Islamic Republic bitterly divided, while its ultimate arbiter, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, remains in hiding.

Winning the peace

Tehran’s competing politicians maintain publicly that Iran has emerged triumphant in the war.

Yet, a deep ideological schism remains over what victory for the Islamic Republic should look like.

On one side stand pragmatists and technocrats led by President Masoud Pezeshkian, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

They back a conclusive agreement, pointing to a war-battered economy, an exhausting US naval blockade and damage to the nation’s infrastructure.

USS Abraham Lincoln conducts US blockade operations related to the Strait of Hormuz on April 16 in the Arabian Sea. US Navy/Getty Images

They have publicly warned that the window to settle the conflict from a position of strength is closing. They speak for Iranians who believe that ending the 47-year conflict with Washington is the surest way to ease the country’s domestic crises and keep the Islamic Republic alive by breaking its global isolation.

“The war must end at some point,” Pezeshkian said this month. “It would be better to end it today, while we are in a position of strength and dignity, and the entire world acknowledges our victory.”

On the other side stand hardline conservatives. Their ideology centers around a distrust of a Washington they see as hell-bent on destroying the Islamic Republic. For more than half a century they’ve warned against US intentions, and now they stand vindicated against their moderate opponents by Trump’s war.

They also accuse sitting officials of being “Western-oriented” and of trying to influence public opinion toward a deal by exaggerating domestic issues.

“They see the US as a deeply untrustworthy actor… and (have) been burnt so many times by Trump himself that they think that this is exactly what will happen again,” Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and North Africa program at London’s Chatham House think tank told CNN.

“In their minds, by not losing (the war), they’ve won, and they’re not just trying to win out with a better deal from Washington, but they’re looking for internal longevity in their competition with their opponents.”

They see Pezeshkian as a weak president who took office by chance after his hardline predecessor died in a helicopter crash. And his signature beside Trump’s on the June ceasefire agreement has ostracized him further, empowering their campaign to blame him for the shattered economy and the failed deal with Washington.

People walk past shops and browse for goods at the Grand Bazaar in Tehran on August 24, 2026. Oil prices fell on August 24 as investors braced for details of a US plan to isolate the Iranian economy that President Donald Trump billed as the “most crushing” financial operation ever against Tehran. AFP/Getty Images

So deep are the divisions that hardliners have accused officials of deliberately mismanaging the economic crisis to pressure an exhausted public into accepting a deal. Some allege that the government has engineered fuel shortages to make an agreement unavoidable, others go further, accusing moderates of staging a coup.

“Economically, are we really in a dead end, or are you just projecting a dead end?” asked hardline lawmaker Mohammad-Manan Raisi. “It has all been blamed on the war, while it is not all related to the war.”

What do the hardliners want?

The hardliners point to failed past deals with the US, including a nuclear agreement signed in 2015 with the Obama administration that Trump later tore up, and they cite the two times that the US attacked the Islamic Republic amid negotiations.

This camp wagers on the Islamic Republic’s endurance, and claim that a policy of confrontation supported by armed regional proxies, missiles, drones and Shia religious belief has guarded the country more effectively than the diplomacy championed by the “Western-oriented” politicians.

“Hardliners concluded they will achieve no deal with Trump and perhaps they’re now just living in the war between the wars,” Vakil said. “They think that they can wear Trump down and they can play for time to weaken him by extending economic pain.”

Diesel and gas prices are displayed at a Allsup’s gas station on August 13, 2026 in Nortrees, Texas. US President JD Vance said that top US priority was no long Iran’s nuclear program but to bring gasoline prices down. Brandon Bell/Getty Images

A hardline lawmaker described those advocating for a deal with the US as standing against former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei – killed in US-Israeli strikes at the beginning of the war.

“They want to prepare public opinion to accept an agreement and a humiliating peace,” Kamran Ghazanfari told parliament on Thursday, referring to those in favor of diplomacy with the US.

“Yet the enemy has repeatedly shown that no matter how many concessions we make to it, no matter how much we retreat before it, it will never be satisfied and will continue to demand other things from us, and it will settle for nothing less than our complete surrender.”

‘Trump isn’t helping’

As Iran’s pragmatists play a high-stakes poker game with Washington, hardliners’ warnings against a deal with the US have gained force amid an erratic strategy from Trump’s and uncertainty about his commitment to a potential agreement.

“Trump is not helping. He says he wants to make Iran great again then threatens Iran in the next tweet, and that fans the flame of paranoia within the Iranian system,” Vakil said.

An American flag is reflected off bulletproof glass as U.S. President Donald Trump watches the end of the NTT INDYCAR Series on August 23 in Washington, DC. Mike Kropf/Getty Images

The conservatives, who have elements controlling newspapers, state broadcasters, protesters on the street and followers in the military, believe Trump is using diplomacy to prepare for another military campaign and that “every time they go down the road of diplomacy” with Trump he “betrayed them,” she added.

Mojtaba Khamenei has remained quiet amid the divide. It appears that he understands that choosing a side on negotiations with an unreliable Trump could harm his office just as he is working to secure legitimacy.

On Friday, he praised the government’s performance under pressure but urged officials to address the country’s weaknesses without dwelling on them publicly, warning that doing so could embolden Iran’s enemies and demoralize its allies.

With no one to rein them in, hardliners are pressing ahead with their campaign against a deal.

“Our martyred Imam (Ali Khamenei) warned them dozens of times – how do they not understand?” said Ghazanfari about his domestic opponents. “They speak in a way that reeks of nothing but capitulation and surrender.”

Additional reporting by Aida Karimi

World.title: Iran says 40% of capacity at its giant gas field has been restored
World.content:
Iran said that 40 percent of the damaged capacity of the South Pars gas field has been restored, according to the semi-official news agency Fars – adding, however, that it will take at least two years to rebuild the facility attacked by Israel this year.

“With the tools we have, we managed to restore about 40 percent of the damaged capacity. However, the damage that has been inflicted is very severe. It will definitely take at least two years of work just for those sites to be rebuilt,” Iran’s deputy oil minister, Ahmad Zeraatkar, told Fars on Thursday.

Iranian officials have acknowledged the desruptions to energy exports that are vital for government finances, but have sought to play them down.

Zeraatkar said that by targeting energy, the US and Israel seek to curtail the government’s ability to provide for the public.

“We know this gas belongs to us and has created a semi-welfare state in our country. The goal of the damage is to hurt that, which would cause us to fall into trouble during the seasons when we have difficulties,” he said.

Earlier this week, Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad acknowledged that oil sales have “decreased to some extent” during the US blockade, but said they have “continued” nonetheless.

South Pars is part of the world’s largest natural gas reserves, located offshore in the Persian Gulf. It is shared between Iran and Qatar, which calls its part of it the North Field.

In March, an Israeli strike on Iranian facilities in the South Pars gas field marked a significant escalation in the war, prompting a furious Iran to attack major energy facilities of its Gulf neighbors, sending oil prices surging, and leading US President Donald Trump to threaten to “blow up” South Pars if Iran didn’t stop.

World.title: She fled Iran. America sent her to Africa
World.content:
Bangui, Central African Republic —

“It’s okay now, I’m safe,” she remembered thinking. “I can make one new life here.”

She described her joy at reaching “one of the best countries in the world,” but her happiness would prove fleeting.

Nika is among a growing number of migrants deported by the Trump administration to countries they’ve never been to – countries that can hardly be considered safe havens. It’s a loophole. Judges have stopped the US government from sending some migrants back to their home countries. So it has inked dozens of arrangements with third countries, where people like Nika are increasingly festering. Because she fears for both her and her family’s safety, Nika is a pseudonym.

‘If I was in Iran, they’re going to kill me’

Telling her story for the first time, Nika says she spent much of her youth protesting against the Iranian regime.

“I lost too much of my friends. They [the Islamic Republic] killed them. And some of them are still in prison,” she said tearfully. “I know if I was in Iran, they’re going to kill me.”

Her story unfolds at a remarkable time in US-Iran relations. Earlier this year, Iran was rocked by widespread anti-government protests. The regime launched an unprecedented crackdown, killing thousands. President Donald Trump encouraged protesters to “take over your institutions” and said, “help is on its way.”

Iranians block a street during a protest in Tehran, Iran on January 9, 2026. MAHSA/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images

On the last day of February, the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and attacking targets across the country.

Nika followed the events closely from the United States. She allowed herself to hope it might mean the end of the Iranian regime, and a return home. In reality her fate had already been decided.

One of the hardest days

After being detained at the border and months in ICE detention, Nika had briefly been allowed to live freely in California. She received a Department of Homeland Security notice asking her to attend what she understood to be a routine meeting in June. But according to documents reviewed by CNN, US authorities had decided weeks earlier to deport her. When she attended the meeting, she was arrested.

Three days later, on the evening of June 11, she says she was handcuffed, shackled and placed on a deportation flight along with 17 other migrants, including those from Afghanistan, Iraq and Georgia.

“This is one of the very hard days in my life,” said Nika, describing how her whole body shook with fear. She said it was only on boarding the flight that she learned where she was going. The destination was shown on the small screen attached to the seat in front of her.

Sahar Jalili Pawelski, Nika’s current immigration lawyer, said she tried desperately to get her off the flight.

“I remember when the flight took off, I just sat on the floor, called my mom and cried. I live those moments. You know what that person must’ve been feeling. The loneliness she must have felt,” said Pawelski.

Legal protection

Like many of the other migrants she was deported with, Nika had won a protection order from an American judge. Such orders are intended to prevent migrants from being returned to places where they could face persecution, torture or death.

Until recently, it was extremely rare for people with these types of protection orders to be deported.

But since Trump returned to power last year, promising mass deportations, that’s all changed. Trump’s top anti-immigration advocate, deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, has stated “America’s doors are closed, fully, to asylum seekers.”

Isobel Yeung speaks with a young Iranian activist who was deported from the US to Bangui, in the Central African Republic. Mick Krever/CNN

The Department of Homeland Security has defended its actions, telling CNN in a statement that those deported received due process and had final orders of removal.

“These third country agreements, which ensure due process under the U.S. Constitution, are essential to the safety of our homeland and the American people. We are applying the law as written. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period.”

Malaria and fear

Since her arrival in the Central African Republic’s capital city of Bangui over two months ago, Nika says that she’s usually too scared to leave her apartment block and spends most of her time in her room.

When she does go out to buy groceries or essentials, she claims the local police have often stopped her to demand bribes and threaten arrest if she doesn’t pay – claims the police denies. She’s also spent a stint at a local hospital, after contracting malaria.

“I couldn’t believe I’m here,” Nika said. “Really, for me this is unbelievable.”

The US State Department itself has advised against all travel to the country due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, disease and terrorism. It urges anyone who does make the journey to leave a DNA sample so they can be identified by their family in the event of their death.

Why the Central African Republic agreed to accept migrants from the US is still something of a mystery. No details of the deal have been made public.

But there are clues.

This year the US has given a surprisingly large $85 million to the UN’s International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) operations in the Central African Republic, up from just a few million in previous years, as well as committing an additional $50 million to the country’s Humanitarian Fund.

It comes at a time when the US is slashing foreign assistance.

The State Department has hinted that that funding was a direct quid pro quo for accepting deportees. A DHS spokesperson told CNN that “the United States will use foreign assistance to support countries that help us achieve our immigration priorities.”

The IOM, which does not facilitate deportations, did not reply to CNN’s specific questions but said in a statement it has a longstanding presence in the country. “As in other contexts, IOM benefits from funding from a range of donors in Central African Republic.”

No one in the CAR’s government has spoken publicly about the deportation agreement, and rebuffed CNN’s requests for an interview.

Life in limbo

It’s unclear how life might unfold for Nika.

She and the migrants she arrived with were told they were only being granted a temporary, three-month stay. A second deportation flight to the country left the US on July 31, this time carrying 31 deportees, and there’s a fear among the migrants that, as accommodation runs out, they will be forcibly repatriated to their countries of origin.

If that were to happen, Nika does not rate her chances of survival.

Her lawyer, meanwhile, is filing a federal lawsuit in an attempt to get her back to the US and re-open her claim for asylum.

While Nika awaits her fate, she struggles to understand how the country she believed would protect her would be the one that sent her away.

World.title: Trump is staking out extreme positions on White House secrecy, legal experts say
World.content:
At this point more than two months before the midterm elections, Democrats retaking control of Congress and its subpoena power is far from certain. But President Donald Trump is already laying down legal markers for how he’ll fight any attempt by lawmakers to investigate him.

In a Justice Department memo and legal filings, the Trump administration is arguing that the president can keep secret not just the conversations he has with his advisers within the White House, but that his dealings with individuals outside the government can be shielded as well. The White House is also saying in court that even disclosing the identities of the people who worked on significant policy efforts would infringe upon the presidential confidentiality to which Trump is entitled. And the administration has taken the stance that it can ignore a Watergate-era law prohibiting the destruction of White House documents.

The posturing comes as Trump, in his second term, has been notably reliant on a constellation of business moguls, non-government attorneys and old friends to help shape his agenda.

“There has been an unprecedented amount of interaction between the Executive Branch — particularly the White House — and the private sector that Congress has made clear is going to be the subject of oversight,” said Jamie Bair, a partner and head of congressional investigations at the law firm Crowell & Moring.

Congressional Democrats are already probing the administration’s interactions with FIFA, how Trump’s ties to the crypto-industry are affecting federal policy, and other examples of Trump family business maneuverings that Democrats say can be tied to government policies.

Trump’s opponents are confident that he will not prevail in the most extreme version of his secrecy claims. But they also acknowledge that the process for litigating those questions is a slow one that can drag out beyond January 20, 2029, when he leaves office.

Democrats on the Hill are watching the Trump administration’s legal arguments closely, as they plot the various of tools they’ll have at their disposal to fight back — including pressure points that go beyond pressing for compliance in court.

“There are the collateral consequences of being held in contempt, of refusing to provide documents, and standing behind a blatantly unlawful assertions of executive privilege,” a senior House aide, who spoke on the condition of not being named so they could talk openly about Democrats’ thinking, told CNN.

Democrats believe that the threat of pushback from the public, investors, state authorities and future administrations will encourage business leaders and others targeted with subpoenas to participate in oversight probes, even if Trump is claiming privilege could shield them.

“The private sector folks are going to be completely caught in the middle of this,” Bair, who did congressional oversight work for the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said. He predicted that lawmakers “are going to make it as painful as possible” for any company that doesn’t hand documents sought by Congress.

“They will say your name on television as many times as possible until the public pressure builds up enough for compliance,” Bair said.

President Donald Trump holds papers in the Oval Office of the White House before signing an executive order in Washington DC on March 31. Alex Brandon/AP

The president’s position on executive privilege for outside advisers could soon be tested in a Justice Department effort to block a subpoena to Boris Epshteyn – a legal adviser for Trump who does not work in the government – in a case brought by the American Bar Association to challenge the administration’s pressure campaign on law firms.

In a letter to the White House this week, Senate Democrats led by California Sen. Adam Schiff demanded the White House inform them which other non-government advisers if believes the presidential privilege covers.

Executive privilege, they wrote, “is not an unlimited shield designed to insulate private citizens, informal advisers, and non-governmental actors from congressional oversight and public accountability.”

The White House, in a statement to CNN, defended its legal positions on the records law and on executive privilege.

“Throughout history, Presidents have relied on advisers outside of the executive branch. Restricting executive privilege to only communications with executive branch officials would make it impossible for the President to rely on important outside sources,” said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.

Can Trump keep his conversations with non-government advisers secret?

The DOJ’s Office of Legal of Counsel – which gives legal advice to agencies across the executive branch – has a longstanding tradition of pushing expansive views of executive powers and privileges. Still, legal experts – including former, high-ranking government lawyers from administrations of both parties – say that DOJ grossly exaggerated the case law supporting their arguments.

The claim will soon be tested in the American Bar Association case but could take many months or even years for the question to go up the chain of higher courts. Beyond how the argument is functioning in that Epshteyn dispute, the DOJ’s release of the opinion was viewed as a signal for how the administration would responds to attempts by a Democratic Congress to subpoena non-government individuals and entities for information about their dealings with the Trump administration.

Historically, lawmakers have focused their investigatory efforts that way because those individuals are viewed as not having the same constitutional protections as those within the executive branch, according to Tara Ganapathy, who has worked on congressional investigations both as a lawyer for several committees on the Hill as well as within in the Executive Branch, in roles advising agencies that were targeted in legislative probes.

Even if courts don’t ultimately uphold the administration’s arguments, it can be a bargaining chip those individuals can use in their negotiations with Congress over compliance with subpoenas.

There is “a lot of procedural value to having this OLC opinion” said Ganapthay, now a lawyer at the firm K&L Gates.

Does the White House even have to say who advised the president?

Last week, the administration pushed its executive privilege arguments even farther. In the same ABA case, the White House also told the court that Trump was asserting privilege to shield the identities of anyone who was advising Trump on how to craft his assault on law firms.

The White House said in court filings that disclosing those names “would have a chilling effect on communications within the Executive Office of the President, making it more difficult for the President to obtain candid advice from and explore alternative with a wider of senior advisers and their staffs.”

While the administration has framed those disclosures as protected under the presidential communications privilege – which courts have found to be established within the Constitution – legal experts predicted that judges may be more inclined to see such a claim as fitting under the framework of the “deliberative process” privilege.

That privilege sits on far shakier legal ground, according to Michael Bopp, the chair of Gibson Dunn’s Congressional Investigations Practice Group who previously worked in several investigative roles in the House and Senate.

Still, if Trump uses a similar strategy to obstruct the investigations of Democratic lawmakers, “Congress has not a lot of levers to pull to force the administration to produce that kind of information, unless it were to go to court, and it’s been reluctant to do so,” Bopp said.

Can Trump ignore the Presidential Records Act?

The Justice Department is also trying to relieve Trump and his staff of their obligations to follow a Watergate-era law requiring that the White House preserve and hand over to the National Archives presidential records at the end of Trump’s term.

The fight over the Presidential Records Act, or PRA, was kicked off in April with an Office of Legal Counsel memo asserting the law was unconstitutional and that Trump no longer must comply with it.

“The Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional and a clear violation of the separation of powers,” Bis, the White House spokesperson, told CNN. “For over 200 years, the president owned his own papers and correspondence.”

Of particular concern to Democrats is that DOJ’s extraordinary attempt to nullify the law could be used to justify the deletion of communication sent on non-government messaging apps. (After the DOJ memo, the White House revised its document retention policy to give staff more leeway to delete certain text communications. The White House claimed the policy was still in line with the PRA; a federal judge disagreed.)

A federal appeals court is currently considering the ruling from US District Judge John Bates rejecting the administration’s claims that the PRA is unconstitutional, with oral arguments scheduled in October.

If the White House no longer had to preserve records of its activities, the administration could “could straight up lie about” what was happening behind the scenes, Bair said, and “there would be no contemporaneous records that would disprove it.”

The administration is framing its objections to the law around the idea that the statute amounts to unconstitutional effort by Congress to dig into White House operations—an argument that, if adopted by courts, could have knock-on effects on other oversight battles.

In briefs submitted to the appeals court, critics of DOJ’s arguments – including over 100 Democratic lawmakers – have stressed that the law protects not just the public and Congress’s access to those records, but the access future presidents to understand the decision-making of their predecessors.

“Harm to the public occurs the instant the White House destroys an official record, regardless of when the injury is actually felt,” the lawmakers wrote.

World.title: At least 37 dead after Russian drone attack triggers multiple blasts and fire at warehouse near Kyiv
World.content:
At least 37 people have been killed and dozens wounded after a Russian drone attack triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted for hours at a warehouse in a residential area near Kyiv.

The attack in the Bucha district came amid near constant aerial assaults from Russia, but initial reports suggest a likely storage of ammunition at the warehouse has had catastrophic consequences. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky vowed to punish those responsible.

Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv region military administration, said the that as of Saturday afternoon, 37 people were known to to have died. This makes the incident one of the deadliest Kyiv has seen since the start of the war more than four years ago.

“This is a terrible and irreparable loss. Our heartfelt condolences go out to the families and loved ones of those who have died,” Tkachenko said.

He said earlier that more than 40 people were injured in the attack and more than 380 others, including dozens of children, had to be evacuated from the area. He said at least 50 residential buildings were damaged.

Videos and photos shared by local residents show several completely destroyed buildings, with a little more than a few bare walls and scorched earth left.

Russia’s defense ministry said its forces struck an arms depot storing drone making equipment.

Speaking about the attack, Zelensky did not explicitly reveal the details of what kind of a warehouse was hit by the Russians, but said an investigation would be opened into the incident because “ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas.”

Separately, the office of Ukraine’s Prosecutor General said in a statement that “explosive objects and materials” were stored in the premises and that an investigation would be opened into “the circumstances surrounding the explosion on the premises of the facility and the actions of the officials responsible.”

Zelensky said a care home for elderly citizens and people living with disabilities was among the dozens of building damaged in the attack, and that more than 300 emergency services personnel were responding on the scene.

Days of non-stop terror

The deadly blast came as Kyiv has endured more than two days of near non-stop Russian attacks. According to a CNN tally, there have been 28 air raid alerts between midnight on Thursday and midday on Saturday, lasting more than 28 hours in total.

While some missile strikes were recorded on Thursday, most of the attacks over the past few days were by jet-powered drones. These are a relatively new addition to Russia’s arsenal, having been first spotted around the start of the year.

They can be exceptionally dangerous.

Jet-powered drones fly at speeds of up to 500 kilometers per hour (310 miles per hour), evading Ukraine’s air defenses. They are also too fast for Kyiv’s mobile fire groups, so the only way to shoot them down is with ground-to-air missiles or fighter jets – both of which are in extremely limited supply in Ukraine.

This story has been updated.

World.title: Central Bank of Egypt issues urgent message regarding OTPs
World.content:
The Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) warned bank customers and users against sharing their One-Time Password (OTP) with anyone, explaining that disclosing this code could expose them to risks related to their transactions and bank account.

The CBE published an awareness warning on its official Facebook page, urging users to be vigilant against fraud attempts targeting the verification code sent to their mobile phone, which is used to confirm payments.

What is an OTP Code?

The OTP code is a security code used during banking transactions.

It is sent to the user’s phone to confirm a payment.

This code is designated for the account holder’s use and is valid for one-time use only, making it a crucial part of the transaction security measures.

According to the Central Bank’s warning, handling this code requires caution as sharing it with anyone else could expose users to risks related to their bank account or financial transactions.

Don’t share OTP codes

CBE also posted an awareness image on its official Facebook page, titled “Always Beware of Fraud Attempts,” highlighting the dangers of sharing OTP codes with others.

The Central Bank stressed the importance of not sharing this code with anyone, explaining that disclosing it could expose users to fraud and scams.

This warning comes in light of the importance of OTP code in securing certain banking transactions. The code is sent to the phone number linked to the user’s account to confirm payments.

Therefore, sharing it with someone else could allow them to use it to conduct transactions in the account holder’s name.

Why the warning?

Disclosing OTPs could lead to users falling victim to scams, the CBE warned.

The bank explained that sharing these codes with someone else could enable them to carry out several actions that pose a risk to the user, especially if they manage to use the code to complete a transaction that requires confirmation.

Risks of sharing OTP

The Central Bank pointed to several risks that may arise from sharing OTP codes, explaining that the person who obtains the code could be able to execute transactions in the user’s name.

The CBE highlighted the following risks:

The person who obtained the code could use it to make purchases in the account holder’s name.

Sharing the code could allow another person to access the bank account, posing a risk to the user’s data and transactions.

The person who obtained the code could transfer funds to other accounts.

Keep Your OTP Confidential

The awareness warning issued by CBE emphasizes the importance of keeping your OTP code confidential and not sharing it with anyone, especially since the code is used to confirm transactions and is used only once by the account holder.

Be Aware of Fraud Attempts

The CBE urged users to be vigilant against fraud attempts and not to treat their OTP code as a number that can be shared with others.

The code is sent to the account holder’s phone to confirm the payment process; therefore, keeping it confidential and not disclosing it is a fundamental aspect of using banking transactions securely.

What You Should Know About OTPs?

The OTP code is unique to the account holder and is sent to their phone to confirm a payment.

It is for one-time use only, so sharing it with anyone else could expose you to the risk of fraud.

The CBE explained that sharing the code could allow someone else to use it to conduct transactions in the account holder’s name.

This makes keeping the code confidential essential when conducting banking transactions.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: High-speed train from Ain Sokhna to Marsa Matrouh to begin operating mid-September
World.content:
The Egyptian Transport Ministry is preparing to launch trial operations for the first line of the high-speed electric train network, connecting Ain Sokhna, al-Alamein, and Marsa Matrouh, from mid-September until early October 2026.

The trial period for the first line will last for six months before official launch and the opening of service to the public.

The first line of the high-speed electric train network extends for 660 kilometers and is part of the Ain Sokhna-Dekheila logistics corridor.

It includes 21 stations in addition to a control center.

Trial operations

Trial operations are scheduled to begin gradually from the Hadayek October area, with service then gradually extending to Wadi al-Natroun, Nubaria, and finally Alexandria, according to the operational plan.

The planned operation of Line I includes 15 high-speed trains, 34 regional trains, and 14 freight locomotives.

The high-speed electric train’s operation and safety systems rely on security systems provided by specialized foreign companies, in addition to securing stations and surrounding areas through a sophisticated surveillance camera system.

The high-speed electric train network currently under construction in Egypt consists of three lines with a total length of 2,000 kilometers.

It aims to support the modern transportation system, connect cities, industrial zones, and ports, and enhance passenger and freight transport.

World.title: We Must Not Forget The Victims Of Liberia’s Civil War
World.content:
Liberia’s fourteen years of civil conflict ended long ago, but many of its victims are still suffering. Some live with bullets and fragments in their bodies, lost limbs, impaired vision, chronic pain and emotional trauma. Others remain in poverty because the war destroyed their homes, farms, businesses and families. Many feel abandoned and forgotten by the country for whose conflict they paid such a terrible price.

By Tiawan Saye Gongloe

At the end of the war, former fighters received disarmament and demobilization packages, including money, vocational training and other forms of assistance to help them return to civilian life. That support was necessary for peace. But it created a painful imbalance: those who carried the guns received organized assistance, while many of the people injured, widowed, displaced and impoverished by the war received little or nothing. Liberia must correct this historic injustice.

I therefore propose the creation of a National War Victims Relief Fund for an initial period of five years. Every unemployed adult Liberian who is able to contribute should pay L$100 per year. Every employed Liberian should contribute US$1 per year, and Liberians living abroad should also be encouraged to contribute at least US$1 annually. The Government should match these contributions at a ratio of US$5 for every US$1 contributed under the national scheme.

The fund should be used to provide medical treatment, medication, prosthetic devices and modest welfare support to severely disabled victims. It should also provide interest-free microloans to victims who can engage in farming, trading or small businesses. The goal should be to reduce suffering, restore independence and give victims renewed hope in a caring Liberia.

This fund must be completely separate from the establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court. The court concerns accountability for crimes committed during the conflict. The relief fund concerns care and responsibility for people who are suffering today. A wounded victim who needs medicine should not have to wait for a prosecution, and a widow living in poverty should not have to wait for the creation of a court before receiving assistance. Liberia can pursue justice and care for victims at the same time.

The fund must also be transparent and protected from political interference. A credible national registry of qualified victims should be established, and the General Auditing Commission should audit the fund annually. Most importantly, administrative expenses should not be deducted from the victims’ money. Salaries, offices and other operating costs should come from a separate appropriation in the national budget.

Someone may ask, “Why now?” The answer is simple: it is better late than never. The passage of time does not erase the suffering of those who still carry the physical, emotional and economic scars of the war. Delay is not a reason for continued neglect; it is a reason to act now.

This is more than a financial proposal. It is a national statement that Liberia remembers its victims, cares about their suffering and accepts responsibility for helping them rebuild their lives.

Such collective care can help heal old wounds, restore hope and make victims feel that their country has not abandoned them.

The fighters were assisted because Liberia needed peace. The victims must now be assisted because justice, compassion and national responsibility demand it.

We must not and cannot forget the victims of Liberia’s civil conflict.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court Denies Koffa, Co-Defendants’ Prohibition Petition, Clears Way for Capitol Arson Trial
World.content:
High Court Upholds Judge Willie’s Authority to Disband Jury; Koffa Team’s Challenge Rejected

By:Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia-The Supreme Court of Liberia has denied a petition for a Writ of Prohibition filed by former House Speaker J. Fonati Koffa and several co-defendants in the Capitol Building arson case, clearing the way for Criminal Court “A” to proceed with the prosecution.

The ruling represents a major victory for the prosecution and effectively rejects the defendants’ attempt to overturn Resident Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie’s decision to disband the jury previously empaneled to hear the case.

The petitioners, including Koffa, Dixon W. Seboe, Abu B. Kamara, K. Jacob C. B. Debee, Christian Kofa, John Nyanti, Eric Susay, Thomas Isaac Etheridge and Stephen Broh, had asked the Supreme Court to restrain Judge Willie from proceeding after he dissolved the jury following allegations of juror misconduct.

The Supreme Court, however, found no sufficient legal basis to issue the extraordinary writ, holding that Judge Willie acted within his lawful authority in making the decision concerning the jury.

The decision does not determine the guilt or innocence of Koffa and his co-defendants.

Rather, it resolves the immediate legal challenge over whether the trial judge acted unlawfully in disbanding the jury.

Why Judge Willie Disbanded The Jury

The controversy arose after prosecutors asked the trial court to dissolve the entire jury, alleging that the panel had become compromised and could no longer fairly and independently adjudicate the case.

The prosecution pointed to several incidents involving jurors during testimony, including questions raised concerning evidence presented by the State.

One of the disputed incidents occurred during the testimony of LNP Chief Superintendent Rafael A. Wilson.

A juror questioned Wilson after he testified concerning photographs and evidence gathered during the investigation of the Capitol Building fire.

According to the proceedings, the juror questioned how photographs had been obtained when Wilson had earlier indicated that there was no CCTV camera inside the Capitol Building.

The juror subsequently asked that a photograph be produced and, after it was exhibited, raised a question concerning whether a person appearing in the image resembled defendant Thomas Isaac Etheridge.

Prosecutors argued that the nature of the questioning suggested that the juror had already begun evaluating the evidence and forming an opinion about a defendant before the conclusion of the trial.

The State further alleged that some jurors had consulted among themselves before putting questions to witnesses, which prosecutors argued demonstrated a loss of impartiality and undermined their ability to fairly determine the case.

Defense Rejected Claims Of Juror Misconduct

Koffa and his co-defendants strongly challenged the prosecution’s allegations.

Their legal team argued that prosecutors had failed to identify specific jurors who had committed misconduct and had, in some instances, mischaracterized or misquoted the jurors’ remarks.

The defense maintained that jurors asking questions about evidence did not, by itself, constitute misconduct.

They further argued that even if misconduct had been committed by an individual juror, such conduct could not automatically be attributed to the entire panel.

According to the defense, there was no sufficient evidence that the jurors had received outside influence, improperly communicated with outsiders or reached conclusions concerning the defendants’ guilt before deliberations.

The defense therefore argued that there was no legal basis to dissolve the entire jury or declare a mistrial.

Political Affiliation Also Became An Issue

The jury controversy was further complicated by the removal of one juror after the court determined that she had failed to disclose during jury selection that she held a leadership position within the Congress for Democratic Change

The prosecution raised concerns about potential bias because some of the defendants have political associations with the CDC.

Another juror was challenged after prosecutors presented photographs they claimed showed her among supporters at an event associated with defendant Abu B. Kamara.

Judge Willie, however, rejected that challenge after finding that the photographs had not been sufficiently authenticated to establish that the person depicted was the juror.

The juror denied that she was the woman in the photograph and maintained that the person shown was her mother.

Supreme Court Says, Prohibition Cannot Lie

The defendants subsequently turned to the Supreme Court, arguing that Judge Willie’s decision to disband the jury was unlawful.

The High Court had previously intervened in the matter, including ordering a stay of proceedings while the prohibition petition was considered.

But after scrutinizing the arguments, the Supreme Court has now declined to grant the requested relief.

The Court essentially determined that the trial judge had acted within the authority vested in him to make the disputed ruling concerning the jury.

The petition for prohibition was therefore denied.

The case stems from the December 18, 2024 fire at Liberia’s Capitol Building, an incident that damaged portions of the country’s legislative complex and triggered a major criminal investigation.

The government subsequently charged Koffa and several others in connection with an alleged conspiracy surrounding the fire.

The defendants have pleaded not guilty to all charges and have consistently challenged the prosecution’s allegations and evidence.

The proceedings have involved contentious disputes over witness testimony, photographs, videos, audio recordings and other evidence the prosecution intends to use to establish its case.

The jury controversy became one of the most consequential procedural battles in the trial after prosecutors argued that questions raised by jurors demonstrated that the panel had become compromised.

Judge Willie ultimately sided with the prosecution and disbanded the jury.

Koffa and his co-defendants then sought Supreme Court intervention.

World.title: Liberia: Fundamental Weaknesses In State’s Evidence Against Murder Suspect Kaiser
World.content:
Supreme Court Overturns Lower Court’s Conviction, Orders His Release, After Years In Prison

‘State’s Evidence Failed to Corroborate’, As High Court Restores Rights of Man Convicted in Fatu Blasuah Murder

By Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia- The murder conviction of Valington B. Kaiser, alias “Bishop,” has been overturned by the Supreme Court of Liberia, declaring that the evidence presented by the prosecution failed to sufficiently corroborate the case against him and ordering that his rights and dignity be restored.

Kaiser, who has spent more than three years behind bars at the Monrovia Central Prison, walked away from the country’s highest court a free man Friday, following the landmark decision.

The ruling brings a dramatic turn to a murder case that began with the brutal killing of 18-year-old Fatu Blasuah at the former LPRC compound in Monrovia in May 2022 and culminated in Kaiser’s conviction before Criminal Court “A” in March 2023.

The Supreme Court, in reviewing the lower court’s judgment, found fundamental weaknesses in the State’s evidentiary case, concluding that the pieces of evidence relied upon by the prosecution did not sufficiently corroborate one another to sustain Kaiser’s conviction.

With the conviction overturned, the Supreme Court has restored Kaiser’s legal standing and liberty, bringing an end, at least for now, to more than three years of incarceration stemming from a conviction the nation’s highest court has now rejected.

From Murder Scene To Prison Cell

The case dates back to May 16, 2022, when the body of Fatu Blasuah was discovered at the Old LPRC Compound in Monrovia.

Police reported that the 18-year-old had suffered multiple stab wounds.

Investigators reportedly recovered a silver knife with a green handle from the scene.

Kaiser, who was then about 20 years old, was subsequently arrested and accused of involvement in the killing.

Investigators also pointed to CCTV footage which they said placed Kaiser in or around the area where Fatu’s body was discovered.

The prosecution further alleged that Kaiser and Fatu had been involved in a romantic relationship before her death.

Those allegations formed part of the evidence presented against him at trial.

A Mother’s Testimony

During the trial, Fatu’s mother, Maima Sackie, testified about her daughter’s relationship with Kaiser and the events preceding her disappearance.

She told the court that Kaiser was known to the family and frequently visited Fatu.

According to her testimony, Fatu left home after telling her that Kaiser had contacted her concerning a phone he had left with her.

Fatu did not return home that evening.

The family later became alarmed and eventually learned that a body had been discovered around the LPRC area.

The prosecution relied on the testimony, along with the CCTV footage, the knife reportedly recovered from the scene and other evidence, to build its case against Kaiser.

Jury Found Kaiser Guilty

After approximately a month-long trial before Criminal Court “A,” a 12-member jury returned a guilty verdict against Kaiser on March 1, 2023.

Reports from the time indicated that 10 of the 12 jurors voted to convict him.

The verdict resulted in Kaiser’s continued detention at the Monrovia Central Prison, where he remained for years while pursuing legal remedies against his conviction.

But the case did not end with the jury’s verdict.

Kaiser challenged the judgment, eventually bringing the matter before the Supreme Court—the final judicial authority in Liberia.

Evidence Did Not Corroborate

In its review, the Supreme Court scrutinized the evidence upon which the conviction rested.

The High Court determined that the various pieces of evidence presented by the State failed to adequately corroborate one another, raising serious questions about whether the prosecution had met the legal threshold required to sustain a criminal conviction.

The significance of the ruling is profound.

A guilty verdict by a trial jury cannot stand simply because suspicion surrounds an accused person.

The prosecution must establish guilt through legally sufficient evidence.

In Kaiser’s case, the Supreme Court has now determined that the evidentiary pieces relied upon by the State were insufficiently corroborated to sustain the judgment against him.

From Convicted Murderer To Free Man

The decision dramatically changes Kaiser’s legal status.

For more than three years, he lived behind the walls of the Monrovia Central Prison after being convicted of one of the most serious crimes under Liberian law.

On Friday, August 28, that conviction was overturned by the Supreme Court.

The ruling restores his liberty and, with it, the presumption of innocence that stands at the heart of Liberia’s criminal justice system.

Kaiser is now a free man.

World.title: Liberia: Maryland County Senator Engages Liberian Embassy, Diaspora Leaders in France
World.content:
Amb. Teeko Tozay Yorlay, Sr. (left) and Senator James Biney of

Maryland County.

PARIS, France – A Maryland County Senator, who chairs the Liberian Senate Committee on Executive and serves as ranking member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, has held separate engagements with officials at the Liberian Embassy in Paris and leaders of the Liberian community in France.

By Jaheim T. Tumu

According to a release, the Senator visited the Embassy of Liberia in Paris on Thursday, where he was received by Liberia’s Ambassador to France, Dr. Teeko Tozay Yorlay, Sr., and members of the diplomatic staff.

During the meeting, the Senator commended Ambassador Yorlay and the Embassy staff for their service to Liberia, particularly the sacrifices and challenges associated with representing the country abroad.

He praised the mission’s dedication, resilience and commitment to duty, noting that Liberia’s diplomatic representatives play an important role in advancing the country’s foreign-policy interests, providing services to Liberians abroad and strengthening relations with France and other countries of accreditation.

The Senator encouraged the Embassy staff to remain committed to their national responsibilities and continue upholding Liberia’s interests in their diplomatic engagements.

Senator Meets Liberian Community Leaders

Following his engagement at the Embassy, the Senator met with the leadership of the Federation of Liberian Associations in France as part of his outreach to Liberians living in France and across Europe.

The meeting provided an opportunity for the Federation’s leadership to present its vision, priorities and ongoing efforts to promote unity, cooperation and community development among Liberians in France.

The group also briefed the Senator on preparations for the upcoming Liberian Independence Day celebrations in Europe under the European Federation of Liberian Associations (EFLA).

The Federation described the annual gathering as an important platform for promoting Liberian culture, national identity, diaspora solidarity and stronger connections between Liberians abroad and their homeland.

Discussions also focused on the need for greater and sustained engagement between the Government of Liberia and diaspora organizations across Europe.

The Federation highlighted the potential contribution of the Liberian diaspora to national development through investment, knowledge and skills transfer, advocacy, tourism promotion and other forms of constructive engagement.

Call for Stronger Government-Diaspora Engagement

The Senator welcomed the concerns and recommendations presented by the Federation and acknowledged the significant contributions Liberians abroad continue to make to the country’s development.

He emphasized the importance of maintaining effective channels of communication between the Government of Liberia and organized diaspora communities, particularly those in Europe.

The Senator encouraged the Federation to continue working collaboratively to promote the interests and welfare of Liberians in France while contributing to Liberia’s broader national development agenda.

The engagements in Paris concluded with a shared commitment to strengthening Liberia’s diplomatic service, deepening Government-diaspora relations and ensuring that the concerns, aspirations and contributions of Liberians living in Europe remain an important part of national development discussions.

World.title: Liberia: Finance Unlocks Jobs, Hope”-Governor Saamoi Declares as CBL Launches Enhanced Collateral Registry Aimed at Boosting Secured Lending
World.content:
As CBL Launches Enhanced Collateral Registry Aimed at Boosting Secured Lending

Congo Town– The Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) has launched an Enhanced Collateral Registry System, a major financial sector reform aimed at expanding access to credit for businesses and individuals by allowing lenders and borrowers to more efficiently register and verify collateral through a modern digital platform.

By Jaheim T. [email protected]

The launch, attended by senior government officials, development partners, representatives of financial institutions, and members of the private sector, marked what CBL Executive Governor Henry F. Saamoi described as an important step toward strengthening secured lending, promoting responsible borrowing, and deepening financial inclusion across Liberia.

In his keynote address, Governor Saamoi said the new system is designed to help unlock financing opportunities for entrepreneurs, small businesses, farmers, and other productive sectors of the economy that often struggle to access formal credit despite owning valuable assets.

“We are not merely launching a technological platform. We are launching a powerful instrument for economic empowerment,” Saamoi said.

“We are launching a reform that will help unlock capital, expand opportunity, and strengthen the foundations of inclusive economic growth in Liberia.”

The Governor explained that many Liberian businesses possess assets such as equipment, contracts, vehicles, inventory, and land, but have historically faced challenges converting those assets into bankable collateral due to weaknesses in the country’s credit infrastructure.

According to him, the enhanced registry addresses that challenge by creating a more transparent, reliable, and accessible framework for secured transactions.

The modernized system allows both movable and immovable assets to be registered through a unified digital platform that can be accessed around the clock.

Financial institutions can electronically register, amend, assign, discharge, and search security interests more efficiently, reducing delays and uncertainty in lending transactions.

Saamoi said the initiative forms part of Liberia’s broader effort to build a modern financial system capable of supporting investment, job creation, and sustainable economic growth.

He noted that the reform is aligned with the government of Liberia’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development, which emphasizes inclusive economic growth and expanded access to financial services.

“We are not simply introducing new technology,” the Governor said. “The Enhanced Collateral Registry represents another important milestone in our collective efforts to modernize Liberia’s financial infrastructure and create a financial system that works for every Liberian.”

One of the key features of the upgraded platform is its ability to connect with other national databases and institutions.

The registry is linked with institutions such as the National Identification Registry, the Liberia Land Authority, the Liberia Business Registry, and vehicle registration systems.

This interoperability enables lenders to verify ownership information, identity records, and existing claims on assets with greater confidence.

According to the Saamoi, better access to reliable information will help reduce lending risks, strengthen transparency, and improve confidence within the financial system.

Experts say these improvements could encourage financial institutions to expand lending to sectors that have traditionally been underserved.

Saamoi emphasized that the reform could have a particularly strong impact on micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), which remain the backbone of Liberia’s economy.

He said many entrepreneurs possess productive assets but are unable to access financing because traditional lending models often favor conventional forms of collateral.

“For too long, many small businesses, women-owned enterprises, young entrepreneurs, farmers, and rural producers have lacked access to traditional financing despite owning productive assets,” he said.

“A more inclusive financial system is not merely a banking objective. It is a national development imperative.”

Governor Saamoi said the true success of the registry would not be measured by the technology itself but by its impact on people’s lives and businesses.

“The real value of this platform will not be measured by the technology itself,” he said. “Its true value will be measured by the businesses it helps grow, the investments it supports, the jobs it creates, and the lives it transforms.”

The Governor summarized the broader vision behind the reform. “Today, we launch an enhanced system. Tomorrow, we unlock finance. Finance unlocks enterprise. Enterprise unlocks jobs. And jobs unlock hope.”

During his remarks, the Governor pointed to results achieved under the Liberia Investment, Finance and Trade (LIFT) Project as evidence that increased access to finance can produce positive economic outcomes.

He disclosed that a US$6 million line of credit established under the project had been fully deployed through seven participating financial institutions by the second quarter of 2026.

According to the Central Bank, the facility helped 358 MSMEs obtain affordable financing, with some businesses receiving loans of up to US$100,000.

The Governor further revealed that women-owned businesses accounted for 64 percent of all loan disbursements, while 130 beneficiary enterprises were located outside Montserrado County.

Reflecting on those achievements, Saamoi said the data demonstrates that Liberian entrepreneurs have the capacity to grow if given adequate support and access to financing.

“The truth is that Liberian entrepreneurs do not lack ambition. Liberian entrepreneurs do not lack innovation. Liberian entrepreneurs do not lack determination,” he said. “Too often, they simply lack access.”

Development partners also welcomed the launch and described it as an important milestone in Liberia’s economic development agenda.

World Bank Country Manager, Georgia Wallen said access to finance remains one of the biggest obstacles facing Liberian businesses.

She noted that many entrepreneurs possess productive assets but lack the traditional collateral required by lenders to secure financing.

“The Enhanced Collateral Registry System helps to bridge this gap,” Wallen said. “It will give lenders greater confidence to accept a wider range of assets, and it will help borrowers unlock the value of the assets that they possess.”

She recalled that Liberia’s first collateral registry, launched in 2014 with support from the International Finance Corporation (IFC), had produced encouraging results by facilitating more than US$237 million in financing within its first two years of operation.

According to Wallen, the enhanced version seeks to build upon those gains while addressing challenges identified over time.

Wallen stressed, however, that technology alone would not guarantee success. She said widespread adoption by banks, businesses, regulators, and other stakeholders would be necessary to ensure the registry achieves its intended objectives. She disclosed that training programs and public awareness campaigns are already being planned to support implementation.

The judiciary also expressed strong support for the reform. Commercial Court Judge Eva Mappy Morgan described the enhanced registry as a critical development that could improve transparency in lending transactions and strengthen the enforcement of financial agreements.

Morgan explained that disputes often arise when collateral cannot be properly identified or when multiple claims exist over the same asset.

She said the new system would help provide clarity regarding ownership and security interests, reducing legal uncertainties that have historically complicated the recovery of non-performing loans.

A more reliable collateral framework, she added, could increase confidence among lenders and investors while strengthening the overall business environment.

As Liberia continues its broader financial sector modernization agenda, the Central Bank says the Enhanced Collateral Registry will work alongside a modernized Credit Reference System currently being developed under the LIFT Project. Both systems are expected to improve credit information, support better lending decisions, and strengthen confidence throughout the financial sector.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court Recalls US$50,000 Fines Against Martin Kollie, Alex Williams
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Supreme Court of Liberia has recalled and corrected a portion of its ruling delivered Thursday, August 27, in a damages case involving former LISGIS Deputy Director General Wilmot Smith and Ecobank Liberia.
