World.title: Opinion: Remembering Dolly Parton
World.content:
Opinion: Remembering Dolly Parton

toggle caption Mark Humphrey/ASSOCIATED PRESS/AP

Dolly Parton was brilliant, melodic, and trailblazing. Her lifetime art was to be both spangly and utterly genuine.

When Dolly died this week, I thought I could see her bright, wide smile shining down from the sky, with the clouds billowing into her signature blond curls.

Dolly Parton was lauded and loved. Tributes poured in as they would for a head of state—more, I daresay, than many heads of state. American flags were lowered to half-staff, the top of the Empire State building sparkled in pink, and the royal guards at Buckingham Palace played "9 to 5" in tribute.

Sponsor Message

Dolly Parton sold more than 100 million records. She delighted, amused, and moved millions more, starring in movies and appearing on TV. She was charming, and she was savvy.

When Dolly was born, the 4th of 12 children, her parents had to pay the doctor in cornmeal. Her life reminds us that in America, someone can be born in a one-room cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River, and still be a queen.

Dolly Parton's success in show business gave wings to her natural generosity. She helped families rebuild after floods; sponsored scholarships; funded the development of a COVID vaccine; and started a program that sent books to more than 300 million children around the world.

But enough of a journalist's words—let's listen to the queen.

In 1972, Dolly wrote and recorded My Tennessee Mountain Home. It had the gift, as great songs do, of helping us to see simple things that were always right before us.

"Sittin' on the front porch on a summer afternoon

In a straight back chair on two legs leaned against the wall

As I watch the kids a-playin' with their June bugs on a string

And chase the glowin' fireflies when evenin' shadows fall

In my Tennessee mountain home

Life is as peaceful as a baby's sigh

In my Tennessee mountain home

Crickets are singing in the fields near by..."

World.title: The bridges of Rwanda open up new worlds
World.content:
The bridges of Rwanda open up new worlds

toggle caption Claire Harbage/NPR

MUKUNGA RIVER VALLEY, Rwanda — For Naomi Nibishaka, there's life before the bridge, and life after the bridge.

On a sunny summer day, the 76-year-old crosses the rushing waters of the Mukungwa river on a pedestrian suspension bridge.

Made of concrete and cable, it's only 230 feet long — roughly the length of a city block. But it's a game changer.

The bridge connects two settlements in a valley in northwest Rwanda that are separated by the river. People cross for all sorts of reasons. Certain services are only available on one side –- a health clinic, a school, a market. Farmers may cross to seek supplies or sell their harvest. Nibishaka is on her way to see her son and grandchildren, who live across the river from her settlement.

Sponsor Message

Before the bridge was built, there were crossing options — none of them great. You could hire a boat but it was expensive. Local authorities would rope together timber logs for a makeshift bridge, but in the rainy season, the logs would grow slippery and floods would wash them away.

toggle caption Claire Harbage/NPR

The other alternative was hiking to a narrower crossing — but that took 3 hours each way.

"When someone [who attempted the crossing] went missing, we would look for them, but if it was a rainy day, we would ask the other side if that person slept over,"

Nibishaka says. "And if they can't find them, we would look for the body."

Many people in the community drowned, Nibishaka says. Fearful parents pulled their children out of school if a river crossing was part of their commute. Farmers unable to cross saw their business suffer.

Then in 2025, this footbridge — called Cyangoga — was built. It's one of 96 built in Rwanda since 2020 by the bridge-building nonprofit Fika. The name for this Kigali-based charity means "to arrive" in Swahili. Funding for the program came from the Rwandan government and donors like the U.S. Agency for International Development, before it was dismantled by the Trump administration.

toggle caption Claire Harbage/NPR

Until now, researchers had not studied the impact of the bridges Fika built. The Rwanda project offered an opportunity to assess what this simple piece of infrastructure might be able to accomplish.

Sponsor Message

Evan Thomas , professor of environmental engineering at the University of Colorado Boulder, is one of the researchers. "We collected tens of thousands of surveys from hundreds of villages and thousands of households to try to figure out: What changes when you get a bridge?"

Results are in

Their results, released in July, attest to a remarkable series of improvements.

"We found an increase in household consumption, an increase in household income, an increase in the amount of land people are cultivating, an increase in use of fertilizers, even an increase in the number of children going to school," Thomas says.

For Nibishaka, the bridge has brought her freedom to move around — and a full stomach.

"Before, I would have to wait for my grandkids to bring me food every day. Some days I would be very hungry" she says. Now, the children can easily get food to her, and she can cross the river herself to visit them.

A tough terrain

Rwanda, known as the land of a thousand hills, is particularly challenging for infrastructure projects.

"The whole country is very mountainous, very steep and very wet," says Devin Connell, Fika's vice president of programs. "So to build infrastructure, or provide electrification across the country, it's just a logistical and physically difficult task to do."

The group mainly builds two types of bridges.

"This one is a suspension bridge, which is the type of bridge we build in valleys," says Connell. "It has steel towers and a dead man anchor buried in the ground. And brings the walkway up above the floodplain."

toggle caption Claire Harbage/NPR

The other kind of bridge is built for steep gorges, with hills on both sides.

"That's where we build a suspended bridge and the cables sag down below, kind of classically like an Indiana Jones-style bridge," he says.

Sponsor Message

Because of the challenging terrain, the bridges are designed to be constructed without heavy machinery.

On average, each bridge costs about $100,000. Thomas says it's a cost-effective figure, especially considering the price of building in Rwanda's terrain.

The results of the study offer up many instances of the power of the bridges.

In the Mugunkwa river valley, farmers who make banana wine more than tripled their output. And since services such as a health clinic, school and post office are only on one side of the bridge, communities on the other side have easier access. The health clinic saw a 40% increase in the number of people coming in.

toggle caption Claire Harbage/NPR

The rate of return on investment was 120%, meaning the bridge paid for itself and more in the year since it was built.

The impact on schools is especially striking, says Marie Gorette Mutuyimana, a primary school teacher of 28 years who crosses the river twice every weekday to get to and from work.

For years, Mutuyimana had worked with parents in the valley, encouraging them to send their children to school, but deep down she knew it was the river that kept drop-out levels high.

toggle caption Claire Harbage/NPR

"Sometimes I invested my own money in renting bicycles for those students for a faster commute, and the parents were relying on me to ensure their safety," Mutuyimana says.

"If it started raining while we were at school. I wouldn't be able to concentrate on teaching, I would just worry about how we were all going to get home," she says. The responsibility weighed heavily on her.

Now she says things are different: More than 134 students re-enrolled in the school. She says they're excited to be back with their friends. And she can focus on teaching.

toggle caption Claire Harbage/NPR

Lessons learned

The research shows how transformative infrastructure investments can be, according to Edward Miguel , a development economist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not part of the research team.

Sponsor Message

"Solving that one fundamental transportation problem changes lots of economic decisions, farming decisions, and the payoff can be really big in the long run," Miguel says.

It's especially relevant, he says, in light of the funding shortages that have rocked the world of development assistance after the Trump administration's overhaul of U.S. foreign aid. USAID used to be a big supporter of programs like this all over the world, Miguel says. Now, many lower income countries are struggling to fill the gap. A study like this can show them what's worth investing in, according to Miguel.

"If I were in the government of Rwanda, looking at how important these investments are, in next year's budget, I would start thinking about maybe allocating more money to transportation investments," Miguel says.

What else is needed

Yet a bridge can't solve all challenges that face remote communities.

Asked what they need for a better life, villagers told NPR they urgently needed roads, electricity and clean water. Miguel says the problems facing rural populations can be daunting.

"And sometimes people look at it and throw up their hands and go 'oh my god, we solved the bridge, but now we need the road … we need electricity," says Miguel. "But every time you make one of those investments, you improve people's lives."

For schoolteacher Marie Mutuyimana, the bridge was the start.

toggle caption Claire Harbage/NPR

"Primarily, we needed to ensure the safety of ourselves and our children, and the ability to access services," she says. "Now that we have that peace of mind, we can ask for the other things we need to improve our lives."

World.title: Lights out, Instagram off? The changes to Meta for teens could be a big deal
World.content:
Lights out, Instagram off? The changes to Meta for teens could be a big deal

toggle caption Manuel Arias Duran/Moment RF/Getty Images

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

The social media company Meta has agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion in a settlement in a federal lawsuit alleging the company's social media platforms have harmed children and teens. The company denies the allegations, but has agreed to make a suite of changes to its social platforms — Facebook and Instagram — to make them less compelling and potentially dangerous to minors.

This comes at a time when healthcare providers are increasingly seeing symptoms of social media addiction among youth, says psychologist Mitch Prinstein, who is the Co-Director of the Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.

"We know that about 50% of kids are reporting at least one symptom of clinical dependency on social media," he says. "We know that kids who are having a difficult time getting off social media are also reporting more depression, loneliness, anxiety, even suicidality over time."

Sponsor Message

While Meta denies the allegations that it designed its social platforms to be addictive for kids, child safety advocates and researchers have welcomed the settlement as a major development in holding tech companies accountable.

"This settlement isn't perfect, but I do think it's a critical first step in making sure platforms are safer for our children and that our kids can grow up healthy," says Julie Scelfo, founder of the grassroots organization Mothers Against Media Addiction.

The changes Meta will have to make are intended to reduce the addictiveness of Facebook and Instagram. For example, it will have to give minors the option of having a non-personalized feed, where it doesn't use an algorithm to tailor content based on individual preferences to keep kids scrolling. The changes are detailed in a press release from California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led a coalition of 50 states and territories and the District of Columbia that settled with Meta.

The other reforms Meta has agreed to for people under 18 include:

a default daily time limit of two hours for minors, with only parents having the ability to opt kids out.



a default block on nighttime use from midnight to 6 a.m.



a default block on notifications to minors – both overnight, and from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year.



a ban on showing minors how many likes or reactions their posts receive.



a ban on cosmetic procedure image filters.



a better system for teens to report potentially harmful content and a commitment that Meta respond to 90% of those reports within six hours.



Sponsor Message

Meta is also promising to do a better job of verifying users' ages and has agreed to report regularly to an independent auditor.

Meta is calling on other social media companies to make the same changes, and has negotiated that $5 billion of the settlement will be paid to states if other companies join the effort. Texas negotiated an additional $1 billion settlement with Meta.

"This framework will only work if all our peers join us," Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. "Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away."

Enthusiastic reception from experts

"It is very exciting to see that a lot of the changes that are written into the settlement are very similar to what we saw scientifically," says Prinstein, who was scheduled to testify next week in the case brought by the states.

For example, he says, studies show why the design elements of Facebook and Instagram are particularly addictive for teens and pre-teens.

"By the time a kid turns around ten or 11, the part of their brain that makes them suddenly super interested in things like popularity and who sits at the lunch table are really showing a hypersensitivity to social signals," he says. And so, when kids encounter constant notifications about followers, likes, and dislikes on social media accounts, it easily leads to time spent on these platforms.

"We saw kids unable to stop themselves on these platforms," explains Prinstein. "They would tell us, 'I have tried to quit and I can't. It's interfering with my daily roles and routines.'"

So turning off notifications during school days and overnight should help lower problematic use by minors, he adds.

Making sleep a priority

Similarly, the block on nighttime use could make a big difference to teen mental health, says Dr. Jason Nagata, a pediatrician and researcher at the University of California, San Francisco.

Sponsor Message

His analysis of the longitudinal Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, where researchers have followed thousands of children as they grow up, shows that a big proportion of teens are using their cell phones between midnight and 4 a.m.

"The most used app category during this period was social media," says Nagata. "So I think that it is likely that most of these teenagers are … on social media and getting the notifications and kind of distractions that are impairing their sleep."

And sufficient sleep is key to teen brain development and mental wellness.

Implementation will be important

But Nagata and Prinstein also caution that it remains to be seen whether these changes required by the settlement actually will have the desired effect on kids' experience of social media and their mental health.

"I do think that the details of the implementation are really important," says Nagata. "What we have found, even in some of the testimony during this case, is that it's actually very hard to get some of these things to work."

He is referring to some of the changes Meta had already made on its apps, like the "Take a Break" feature on Instagram, which reminds teen users to close the app after they have been on it for a certain length of time. As Instagram head Adam Mosseri testified in court, the feature wasn't as effective as they had hoped.

"We really need to know how this is going to be implemented," says Nagata, "and then I do think that this needs to be rigorously evaluated. It's not just like we're going to make some changes and then that's it."

Prinstein agrees. "We still need research to make sure that these changes are actually helping, and they're not in some ways making kids worse or kids are finding sneaky ways around them," he says. "So we still have some work to do."

Sponsor Message

The settlement does include an agreement from Meta "to maintain, review, and improve existing teen content safety measures" and to "create enhanced parent supervision tools."

World.title: In Ohio, Canada-U.S. trade war sparks anger and uncertainty
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The rat-a-tat-tat of a nail gun and high-pitched whine of a buzz saw echo through the two-storey home as Joe Koch’s carpentry crew completes the final touches.

Koch, the vice-president of operations for his decades-old family business, had hoped there would be three or four other new builds going up in this Ohio subdivision about now, but the U.S. trade war with Canada and many other countries has scuttled that plan.

"People are just going to not build that house this year. They're going to wait 'til interest rates lower. They're going to wait 'til the tariffs subside or the political landscape changes," Koch said.

He sees his business challenges as a microcosm of what’s happening across Ohio. President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canadian and other nations' goods have not only raised the prices he pays but costs for consumers more broadly.

Koch used to buy Canadian shingles. Now he buys from a local company.

"If there's any benefit [to the trade turmoil], it's that you get that much more resourceful," he said.

The uncertainty and instability of the trade war has made financial planning and supply management difficult. Koch believes when it comes to trade, building relationships and making compromises is important.

"When it comes to the real volatile landscape of the globe, you need partners within your backyard that you're able to go to," he said. "I think it may be great to be able to have everything homegrown — but is that the reality of the world? I'm not so sure."

Youngstown, Ohio, used to be the heart of steel country. Even though it has diversified its economy, it still has more than 20,000 jobs in manufacturing, which could be impacted by the ongoing trade war between Canada and US. (Katie Nicholson/CBC)

Koch feels caught in the middle of a trade storm but he’s determined to tough it out.

"It's a game of chess," he said. "There's no victory. It's just battle after battle and you win where you can. You try to minimize the damage wherever there is damage. And then you live to fight another day."

"But we're used to it," he said. "We're Youngstown, Ohio."

'It makes me angry'

Youngstown/Warren, which has a population of around 425,000, has faced economic challenges before. It was once known as the heart of U.S. steel country, until the closure of Youngstown Sheet and Tube in September 1977 put 5,000 workers out of work overnight.

While Youngstown diversified its economy in the decades that followed, more than 20,000 jobs are still tied to manufacturing, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That's across numerous sectors, including steel tubes and pipes, plastics and advanced materials.

WATCH | We asked Americans what they think of the trade war: ‘Nonsensical’: We asked Americans what they think about the trade war | Duration 1:30 Nearly two years into Trump's second term, Americans in Ohio and Pennsylvania have found themselves caught in the crossfire of a trade war with Canada as Washington levies tariffs on Canadian imports and Ottawa responds in kind. CBC’s Katie Nicholson spoke to some locals in Ohio to see how trade negotiations are becoming pocketbook issues for voters as the November midterms approach.

Last year, Ohio exported $17.5 billion US in goods to Canada — roughly a third of its total exports. Ohio’s top exports to Canada included $2.7 billion US in engines and turbines, $1.8 billion in auto parts, $1 billion in plastics and $692 million in iron and steel alloys and semi-finished products, according to data from the Embassy of Canada in Washington, D.C.

Conversely, Ohio imported $3.2 billion US in Canadian crude oil, $1.1 billion in vehicle parts, $1 billion in plastics, $915 million in steel and semi-finished products, and $672 million in aluminum and aluminum materials.

Youngstown sits in a wider congressional district known as OH-6 with a population of more than 775,000.

It exports more than $820 million US in goods to Canada every year, including coal and petroleum, iron steel and ferroalloys, resins and synthetic fibres, aluminum products and plastics.

While not all of these imports and exports are caught in the crosshairs of the escalating tariffs, a prolonged trade war could threaten some businesses in those sectors.

WATCH | What Canadian products is Trump targeting with latest tariffs?: What Canadian goods is Trump targeting with his latest 50% tariffs? | Duration 0:53 U.S. President Donald Trump is imposing new 50 per cent tariffs on dozens of Canadian goods under section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act. Some of these targeted items correspond with the dairy and alcohol grievances the U.S. is raising, but a swath of tariffed goods, mostly listed under the auto grievance, are seemingly unrelated.

At a local ballpark recently, players were hanging out for a post-game beer in the parking lot under the glow of a warm sunset. But there were also heated words about the Trump administration's trade war with Canada.

“It makes me angry. Why is that? Because, first of all, Canada and us have been very good allies forever, and to do something like this makes no sense at all," said Pam Hall. "It's just ridiculous.”

Next to her, Patricia Vandervoort chimed in: “We don't want Canada to hold it against us citizens — it's not us.”

Hall said the administration’s trade war with Canada and other countries is hitting Ohioans in the pocketbook.

“Everything you buy is more expensive, no matter where it comes from, because of these tariffs. Groceries, basic day-to-day items that you need,” she said. “The tariffs have … done a lot to destroy the economy.”

From left, Cindy Burns, Patricia Vandervoort and Pam Hall say the trade war has made life more expensive for people in the U.S., and question why the Trump administration is targeting its long-time ally Canada. (Katie Nicholson/CBC)

Their friend Cindy Burns fears Canada may permanently take its business elsewhere.

“I'm sure you're going to strengthen trade with other countries to supplement what we're not giving you or trading with you. You'll go elsewhere and maybe it'll be better and you'll never come back,” Burns said.

“It'll affect our factories, because there won't be a demand that there has been. People will lose their jobs. I mean, it's gonna spiral,” said Vandervoort, a Pennsylvania native.

Not far away, Larry Kelly believes the tariff war could flip seats blue in this red state in the November midterms.

Some polling in the Buckeye state has shown Democrats competitive and even ahead in some key races, including for a Senate seat currently held by Republican John Husted, who was appointed by the Republican governor to replace now Vice-President JD Vance.

“I think it's going to have a dramatic effect on the midterms," said Kelly.

His teammate Mike Glinatsis says the trade war hasn’t affected him that much.

“I mean, I can afford to eat,” he said. “I think Canada had … high tariffs on our stuff. And then Trump made it equal. And that's when people started getting all pissy.”

Tariffs 'a mixed bag'

Others in the business community share Glinatsis’s more positive view of the tariff war.

“There's a mixed bag — it hurts some, it helps some. And there's some companies where it hurts on one side, it helps on the other," said Guy Coviello, president and CEO of the Youngstown/Warren Regional Chamber.

Guy Coviello, the president and CEO of the Youngstown/Warren Regional Chamber, says the U.S. tariffs have been a mixed bag for local businesses, with some being hurt and others benefitting from them. (James Young/CBC)

One of the major steel companies in town is in favour of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel, Coviello said.

“Sometimes in those meetings, I've got a chamber member that is trying to argue against tariffs sitting across the table from a chamber member that's embracing the tariffs, and it is interesting to hear them talk it out.”

Companies and agriculture producers in Ohio are still trying to figure out how the Canadian counter-tariffs, set to begin on Sept. 8, will affect them.

Coviello said data from Youngstown State University’s Export Assistance Network suggests overall, the trade war has been a “net negative.”

Americans 'rethinking who truly has their back'

The trade war has stymied growth potential for some Ohio businesses, such as Shapes Unlimited, which fabricates aluminum gates, fences and other materials. It employs roughly 40 people in the Youngstown/Warren area and has just moved into a new facility with major investments in technology.

"We'd like to further extend our reach into the provinces, but it isn't cost-effective right now,” said CEO Doug Rende, who has been eyeing markets in Ontario and Quebec, given their proximity to northeastern Ohio.

“The issues associated with transportation surcharges, rising fuel costs and obviously the 50 per cent issues associated with tariffs make it untenable.”

Rende’s business has had to work hard to source aluminum amid the tariff war, with levies ranging from 25 to 50 per cent on imported aluminum and an elevated demand for domestic and scrap supply.

“You can't cut off your nose to spite your face until such time as you're finding ways to more aggressively invest in the capacity,” Rende said.

WATCH | CBC speaks to steelmaker about tariff impacts: CBC speaks with steel-making company owner Rahim Moloo on the impact of tariffs | Duration 6:58 Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis.

The U.S. did once make more of its own raw materials, he said.

“This country abandoned investments in aluminum manufacturing in the 1980s, where there were 30 smelters. Now there's four. So again, [the government's] fire-ready-aim approach is unnecessarily raising costs to the end consumer, making housing costs less [affordable], and certainly negatively impacting by millions of dollars our ability to be more profitable in utilizing this material on an ongoing basis.”

Rende said he’d like to buy Canadian aluminum because of its quality and its proximity to Ohio, which would help significantly shorten the lag time in its supply chain.

Rende’s patience with the trade war is growing thin.

“Regardless of the political affiliations and points of view of your prime minister and our president, the bottom line is it's affecting us as individuals, as consumers, it's affecting us as businesses and business owners, and it's driving up issues that can be easily averted,” he said.

He believes this spat and its knock-on effects will play a role in how Americans vote in November.

“I think the U.S. population is now rethinking who truly has their back — and we'll see.”

World.title: An island mysteriously appeared — then disappeared — on B.C.'s largest reservoir
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

No one knows where it came from or where it went, but a massive new island might be floating out somewhere in the Williston Reservoir in northern B.C.

The forested land mass caught the attention of B.C. Hydro and local residents earlier this month after it was spotted bobbing in the massive man-made lake north of Mackenzie.

Rocky Avery says video and pictures of the island were taken by a boater and later shared with him. He posted them on social media, and they quickly went viral.

"It was a pretty amazing sight to see, never seen anything like that in my 40 years in this country," said Avery.

"There was a big fishing derby coming up, so I wanted to make sure everybody was aware of what was going on. And I wanted B.C. Hydro to know too that it was out there, just in case it was floating down their way."

The discovery left a B.C. Hydro spokesperson incredulous when CBC News first inquired about the island's origins.

Bob Gammer says he was first skeptical about the origins of the video because of the rise of generative AI technology. Not everything posted online can be trusted as being credible at first glance, he said.

"It's certainly something we've not heard of before," said Gammer. "And with not very many people reporting it, it was difficult to locate."

LISTEN | Floating island on Williston Reservoir: Radio West 3:57 A floating island in northern B.C.'s Williston Reservoir

But satellite imagery dated July 21 confirmed the island was in fact real, and floating in the main body of the reservoir west of Finlay Bay, about 100 kilometres west of the W.A.C. Bennett Dam.

Gammer says the island was estimated around 70 metres wide and 140 metres long, or about 9,800 square metres in area.

According to those estimates, that's roughly the size of two NFL football fields.

By Aug. 5, the island was no longer showing up in satellite data.

"We've been taking more updated snapshots and we can't see the object anymore. So it's disappeared now," Gammer said.

"It doesn't mean it's gone to the bottom of the reservoir. It may have returned to a more sheltered area along the shoreline."

Gammer says no operational impacts are expected, though B.C. Hydro is monitoring for the island's possible reappearance.

Satellite data provided by B.C. Hydro shows the location and size of a floating island found in the Williston Lake reservoir in northern B.C., about 100 kilometres west of the W.A.C. Bennett Dam. (B.C. Hydro)

First full reservoir in 14 years

The Williston reservoir, impounded behind the W.A.C. Bennett Dam in 1968, is the seventh-largest reservoir in the world and visible from space.

High winter snowpacks and steady summer rains have filled it to the brim, forcing B.C. Hydro to open the dam's spillways in June and July to release water.

Gammer says it's likely the island formed over many years somewhere along the shore where driftwood accumulated, allowing plants and trees to take root in the decomposing debris.

As reservoir levels rose, it broke free, and winds carried it out into open water.

"We haven't had a full reservoir in 14 years," Gammer said. "We can't pinpoint the origin of this floating island [but that's] one explanation that seems reasonable."

Avery says this year's high water has washed out shoreline sand dunes popular for quad-biking, and pulled more trees and debris out into the lake than usual.

"There's areas we would never even drive a boat on before, and now we're going up over top of it," said Avery.

High water levels in the Williston Lake reservoir in northern B.C. prompted B.C. Hydro to open the W.A.C. Bennett Dam spillways in June and July to release water. (Matt Preprost/CBC)

Phenomenon seen across the world

While a rare sight in Williston Lake, floating islands are a rather common phenomenon seen in dam building.

In Wisconsin, massive chunks of peat bog broke off from the bottom of Lake Chippewa after it was flooded for the Winter Dam.

One of them, called the "Forty Acre Bog," has to be pushed by boat every year to prevent it from drifting into a local bridge.

In Africa, researchers are investigating how floating islands in Lake Victoria are impacting transportation, fisheries and water quality. The world's second-largest freshwater lake spans across three countries.

Mackenzie, a town north of Prince George, is one of numerous communities along Williston Lake. (Chris Corday/CBC)

Lake needs public help to monitor

Gammer says the power utility relies on public reports in monitoring its reservoirs.

Because the Williston reservoir is so huge, he says it's not feasible to surveil it by water, and that B.C. Hydro will keep an eye out for sightings of the island via satellite.

Avery says local tugboat crews do a good job pulling what logs they can out of the lake, but says people need to be careful boating on the waters.

"When it's calm, it's fine. You can usually see them, but you get a little bit of choppy waves and it's really hard to see them until you're right on top," he said.

"Some are full-size trees and it'll do a lot of damage to your boat. So you got to be super careful."

Subscribe to CBC's Fort St. John Weekly for a roundup of the best news and stories from B.C.'s Peace and Northern Rockies.

World.title: Days after deadly Nepal flood, families of missing B.C. couples desperate for details
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Families of Canadians missing after the Nepal-Tibet flash flood disaster are desperate for any news of their loved ones, with some planning to travel to join the search efforts. Of the 32 Canadians reported missing, none have yet been confirmed dead.

Days after a massive wall of water tore through the Timure region of Nepal, families of two missing Metro Vancouver couples are desperately searching for information about their loved ones.

Port Moody couple Dhaval and Megha Shah and Coquitlam couple Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla are among thousands of people who are missing after the Aug. 26 flash flood struck, killing at least 676 people.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Saturday that one of 32 Canadians unaccounted for in the country had been located safely. The person has not been identified.

Vikram Khosla said his cousin Shubakshi was in the area for a trek to Kailash Mansarovar in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others, as a 50th birthday gift to herself.

WATCH | Fears of second flood as Nepal death toll mounts: Nepal-Tibet flash flood death toll climbs as fears of 2nd flood grow | Duration 2:21

He said the couple had been almost ready to depart for their journey when they spoke with a family member about an hour before the flood struck on Wednesday morning.

No one has heard from anyone in the group since then, he said.

“We are very hopeful that they went up and they are stuck somewhere," he said.

The couple, Singaporean citizens who moved to Canada about four years ago, have two daughters, he said.

Speaking from Mumbai, India, Dhaval's brother Kheval Shah told CBC his brother and sister-in-law were staying at Hotel Kailash, near the border, on Wednesday.

The family last heard from the two that morning as they were having breakfast, about 15 minutes before the flood struck.

“That hotel is completely submerged, there is no hotel anymore," he said.

“We just want to find out where they were when the water hit.... Ultimately I feel that closure is very important.”

The couple have a 24-year-old daughter, he added.

Canada has said it will send $5 million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal, with the money earmarked for organizations like the Red Cross to deliver assistance to people on the ground.

WATCH | Extreme weather researcher breaks down Nepal flood: CBC News Network speaks to extreme weather researcher about Nepal/Tibet. | Duration 7:05 Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis.

But Shah said he wants the Canadian government to push Nepal for more information about the search for the missing.

Khosla, too, shared frustration with the lack of updates.

He said Shubakshi's brother and sister have flown to Kathmandu and are trying to get to the affected area to search for answers.

He wants to see a centralized source of information for the families of missing people to get real time updates.

As of Saturday afternoon, more than 3,700 people had been rescued, but another 2,426 people remained missing.

World.title: Warnings over squishy toy hazards expand globally
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some trendy squishy toys have prompted burn warnings and enforcement action in several countries, while Canadian regulators say they've received dozens of reports but have not confirmed a specific health or safety risk.

The soft, palm-sized toys come in a variety of shapes, including cubes and spheres, as well as food shapes such as dumplings and sticks of butter. Their squishy texture is a defining feature of toys marketed for sensory play and sold through online marketplaces, discount stores and other retailers.

Regulators raise concerns abroad

This week, Cornwall Trading Standards in southwest England, warned that some squishy toys they tested failed U.K. safety standards.

Separately, Hull City Council in northeast England said it seized and destroyed toys from local retailers after testing found high levels of benzene, a carcinogen. Hull officials said high levels of exposure can cause irritation of the eyes, nose and throat, skin irritation and, if ingested, a burning sensation.

The local actions in England followed a recall by the U.K.'s Office for Product Safety and Standards of Squeezy Dumplings in June.

WATCH | Squishy toy hazards in Canada and abroad: Some squishy toys are not safe, health officials warn | Duration 2:04 Popular squishy toys that have taken the world by storm have health officials in multiple countries on alert over concerns about toxic chemicals, burns and even explosions after being left in overheated cars.

Earlier this month, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission reiterated a warning about serious burn hazards associated with fake and counterfeit squishy toys that do not comply with U.S. safety requirements.

Shipments of what the agency called "violative squishy toys" have also been seized at U.S. ports.

In Australia, Schyling, the manufacturer of NeeDoh toys, has reportedly asked the Australian Border Force to intercept counterfeit versions of its products.

Health Canada has received 36 reports

From April 23 to Aug. 24, Health Canada said it received 36 reports involving squishy dumpling toys.

"There were 30 reports of odours, four reports about the sale of these products but with no mention of odour or injury, and two reports of the product exploding, with 6 of these reports mentioning an injury (e.g., headache, skin rash, difficulty breathing)," Health Canada said in a statement to CBC News. "These reports include both children and adults."

Health Canada said it has not identified any failures to comply with health or safety regulations and has not confirmed that the toys pose a specific health or safety risk.

Separately, Amazon Canada said in a statement that it proactively removed some squishy dumpling toys following reported safety concerns.

What is actually inside the toys?

Toy manufacturers are not obligated to disclose the ingredients and may not always know exactly what is in their products, said Miriam Diamond, a professor and environmental chemist at the University of Toronto who studies microplastics and chemicals in consumer products.

"There could be chemicals there that are fairly benign, but there could also be chemicals that are of concern. I don't know, and that's actually concerning in and of itself," Diamond said, calling on manufacturers and importers to be vigilant.

WATCH | Squishy toys ease anxiety: Do squishies actually work? The history of sensory toys | Duration 1:01 NeeDohs and other squishy toys are incredibly popular right now. But the history of sensory toys goes back hundreds, if not thousands, of years. Do they really have therapeutic benefits?

The product safety group Consumer Reports said concerns are not necessarily limited to counterfeit or off-brand products.

"We kind of feel that it's not just about the counterfeit," said Ashita Kapoor, director of product safety and personal care at Consumer Reports. "We're actually seeing incidents of products that are happening that are purchased directly from retail."

Tips for parents

For now, the U.S. Product Safety Commission advises families to:

Keep affected toys away from heat, including hot cars and prolonged sunlight, and never intentionally heat them.

Inspect toys regularly for leaks.

Use caution when cleaning up after a toy bursts to avoid direct skin contact.

Diamond also suggests families declutter and stick with a few simple toys.

Families should also follow recommended age limits.

NeeDoh and Squishy Dumpling did not respond to requests for comment.

World.title: Trump's Venezuelan oil deal: What we know and how it could impact Canada's oil industry
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Besides a social media post from U.S. President Donald Trump, the White House has said little about what he is calling "THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY" in Venezuela.

Trump said the agreement announced Friday night would give the United States a stake in Venezuela's vast oil reserves, a step toward his goal of extracting energy from the country after American forces captured then-president Nicolás Maduro in a middle-of-the-night raid in January and brought him to New York to face federal drug-trafficking charges.

Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, described the deal as a step toward economic recovery that will modernize the country's oil industry.

But the answers to questions such as how soon the reserves could be drilled and who will pay to make it happen were not immediately clear. No text of any agreement has been released.

Here's a look at what we know and don't know — and how the agreement could affect Canada's oil industry, too.

WATCH | Trump announces deal on Venezuelan oil: Trump announces Venezuela oil reserves will be controlled by U.S. | Duration 4:12 In a post on his Truth Social platform, U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal that would allow the United States to control more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil.

What are the terms?

The U.S. government and an unnamed private operator in Venezuela formed a new private company that was given the rights to vast, untapped oil fields for 100 years.

A statement from Rodríguez said the deal involves the development of 17 fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels. It said the agreement could draw $100 billion US in investment into Venezuela's oil industry and yield over $209 billion US in taxes for Caracas.

Trump said the agreement was negotiated by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Rodríguez.

The deal gives the United States 55 per cent effective output of the new private company, including an ownership stake and rights to buy oil at cost. American purchases of the oil will go toward the U.S. strategic oil reserves along with the military, according to a U.S. official who was not authorized to discuss the matter publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The company would be the second-largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco, according to the official.

Rodriguez said the deal will modernize the country's oil industry. (Pedro Mattey/The Associated Press)

Will gas prices go down?

Probably not any time soon.

Trump says the deal will help lower gas prices for Americans — an important objective for the Republican president as the Iran war slows the shipping of Persian Gulf oil and keeps prices elevated months before U.S. midterm elections in November.

But experts have repeatedly warned that Venezuela's dilapidated oil infrastructure will take years and billions of dollars to repair. A substantial boost in production is not expected to happen quickly.

The deal could be "helpful in the long run, but it's not going to do anything to change the price of gasoline at the retail station for Labour Day weekend," said Amy Myers Jaffe, director of the Energy, Climate Justice and Sustainability Lab at New York University.

Neither side made clear who would pay for infrastructure investments and at what cost.

Kevin Book, managing director at ClearView Energy Partners, said Venezuela has room to build on its oil production — in the past it produced more than 2.5 million barrels a day above current levels — but this kind of investment does not come quickly.

"It doesn't happen all at once. It's going to take time — many years — to deploy that much capital and produce the kind of incremental results that history suggests possible," Book said.

WATCH | Trump pushes U.S. oil companies to develop Venezuelan reserves: Trump pushes wary U.S. oil execs to move into Venezuela | Duration 3:09 U.S. President Donald Trump is urging top oil executives to move quickly on developing Venezuela’s vast oil reserves. But few seem eager to jump in with both feet in the days after U.S. forces seized Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

What could the deal mean for Canada's oil industry?

While many details of the agreement remain unclear, experts said earlier this year that a revival of Venezuelan oil production would impact the Canadian oil industry.

Canada and Venezuela produce similar heavy crude, and over the past decades, Canadian oil filled a gap in the U.S. market amid shrinking Venezuelan exports.

U.S. imports of Venezuelan supplies "would compete directly with Canadian crude in the U.S. Gulf Coast market," Marc Ercolao, an economist at TD Economics, said in January after the U.S. said Venezuela would turn over as many as 50 million barrels of oil.

The Gulf Coast accounts for about 10 per cent of Canadian oil exports to the U.S., Ercolao said.

Observers say a rapid and large-scale increase in Venezuelan oil production isn't likely after years of under-investment, sanctions and political uncertainty.

But even a gradual recovery "would reintroduce meaningful competition into the North American heavy crude market," said Christopher Hernandez-Roy, acting director of the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C.

Canadian heavy crude trades at a discount, or differential, relative to benchmark U.S. crude prices, Hernandez-Roy said in May. So a "meaningful increase in Venezuelan crude" could widen that differential and reduce the value Canadian producers get for every exported barrel, he said.

Over the long term, a significant scale-up of Venezuelan oil production also could strengthen Canada's push to diversify its trading partners and become less reliant on the U.S. market, the experts said.

"China, the number one buyer of Venezuelan crude, may need to strategically reorient their import sources, further buoying the case for Canada to diversify its energy trade," Ercolao at TD Economics said in January.

Trump hailed the deal with Venezuela as 'THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY' in a social media post. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

What questions remain?

The identity of the private operator, who will cover necessary investments and how America's stake in the company breaks down all remains unclear.

The U.S. will get 55 per cent of the company's effective output, but it was not clear what portion of that comes from the ownership stake and how much comes from the right to buy oil at cost.

It's also unclear how the industry will react. Persuading big American oil companies to return to the region could prove a challenge given the political uncertainty and damaged infrastructure.

Chevron, the only U.S. oil company actively producing in Venezuela, declined to comment. Separately from Trump's announcement, Chevron already had been in talks to expand investment in the country. Exxon Mobil also declined to comment.

David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said that on its face the deal could double U.S. oil reserves and reduce dependence on crude oil from Canada and Mexico.

But Oxley, writing in a commentary, cautioned that there are logistical hurdles and he said the value of Venezuela's reserves may have been exaggerated under former president Hugo Chávez.

Even with legal and security guarantees, it is not clear that U.S. oil companies "would be eager to invest," he wrote, noting that "there simply might be more enticing commercial opportunities on offer elsewhere."

World.title: Old soup factory takes on new high-tech life as quantum computing firm gets $195M federal boost
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the echoey void of a gutted Campbell Soup factory in Toronto's west end , Canada's minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation announced the federal government's biggest bet to date on homegrown technology that could revolutionize artificial intelligence, medical science and a host of other key sectors of the economy.

Against the backdrop of the Canada-U.S. trade war, and U.S. President Donald Trump's frequent threats to Canada's sovereignty, Evan Solomon leaned heavily into patriotism as he announced $195 million in repayable federal funding for Toronto-based Xanadu Quantum Technologies.

"This is absolutely a great day for Canada, for Xanadu, and I think for science around the world," he said on Friday. "It shows what Canadians do best: We build."

Solomon said Canada is going to take "big swings" in that endeavour.

"We are going to not just make a bet on solving the biggest problems in the world, and being the best in the world.... We're going to do it big, fearlessly. "

Founded in 2016, Xanadu builds software and quantum computers powered by light instead of electricity. Unlike traditional computers that generate heat as electricity moves through metal wires, Xanadu's chips guide particles of light without electrical friction.

Evan Solomon, Canada's minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation, announces $195 million in repayable federal funding for Toronto-based Xanadu Quantum Technologies on Friday in Toronto. (Submitted by Xanadu Quantum Technologies)

While other quantum computers require aggressive, power-hungry cooling to work, Xanadu's units largely operate at room temperature.

Last June, the company unveiled a breakthrough chip capable of generating error-resistant photonic qubits, the basic unit of information for quantum computers.

"The countries that will have built what's called a fault-tolerant quantum computer would have the capacity to break cybersecurity," Solomon said.

"This is why China, the United States, Europe, everyone's racing. And the best companies are right here in Canada, and the IP is in Canada. So, from a sovereign national security point of view, this technology is absolutely critical."

'Like riding a rocket'

Xanadu held the announcement inside a former Campbell's Soup factory in Toronto, where the company plans to set up advanced manufacturing for its fault-tolerant utility-scale photonic quantum computers. The 158,000-square-foot facility is expected to cost $893 million and employ 275 workers.

"If digital computing is like galloping on a horse, quantum computing is like riding a rocket," Solomon said. "It's that much quicker."

In 2023, the federal government launched its $360-million National Quantum Strategy. Friday's $195-million repayable financing pledge to Xanadu represents its largest single financial commitment to manufacturing quantum technology.

Xanadu CEO Christian Weedbrook says the federal money will bolster the company's presence in Canada. (Submitted by Xanadu Quantum Technologies)

Friday's announcement ranks among the government's top single-company investments in Canada's tech sector . One of the largest was in 2024, when the government provided a $2.14-billion loan to Ottawa-based satellite operator Telesat .

In March, Xanadu announced negotiations with the federal government and the province of Ontario for as much as $390 million in combined financial support to establish advanced semiconductor and photonic manufacturing capabilities in Canada.

Xanadu CEO Christian Weedbrook said on Friday that up to $195 million in funding is "still being discussed" with Ontario's government, describing the talks as "final negotiations and discussions."

The company said Friday's announcement represents Ottawa's full share. Unlike a traditional loan, there's no fixed date for repayment. The money will come from Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's Strategic Response Fund, which provided $40 million to Xanadu in 2023 .

'Obligations to keep the jobs here'

Weedbrook, who is originally from Australia, says the money will bolster his company's presence in Canada.

"A building that once fed Canadians will now help the technology of the next generation," he said. "Where we are today will allow us to do most of this work here in Canada, in Toronto."

In May, the U.S. government agreed to invest about $2 billion US in nine quantum companies.

Xanadu is growing its footprint south of the border. In 2025, it secured partnerships with the U.S. Department of War and the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory. The company also works with big-name U.S. firms like Lockheed Martin and chipmaker AMD.

"I think there's obligations to keep the jobs here for some time," said Amy Karam, a business consultant and fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.

"By having the government have a seat at the table in terms of business decision-making, I think that is one way that we as a country can really be more involved, or more part of encouraging companies to stay. Just funding and doing research and creating talent, it's not enough anymore."

Xanadu plans to name its 158,000-square-foot photonics hub, shown here in a digital rendering, after the popular Christopher Nolan film, Inception. (Submitted by Xanadu Quantum Technologies)

In March, Xanadu dual-listed its shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange and the tech-heavy Nasdaq. The latter raises the company's profile among U.S. investors, as its stock trades next to household names like Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia.

"It's a big challenge to get companies to stay here," said Karam.

"If you look at the Global Innovation Index, we are slipping drastically," she said.

"We need to do some serious catch-up. We need to take our global technology leadership back, and I have the confidence that this government knows this, sees this and is executing accordingly."

Matthew da Mota is a senior policy researcher at the Canadian SHIELD Institute. The Toronto-based think-tank was launched by BlackBerry co-founder Jim Balsillie to modernize public policy on tech and national security and safeguard Canadian intellectual property.

From developing new pharmaceutical drugs to cybersecurity, da Mota said Xanadu's work could actually be dangerous in the wrong hands.

The IBM Quantum System Two quantum computer is pictured during the inauguration at the IBM-Euskadi Quantum Computational Center in the Basque Foundation for Science Ikerbasque headquarters in the Spanish Basque city of San Sebastian on Oct. 14. (Ander Gillenea/AFP/Getty Images)

"It allows for really, really fast processing, really, really fast computation and doing multiple things at once in a way that we weren't able to do with traditional computing. It allows for the potential to break existing encryption," he said.

"That's very dangerous for Canada, and for allies, but it's also something that can be an extremely powerful tool for cyber security long-term."

WATCH | What a new generation of chip could do in quantum computing: Why Google's Willow chip could be a quantum computing game changer | Duration 6:59 Google said that it has overcome a key challenge in quantum computing with a new generation of Willow chip, solving a computing problem in five minutes that would take a classical computer more time than the history of the universe.

Speaking to reporters, Solomon downplayed the potential risk of the government making a concentrated bet on a single company pioneering an emerging technology.

"Unless we are at the frontier with Canadian companies on quantum computing, we will be vulnerable in the future," he said.

"It is vital for this country from a security point of view, from a science point of view, from an economic point of view, to make sure that the best companies in the world are here in Canada."

World.title: Canadian women's volleyball team qualifies for Olympics for 1st time since 1996
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Mission accomplished.

Top-ranked Canada earned a coveted spot in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics on Saturday with a victory over the host Dominican Republic in the championship match of the women's volleyball NORCECA Continental Qualifier.

Canada, coached by Giovanni Guidetti and assistants Carolyn O'Dwyer, Vincenzo Mallia and TJ Sanders, won the best-of-five final in four games against the fourth-ranked DR squad — 25-15, 20-25, 25-23, 25-14. The team went 5-0 in the qualifying tournament.

It's Canada's fourth appearance at the Olympics and first since 1996. Canada tied for ninth at the 1996 Atlanta Games.

"I don't think I can put it into words how this feels," said Alexa Gray, who was on the team when it attempted to qualify for the 2024 Games. "I started on the National Team in 2017, and this has been my lifelong dream. We've just come so far since that time.

"We were so, so close last quad and we were heartbroken. I'm just so proud of how we came out today; it was a tough environment, but this team means everything to me and I'm just so happy to represent Canada. So overjoyed!"

Gray and opposite Kiera Van Ryk led Canada's scoring effort with 22 points apiece. Dominican Republic put on a fight in front of their home crowd, but Canada led in attack points 56-40, blocks 8-7 and aces 8-3. Canada, however, gave away more points to errors (27-23).

Veteran setter Brie Fransen recognized the hard work by the team: "It's so surreal. I'm so proud of the team and staff of how much we have battled through. We deserve this and it's such an amazing feeling to feel the reward of all the work."

Before securing an Olympic berth, Canada captured its first-ever NORCECA Continental Championship, defeating the Americans in Wednesday's final.

"I cannot ask for anything better," said Guidetti who credited the hard work of the athletes and staff. "We had two goals in the start of the season — reach the VNL (Volleyball Nations League) finals and qualify for Los Angeles. This team did both and I'm extremely happy."

World.title: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith to meet with U.S. officials next week amid trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is set to meet with U.S. officials next week, after recently saying she wants to see Canada double down on diplomacy and avoid any further escalations of their trade war.

Smith's press secretary, Sam Blackett, said the premier had a previously planned personal trip to the United States but will take time out to speak with the officials, alongside Alberta's senior U.S. representative, Nathan Cooper.

Blackett said in a statement Friday that they will meet with the commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Tourist Development, the head of the Nashville Chamber of Commerce and the CEO of the Nashville Convention & Visitors Corp.

Smith said Wednesday after Canada-U.S. trade talks fell apart last week that the United States had "no excuse for their behaviour" but that she didn't think Canada could win through "brute force."

She said Canadians officials need to keep telling their American counterparts that tariffs are destructive and promise to help once they are reversed.

"These efforts include Alberta's participation in organizations like the Council of State Governments (CSG) Midwest, with MLA Jennifer Johnson serving as Alberta's representative, and other U.S. missions including MLA Shane Getson's upcoming mission to the Ports-to-Plains conference in Del Rio, Texas," Blackett said.

Johnson, a backbencher in Smith's United Conservative caucus, is expected to be joined next week at the U.S. organization's annual Midwestern Legislative Conference by six members of Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe's caucus.

Saskatchewan is a full member of the Council of State Governments Midwest, while Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario are affiliate members.

The Alberta government said lawmakers from 11 U.S. states are to attend the conference, which runs in Saint Paul, Minn., from Sunday to Wednesday. It said Johnson will be advocating for Alberta's interests and shared priorities around energy, trade and agriculture.

Saskatchewan Agriculture Minister David Marit said Wednesday he's among those heading to the conference.

He said he attended another conference last month in Wisconsin, where everyone supported continuing with the Canada-U.S.-Mexico trade agreement.

"I would say that from an agriculture perspective, a lot of the states are onside," Marit said.

Also attending from Saskatchewan are Rural Health Minister Lori Carr, legislature Speaker Todd Goudy and three Saskatchewan Party backbenchers.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.

World.content:
