What the exchange involved

Around 60 soldiers were transported on Thursday, 27 August, to Niger, a Malian security source told the AFP news agency. They were exchanged for Inkinane Ag Attaher and for individuals allegedly linked to JNIM, al-Qaeda’s affiliate in the Sahel.

A second security source said Niger’s government directly oversaw the agreement. Al Jazeera reported the swap on 29 August, and the FLA said some of its own members held in Malian prisons were also freed under the deal.

The FLA, or Azawad Liberation Front, is a Tuareg-led separatist coalition fighting for a northern homeland it calls Azawad. Mali’s military government brands it a terrorist group, a label the FLA rejects.

Who Inkinane Ag Attaher is

Ag Attaher is a former Malian army officer who deserted and joined the Tuareg rebellion. He was a founding member of the MNLA, the movement that led the 2012 uprising, and an adviser to its leader Bilal Ag Acharif before emerging as a prominent figure in the FLA.

He was arrested on the night of 3-4 April 2025 near the border between Niger and Nigeria. Bamako accused him of organising kamikaze-drone training for FLA fighters, coordinating deadly attacks inside Mali and serving as the movement’s international go-between.

FLA spokesman Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane welcomed the release on Facebook. He wished Ag Attaher “courage, strength and serenity for the continuation of the struggle.”

A summer of quiet deals

This is the second such exchange in a week. On 23 August the FLA freed about 20 Malian soldiers in another prisoner swap, and earlier releases in the conflict have involved al-Qaeda-linked fighters and even captured Russian mercenaries.

Algeria, which hosted Mali’s failed 2015 peace accord, has reportedly been involved in mediating the releases. Malian Prime Minister General Abdoulaye Maiga recently travelled to Algiers to restore high-level contacts after months of friction between the two neighbours.

The deals are striking because Bamako publicly refuses to negotiate with groups it calls terrorists. In practice, the swaps show back-channels keep working while the fighting goes on.

The war the swap sits inside

Mali’s conflict escalated sharply on 25 April, when the FLA and JNIM launched coordinated attacks across the country, the largest offensive since 2012. Defence Minister Sadio Camara, an architect of the junta’s turn to Russia, was killed in an attack on the garrison town of Kati outside Bamako.

Two days later Russia’s Africa Corps, the state-run force that replaced the Wagner Group in Mali, confirmed it had withdrawn from Kidal alongside the Malian army. The FLA has held the city since, and the two groups struck army positions again on 4 July, from Anefis and Aguelhok to a prison at Kéniéroba near the capital.

Russia began airlifting weapons to Bamako in early July to prop up the junta of General Assimi Goïta. French military estimates cited by the BBC put the remaining Africa Corps contingent at roughly 2,500 fighters.

What is still unverified

The central figures rest on unnamed security sources speaking to AFP, and Mali’s government had not publicly confirmed the exchange at the time of writing. The number of JNIM-linked individuals included in the deal is also unclear.

Accounts differ on who arrested Ag Attaher in April 2025. AFP reports say Nigerian security forces; regional security trackers credited Nigerien forces, and neither country has detailed the operation publicly.

Frequently asked questions

What did Mali’s rebels get for freeing 60 soldiers? The FLA received Inkinane Ag Attaher, a former army officer turned prominent rebel figure, plus individuals allegedly linked to the al-Qaeda affiliate JNIM. The FLA also said some of its members held in Malian prisons were freed. Who mediated the Mali prisoner exchange? A security source said Niger’s government directly oversaw the swap, which took place on Nigerien soil. Algeria has reportedly helped mediate the recent releases, and Mali’s prime minister recently visited Algiers to reopen high-level talks. What is the FLA in Mali? The Azawad Liberation Front is a Tuareg-led separatist coalition formed in late 2024 from northern armed movements. It fights for an independent or autonomous homeland called Azawad and has held the city of Kidal since April. Is Mali’s government negotiating with the rebels? Officially no; the junta labels both the FLA and JNIM terrorists and rules out talks. But two prisoner swaps in one week, overseen by Niger and reportedly encouraged by Algeria, show working back-channels exist.

World.title: M23 Counteroffensive Shakes Congo’s South Kivu Hills
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Rio Times · Africa

M23 rebels have launched a counteroffensive in Kalehe territory, in the northern hills of South Kivu, and heavy fighting with pro-government forces is still under way. The rebel push has reversed most of the gains the Congolese army claimed in the area earlier this month, according to the Critical Threats Congo War Security Review of 28 August.

M23, formally the March 23 Movement, is a Congolese rebel group that says it defends ethnic Tutsi communities and that, with its Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC) partner, has held the region’s two main cities, Goma and Bukavu, since early 2025.

The road from Kavumu to Kalehe, in South Kivu’s contested Kalehe territory. (Photo: MONUSCO Photos, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Where the Fighting Is

The clashes are concentrated in the Ziralo groupement of Kalehe’s Buhavu chiefdom, in the highlands west of Lake Kivu. Local civil society and administrative sources told Kivu Morning Post that AFC/M23 fighters seized Ku Kivocat/Katenderi, Tushunguti, Matutira and Mutale in mid-August, plus the village of Kashihe in the neighboring Mubuku groupement.

Radio Okapi reported heavy artillery fire around Kusisa, on the Igali axis. The fighting has also spilled north into the Ufamandu I groupement of southern Masisi, across the provincial line in North Kivu, around the localities of Remeka and Kashovu.

Civil society groups warn that a further rebel advance could threaten Wazalendo militia positions along the Mianda-Lulere-Kalamo axis. That would open the way deeper into Kalehe’s interior.

Who Is Fighting Whom

The pro-government side is the Congolese army, the FARDC, fighting alongside Wazalendo militias, whose name means “patriots” in Swahili. In early August this coalition went on the offensive and claimed the localities of Chambombo, Shanje, Lumbishi, Kavumu-Luzirantaka and Numbi.

The M23 counterattack came days later, around 15 to 18 August. Local sources told Radio Okapi the rebels retook control of much of the Ziralo area, undoing the army’s claimed gains.

Civilians Pay the Price

At least four people, among them a mother and her two children, were killed as clashes intensified around Kusisa in mid-August, Radio Okapi reported, citing local sources. Four Congolese soldiers were also wounded.

A week earlier, the army said M23 shelling killed three civilians, including a woman and her two children, in the village of Bunje. The rebels did not comment on that accusation.

Hundreds of families have fled toward neighboring Masisi, and villages on both sides of the front line are emptying. The United Nations says South Kivu was Congo’s biggest displacement hotspot in July, with some 55,500 households newly uprooted, and Kalehe was among the worst-hit territories.

The Wider War

M23 swept through eastern Congo in early 2025, taking Goma in January and Bukavu in February. It still holds both cities and runs parallel administrations there, while fighting burns on across Masisi, Rutshuru and Walikale in North Kivu and in the highlands of Fizi and Mwenga further south.

Government forces re-entered the strategic lakeside city of Uvira in January, after the rebels withdrew under international pressure. It remains the government’s most significant territorial recovery of the war.

Peace Tracks Move Slowly

The Doha process produced a framework peace deal in November and terms for a ceasefire monitoring mechanism on 2 February, with a first UN verification mission deploying to Uvira. But implementation is partial, and fresh bombardments were reported on 24 August at Nyaruhinga, near Minembwe, days before a verification mission was expected in the area.

The United States hosts a separate track between Congo and Rwanda. Washington has demanded that M23 meet its Doha obligations, including pulling back from Uvira.

At home, President Felix Tshisekedi launched a three-month national dialogue on 27 August. His conditions bar groups that fight the state by arms, hold territory or act for a foreign power, which effectively shuts out the AFC/M23, and he ruled out any general amnesty for war crimes.

Rwanda’s Role

UN Security Council Resolution 2808, adopted in December, says M23 operates “with the direct support and participation of the Rwanda Defence Forces”. UN expert panels have documented Rwandan troop deployments and support to the rebels for years.

Kigali denies backing M23 and says its security concerns stem from the FDLR, a Rwandan Hutu militia based in eastern Congo. The Congolese government calls the rebellion a Rwandan aggression.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is M23?

M23, the March 23 Movement, is a Congolese rebel group that says it defends ethnic Tutsi communities. With its AFC alliance it has held Goma and Bukavu, eastern Congo’s two biggest cities, since early 2025.

Where exactly is the new fighting?

In the Ziralo groupement of Kalehe territory, in northern South Kivu, with spillover into southern Masisi in North Kivu. Villages including Tushunguti, Matutira, Mutale and Kashihe changed hands in mid-August.

Is there a peace process?

Yes, but it is fragile. The Doha talks produced a ceasefire monitoring mechanism in February, the US mediates between Congo and Rwanda, and Kinshasa opened a national dialogue on 27 August, yet fighting has never fully stopped.

Sources: Critical Threats – Congo War Security Review, 28 August 2026, Radio Okapi – clashes at Kusisa, Kalehe, Radio Okapi – M23 counteroffensive and displacement, Kivu Morning Post – AFC/M23 retakes localities in Kalehe, ReliefWeb – July 2026 displacement report, Reuters – UN ceasefire monitoring mission to Uvira

World.title: Can Belize feed, power, fund, train and govern itself? Here is the scorecard
World.content:
Can Belize feed, power, fund, train and govern itself? Here is the scorecard

By Horace Palacio:

Forty five years ago we raised a flag and the world called us independent.

This column has spent a full year walking the country beneath that flag, auditing the wiring, the pantry, the ledger, the classrooms, the contracts. Today I gather it all into one place, because scattered diagnoses are complaints, but gathered, they become a blueprint.

So let us begin where every serious project begins, with a definition. What does a strong and independent nation actually mean? Not flags. Not anthems. Not seats at the United Nations. We have owned all three for forty five years while our Prime Minister flew to plead for electricity and a foreign war priced our dinner.

Here is the true definition, and I ask you to keep it forever. Independence is the power to say no.

Count a nation’s no’s and you have measured its sovereignty exactly. Can it say no to a predatory loan, because its books balance? No to a bad investor, because it can build alone? No to a neighbor’s pressure, because its lights are its own? No to the recruiter emptying its classrooms, because home offers better? A dependent nation must whisper yes to everything, and smile. Every pillar we build adds one more no to Belize’s vocabulary. That is the entire national project in a single sentence.

And strength, understand, is not a resource. It is an architecture. Nations drowning in oil have collapsed while a rocky island with nothing built the strongest state in Asia, and a broke, corrupt Georgia rebuilt itself in a decade on structure alone. I gave you the image long ago, the bucket and its holes. Belize was never short of water. So the question is never what we have. It is what we have built to hold it.

Very well. What must be built? Five things. And because this column trusts numbers over speeches, each arrives as a test with a figure attached, measurable, publishable, impossible to orate around.

Test one, the Table Test. Can Belize feed itself? A farming nation that imports its food has a foreign hand on its dinner table and a permanent leak in its foreign exchange. The number to publish, the share of the national food basket grown on Belizean soil. Every school plate sourced from Belizean farms, every imported crate replaced, moves it. A country that feeds itself has earned its first great no.

Test two, the 8pm Test, which readers know by heart. Can Belize keep its own lights on at evening peak, without anyone’s permission? On August 25 the answer was no, by nineteen megawatts, and the whole country marked the exam in the dark. The number, in-country capacity available at peak versus peak demand, published quarterly. The rooftops, the dispatched dams, the batteries, the auctions, all of it exists to move one ratio past one hundred percent. A country that powers itself has earned its second no.

Test three, the Ledger Test. Can Belize pay its own way? Today we buy roughly ten dollars from the world for every one we sell, and the gap is bridged by tourism, remittances and borrowing, three bridges we do not control. The number, exports as a share of imports, climbing year on year, with the invisible western trade finally counted and the champions, the cacao, the pepper sauces, the seafood, the digital services, backed like national teams. A country that earns its keep can say no to any lender on earth.

Test four, the Staircase Test. Can Belize staff itself? Half our population is under twenty seven, the one treasure the aging rich world cannot buy, and it will come recruiting. The test is whether the Belizean can climb at home, or whether the upstairs jobs stay imported while our young board planes. Two numbers, published together, the work permit register, which is secretly our most honest education report card, shrinking, and the count of young Belizeans certified each year in the exact skills that register names. A country that trains and keeps its children owns its future, and can say no to the recruiters.

Test five, the Daylight Test. Can Belize govern itself in the open? This is the pillar beneath the pillars, because every other test is funded through the public purse, and a leaking purse fails them all. The numbers, every contract on the promised portal, a whistleblower law passed, a professional public service restored, the megawatt and procurement scorecards published on schedule. Sunlight is not one reform among many. It is the load-bearing wall. A country that governs in daylight can say no to its own worst temptations, which is the hardest no of all.

Now the insight that turns five tests into one machine. These pillars compound. Pass the 8pm Test and cheap power makes the factory viable, which moves the Ledger. Pass the Ledger Test and foreign exchange steadies the dollar and funds the classrooms, which moves the Staircase. Pass the Staircase Test and skilled Belizeans fill the upstairs jobs and build the farms and firms that feed the Table. And Daylight guards the money flowing through all of it. Strength is not five projects. It is one engine with five cylinders, and every cylinder we fire makes the next one cheaper to build. This is why despair is innumerate. We do not need five miracles. We need one honest start, anywhere on the wheel.

So here is the proposal, concrete enough to demand by name. Let Belize adopt a National Scorecard of Independence, the five numbers above, published every quarter, one page, no adjectives, entrenched beyond any single administration. Because this column proved it with three landslides’ worth of history, elections change the occupants and never the architecture. The scorecard is architecture. Let every government, red or blue, inherit it, answer to it, and campaign on moving it. Let the question at every debate shrink to five lines. What did you do to the numbers?

And beneath the tests, always, the foundation the state cannot legislate, the Belizean. Every column this year came home to the same door. The household that owns instead of only earning. The worker who treats hard seasons as training. The voter who is also a citizen on the seventeen hundred ordinary days. The builder who pools seventy five cents with two friends. Nations are the sum of their households plus their architecture, nothing more, and nothing that grand was ever built by spectators.

Forty five years ago, independence was handed to us in a single glorious day, the easy kind, the flag kind.

The other kind, the kind that keeps lights on and tables full and children home, is never handed to anyone. It is built, test by test, number by number, no by hard-earned no.

So let us name the date, as this column always does. Belize at fifty, five years from now. Five tests, five published numbers, all five moving in the right direction by the time we light the golden jubilee.

The flag we raised in 1981 tells the world who we are.

The scorecard will tell us what we have become.

Raise both, Belize.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: BDF soldier gets full disclosure in $4,600 theft case; trial set for November
World.content:
BDF soldier gets full disclosure in $4,600 theft case; trial set for November

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize Defence Force soldier accused of stealing thousands of dollars in clothing and an Apple MacBook has received full disclosure in her case and is set to stand trial in November.

Marilou Elizabeth Aldana, 35, appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannin Dennison in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday afternoon, where she was provided with 12 pages of disclosure.

Aldana is accused of stealing assorted clothing valued at $4,000 and an Apple MacBook valued at $600, for a total value of $4,600.

The alleged theft is said to have occurred on June 26, 2026.

Aldana was first arraigned on June 29 and was granted bail in the sum of $2,500.

She remains out on bail and is due back in court on November 13, 2026, when her trial is scheduled to begin.

World.title: ‘Ah tired ah jail, tired ah di hole’: Accused burglar tries to change plea to guilty to get out early but still in jail because he still says he didn’t do it
World.content:
‘Ah tired ah jail, tired ah di hole’: Accused burglar tries to change plea to guilty to get out early but still in jail because he still says he didn’t do it

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man who told the court he wanted to plead guilty because he was tired of being in prison had his plea rejected after insisting that he never burglarized the property in question.

Earl Sanchez, 45, of the Morning Glory Street area, appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday on a charge of burglary.

Sanchez has been on remand since October 2025 after being unable to meet bail of $3,000 plus one surety in the same amount.

During Friday’s appearance, Sanchez told the court that the pressure of being incarcerated, including time spent in the “hole,” had taken a toll on him and asked to change his plea from not guilty to guilty.

“I wah change meh plea to guilty. Ah tired ah jail,” Sanchez told the court.

The prosecution’s allegations were then read to him. Police allege that at around 10:30 p.m. on October 27, 2025, Sanchez entered a home through an open metal door and stole a bicycle valued at $350, a black and orange pump valued at $35 and a Bluetooth speaker valued at $50.

After hearing the allegations, however, Sanchez told the court, “I neva burglarized deh place,” while reportedly admitting that he stole the bicycle.

Senior Magistrate Dennison explained that the court could not accept a guilty plea simply because Sanchez wanted to get the matter over with if he was not admitting to committing the offence. His proposed guilty plea was therefore treated as equivocal and a not guilty plea was maintained.

Sanchez remains eligible for bail but has so far been unable to meet the $3,000 bail requirement. His bail conditions include staying at least 100 yards away from the complainant and not interfering with the complainant.

Unable to post bail on Friday, Sanchez was further remanded to the Belize Central Prison until November 23, 2026, when his case is scheduled for trial.

World.title: PI for interdicted cop accused of Hattieville double murder adjourned to September
World.content:
PI for interdicted cop accused of Hattieville double murder adjourned to September

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Preliminary Inquiry for interdicted police officer Orin Justin Williams, accused of killing his former mother-in-law and her twin brother in Hattieville, has been adjourned until September 18, 2026.

Williams appeared before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, when his PI was scheduled to take place. However, the matter could not proceed because the Magistrate who has carriage of the case was unavailable.

Williams was further remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

The accused was previously provided with 160 pages of disclosure on May 6, followed by an additional 42 pages and 10 DVDs on May 18 as part of the prosecution’s case against him.

Williams is charged with the murders of 57-year-old Paula Belisle, his former mother-in-law, and her twin brother, Paul Esquilliano.

The siblings were shot and killed at around 2:00 p.m. on September 15, 2025, in the American New Site area of Hattieville Village.

Williams is due back in court on September 18 for the rescheduled Preliminary Inquiry.

World.title: International News: Ecuador court sentences former President Lenín Moreno to 5 years for bribery
World.content:
International News: Ecuador court sentences former President Lenín Moreno to 5 years for bribery

By Zoila Palma: An Ecuadorian court has found former President Lenín Moreno guilty of bribery in a corruption case linked to the construction of the country’s largest hydroelectric plant, the Coca Codo Sinclair facility.

Moreno, 73, was sentenced to five years in prison and permanently barred from holding public office. Prosecutors alleged that Chinese state-owned company Sinohydro paid about $76.1 million in bribes between 2009 and 2018 through fraudulent consulting contracts connected to the project.

Moreno’s wife and daughter, along with two brothers and their wives, were also convicted and sentenced to two and a half years in prison.

Cai Runguo, China’s former ambassador to Ecuador, received a five-year sentence. Prosecutors alleged that more than $1 million reached Moreno and his relatives while he was vice president between 2007 and 2013.

Moreno, who served as Ecuador’s president from 2017 to 2021, has consistently denied the allegations.

World.title: Taiwan veterans affairs delegation visits Belize
World.content:
Taiwan veterans affairs delegation visits Belize

By Zoila Palma: A delegation from Taiwan’s Veterans Affairs Council, led by Deputy Minister Chin-Kuang Chen, visited Belize from August 24 to 26 as part of efforts to strengthen cooperation and people-to-people ties between the two countries.

Upon arrival at the Philip Goldson International Airport, the delegation was welcomed by representatives of the Taiwan Embassy in Belize and the ROC Veterans Association in Belize.

During the visit, the delegation met with Taiwan’s Ambassador to Belize Amino Chi and held discussions with members of the ROC Veterans Association.

They also visited the Belize Ex-Services League, where they exchanged experiences on veterans’ services and support.

The visit provided an opportunity for both sides to share perspectives on veterans’ affairs while further strengthening the longstanding friendship and close people-to-people connections between Taiwan and Belize.

World.title: Santa Elena shooting leaves Rasheed Hyde dead
World.content:
Santa Elena shooting leaves Rasheed Hyde dead

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A man has been shot and killed in Santa Elena Town, Cayo District.

The deceased has been identified as Rasheed Hyde.

Reports of the shooting reached our newsroom earlier today. Sources confirmed that one person had died at the scene.

Details on the circumstances surrounding the shooting are still emerging.

Police have not yet released an official statement.

This is a developing story and we will bring further details as they become available.

World.title: Homeless Stann Creek man fined $105 for crack pipe
World.content:
Homeless Stann Creek man fined $105 for crack pipe

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 39-year-old man who told the court he is homeless was fined $105 after pleading guilty to possession of a pipe used for smoking drugs.

Rugero Mazariego, originally from the Stann Creek Valley area, appeared before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday morning.

Police said Mazariego was found earlier that day with a white metal pipe measuring about three inches in length and fitted with wire mesh. The object was described as being used or adapted for smoking drugs.

Mazariego pleaded guilty to the charge and told the court he would try to change his ways.

“I will try to do better if given the opportunity to do so,” he told the court.

As a first-time offender for the charge, Mazariego was fined $100 plus $5 in court costs. He has until September 30, 2026, to pay the fine or he will serve one month in prison.

World.title: Top class!
World.content:
Highly rated United States teacher recruitment agency is stepping up its search for Jamaican educators, citing their strong classroom management skills, curriculum knowledge, and positive energy as qualities that set them apart from their peers.

A J-1 designated teacher sponsor recognised by the United States Department of State in Washington, DC, the Foreign Academic & Cultural Exchange Services (FACES) recruits educators from around the world and places them in classrooms in South Carolina for periods ranging from three to five years under a cultural exchange programme.

The programme allows participants to bring their professional expertise, academic qualifications, and cultural experiences into American classrooms, while exposing students to the traditions and practices of other countries.

At the same time, teachers gain certifications, professional development, and skills that they can take back to their home countries when they return at the end of the allotted period.

FACES has recruited more than 2,000 teachers over its 27 years of operation. However, Aleksandra Patrascu, communication director at the agency, said Jamaican educators have distinguished themselves and are frequently sought after by schools participating in the programme.

“We’ve found great success with Jamaican teachers due to the great English that they speak. For them, there’s not a lot of language barrier when they get to South Carolina, as opposed to teachers from other parts of the world where the language might be a little bit strange. Jamaican teachers are strongly trained in the curriculum… We’ve had a lot of very successful English teachers from Jamaica,” said Patrascu.

“They are trained in the British curriculum, which is something that was very popular here in South Carolina and that schools loved a lot,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

“Jamaican teachers have very strong classroom management. I’ve had the honour to observe Jamaican teachers in their elementary school classroom and in their Spanish classroom, and you can see that there was a presence in that classroom… I know how hard it can be to be in a classroom with 30 students that you’re trying to mould and model, and Jamaican teachers have done a tremendous job in doing that,” Patrascu

added.

In addition to the Jamaicans’ skills training, she said the island’s proximity to the United States is a bonus because it is easier for the educators to travel home for special events and celebrations to see their family. She added that Jamaicans are also familiar with American culture, making it easier for them to adapt and face less culture shock.

Above all, Patrascu said the positive attitude of Jamaicans is contagious.

“I think it’s something in the air in Jamaica because our Jamaican teachers are very happy. They’re very positive people… They have sunshine in their heart. They’re just happy people. We see that with a lot of the teachers that come from the Caribbean, and we joke that it’s just the sun in the island and the sea air that make people just be a happy individual. They’re happy to be in the classroom, they’re happy with their career, and they’re proud of their career. We’ve experienced nothing but success with Jamaican teachers in our programme,” she told the Sunday Observer.

According to Patrascu, FACES recruited 12 Jamaican teachers this year, while approximately 60 Jamaican educators have participated in the programme over the past 27 years, with some returning to the United States for more than one exchange period.

With continued demand for educators, she said FACES is hoping to recruit even more Jamaican teachers to participate in the programme in a wide range of areas, including elementary education, English, Spanish, physical education, special education, and science.

She boasted that many Jamaican educators have been recognised for their success on the programme, walking away with awards for teacher of the week, month, and year.

Among them is Jermaine Howell, who taught grade five at Golden Spring Primary in St Andrew before joining the programme. He was named teacher of the year at Cedar Fork Elementary School in Morrisville, North Carolina. Camilla Walsh-Reynolds, a Spanish Town educator with 26 years’ experience and a background as a school principal, also serves as international teacher lead at JW Coon Elementary in Cumberland County.

Additionally, Tamar Blair-Robinson, a May Pen, Clarendon native, was honoured as teacher of the month, international teacher of the year, and adviser of the month at Lillington Shawtown Elementary School.

“For an international teacher to be honoured or to be recognised as teacher of the year at their school, that means they did something to stand out from all of the other American and international teachers in that school, and that is huge,” said Patrascu in congratulating the educators.

“That’s why if there’s a chance that we see Jamaican teachers apply, we get super excited and super giddy because we know that there’s other sponsors recruiting from the island and there’s only so many teachers in Jamaica, but they know our programme, they trust us, and we welcome them,” she told the Sunday Observer.

She invited interested individuals to visit the agency’s website facesinc.org to apply to the programme, noting that the application process is free. Once applications are received, an interview will be conducted to assess the educators’ goals and reason for joining the programme. Individuals are also screened, after which their teaching profile will be posted on the company’s website for school districts to assess and select their desired candidate.

Patrascu said FACES covers the air fare for successful candidates, providing them with assistance to secure housing, transportation, and a cellphone with a monthly plan. She stresses that international teachers receive the same benefits as local teachers and are compensated on the same scale.

World.title: Let’s do more business
World.content:
Trinidad and Tobago High Commissioner to Jamaica Deborah Thomas-Felix speaking at the Jamaica Observer Press Club last Friday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

WITH Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago appearing to have moved beyond the trade tensions that once strained their commercial relationship, the twin island republic’s High Commissioner Deborah Thomas-Felix wants to build on that progress by creating stronger business connections, encouraging investment, and opening up more opportunities for companies to enter each other’s markets.

Thomas-Felix said, as Trinidad and Tobago’s high commissioner to Jamaica, her role is to identify opportunities on both sides and bring businesses and other stakeholders together, with the aim of turning both states’ improving relationship into greater commercial activity.

“One of the things I want is to — and I spoke to your Government about it — I want us to have more trade missions. We have a very strong relationship and I want to continue strengthening that relationship, not only in trade and culture and everything, [but] the mark that I leave should be a mark of strengthening and building the relationship that we have,” she said while speaking during a Jamaica Observer Press Club last Friday at the newspaper’s Beechwood Avenue, St Andrew, headquarters.

Her comments come against a history of difficult trade relations between the two Caribbean countries, including complaints from Jamaican exporters about access to the Trinidad and Tobago market and a significant imbalance in merchandise trade. The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding in August 2022 establishing a Trade Complaints Mechanism intended to provide a channel for resolving trade-related problems.

More recently, however, both sides have been emphasising deeper commercial ties. In July 2025, Trinidad and Tobago’s Government said increasing private sector links between the countries were helping to strengthen bilateral and intra-regional trade, while officials committed to further deepening the partnership.

Thomas-Felix said the shift is reflected in Jamaica’s growing presence in the Trinidad and Tobago market. Figures provided to her, she said, showed a substantial increase in Jamaica’s reach between 2019 and 2025.

“From 2019 — the figures from 2019 to 2025 — it seemed to show a 170 per cent increase, particularly in 2025 in terms of Jamaica’s reach into the market. So I would say that some of the issues before would not be issues now,” she said.

The diplomat said Jamaica’s changing economic profile also creates room for the relationship to evolve beyond the traditional movement of manufactured goods.

Thomas-Felix also acknowledged Jamaica’s growing strength in financial and professional services, digital and technology services, and tourism, which she noted is earning the country greater recognition in Trinidad and Tobago and other international markets.

Therefore, she wants greater emphasis placed on helping businesses identify where their strengths can complement those of companies in other countries.

“So not only in Jamaica, throughout the Caribbean and parts of the world, we supply and export manufacturing and energy products…I think that is why there would be an imbalance because, over the years, Trinidad has significantly had a very large manufacturing and energy sector,” she said.

Rather than treating the imbalance as a problem that leaves one country winning and the other losing, Thomas-Felix said both countries should be looking at how they can expand their economic footprint together.

“I don’t think we should ever look at it as one having more and one having less, but how do we help each other to be out there and be large or big in trade. And that’s the way I look at it,” she added.

The figures illustrate the scale of the challenge. Thomas-Felix said Jamaica exported approximately US$36.6 million in merchandise to Trinidad and Tobago in 2024, compared with about US$249.7 million in merchandise flowing in the opposite direction.

But she also pointed to Jamaica’s strength in services, saying the country exported approximately US$5.6 billion in services globally, against imports of about US$3.46 billion, giving it a services trade surplus of roughly US$1.8 billion. She said that strength should form part of the conversation about how Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago can expand their commercial relationship.

That approach is already being reflected in trade missions. A Trinidad and Tobago Manufacturers’ Association trade mission to Jamaica in May 2025 was aimed at expanding market opportunities and identifying investment prospects, with the association describing Jamaica as a significant market for Trinidadian products while also encouraging Jamaican manufacturers to target the Trinidad and Tobago market.

A Jamaican trade mission to Trinidad and Tobago in September 2024 was similarly described as a step towards deepening economic ties by officials there who highlighted opportunities in food, beverages, manufacturing, and investment.

However, Thomas-Felix wants to create relationships that continue after the missions end by putting entrepreneurs, investors, and private sector organisations in contact with one another.

She also wants, when her tenure ends, to leave the bilateral relationship stronger than she found it, with trade forming only one part of a wider network of links between the two countries.

She noted that the relationship cannot be measured solely by government agreements or trade figures. Trinidadians have established lives and careers in Jamaica, while Jamaicans have done the same in Trinidad and Tobago, creating links that run through families, workplaces, education, and culture.

“So the relationship is way beyond government to government, it’s really about people, and we interact through music, we interact in terms of culture, and so I want to really strengthen those bonds and to make sure that if I can spot connections, opportunities, et cetera, that I share it with people in Trinidad and Tobago, because I’m here to advance the interests of Trinidad and Tobago and also share it to the people in Jamaica,” she said.

World.title: More than beauty: Lu Sierra says Jamaican models bring their ‘hunger’ to international markets
World.content:
Lu Sierra.

There is no shortage of beautiful women in the world. But after decades spent strutting across international runways and preparing beauty queens for some of pageantry’s biggest stages, former model and renowned runway coach Lu Sierra believes Jamaican women possess something beauty alone cannot provide — hunger.

For Sierra, who was recently in the island as an international headliner for the inaugural Jamaica Beauty, Fashion & Wellness Week at AC Hotel Kingston, that hunger may very well be Jamaica’s secret weapon.

“The cheekbones, the jawlines and, most importantly, the hunger. I’m telling you right now that in this business, you’ve got to be hungry,” she said. “Modelling is not just something you show up to and say, ‘I thought I could do this because I’m tall.’ Your women come with a sense of ‘I’m hungry’,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

“They want it, and they get that from a generational kind of thing that if you want something, you’ve got to work for it. It won’t be handed to you. Your ladies come knowing that they’ve got to show up, look good, network, and ask questions. They come with a hunger as well as beauty.”

It is high praise from a woman whose career has afforded her a front-row seat to the international fashion and pageant industries.

Known as Runway Lu, Sierra has modelled for the likes of Bill Blass, Escada, Byron Lars, Bob Mackie, B Michael, Cesar Galindo, and Yves Saint Laurent. She has also worked as a muse fit model for fashion houses and designers including Oscar de la Renta, Givenchy, and Patrick Kelly.

Her career eventually expanded beyond walking the runway to teaching other women how to command it. Named Best Coach by the Global Beauty Awards, Sierra has become a runway expert, confidence mentor, and pageant coach whose work has extended to both the Miss USA and Miss Universe competitions.

It is against that international backdrop that Sierra has developed an appreciation for what Jamaican models bring to the table.

“Let’s face it, there are beautiful women everywhere in the world — Ukraine, Russia, Brazil — but Jamaica gives us some beautiful women who are hungry,” she said.

Long before becoming the coach helping other women navigate rejection, Sierra had to manoeuvre her own struggles. She recalled arriving in New York only to have modelling agents repeatedly point out the things they believed she needed to change.

“When I moved to New York, every agent rejected me. They told me, ‘Clear up your skin, lose weight, fix your teeth,’ and all that stuff,” she recalled.

Those experiences helped shape a philosophy she now passes on to the women she mentors: Rejection does not necessarily mean someone does not belong in the industry.

“You have to love what you do,” Sierra stressed. “There has to be something in you that says rejection doesn’t bother me and the word ‘no’ is not an option.”

Sierra’s own experience with rejection has also informed the way she defines beauty. There isn’t, she insists, a single formula as beauty is indeed in the eyes of the beholder.

“In one day I was told I was too skinny, too tall by one designer, not tall enough by another, too black by one designer, and too Puerto Rican by the other. Too pretty by one client and not pretty enough by the other,” she recalled.

For each client, she explained, their assessment was based on what they needed at that particular moment rather than an objective measure of her beauty or worth.

“There is no one thing. As I always tell girls, don’t get upset if they don’t want you, just find someone that does. Get up every day and do that. But that takes a special mentality to get up after rejection and say, ‘Today is a new day, and I’m going in,’ instead of starting to self-medicate.”

Sierra jetted off the island following the conclusion of the Miss Universe Jamaica pageant on Sunday, but not before dropping a few pointers on how pageant organisers can nab a few more titles internationally. For Sierra, the question isn’t whether Jamaica has women capable of competing with the world’s best, it’s a matter of support from the entire industry, especially local designers.

“Jamaica sends us some of the most beautiful women there is, and body — oh Lord!” she exclaimed. “I personally think it’s wardrobe and practising interviews more.”

After getting a first-hand look at local creativity during Jamaica Beauty, Fashion & Wellness Week, Sierra issued a direct challenge to Jamaican designers: Become more involved in outfitting the country’s representatives for the international stage.

“I’m looking forward to seeing what your local designers have to offer the world, and so I hope Jamaica makes this into something that can grow because Miss Jamaica Universe needs some of you designers to dress her,” she said. “When we go to Universe, the girls are dressed to the T. Some of the countries give these girls an outfit to wear. They walk into rehearsals and we’re like, ‘Oh my God!’ They have hand-painted boots, floral jackets that have been painted and things like that.”

“So I’m challenging the Jamaican designers to step up and have Miss Jamaica Universe go there and rock with her own countrymen’s outfit,” she continued.

But Sierra believes clothes are only part of the equation. If Jamaica wants to add more international crowns to its pageant résumé, she believes contestants must also become more comfortable with selling themselves when it matters.

“Your ladies come with a sweetness, kindness, and an island mentality that everyone is family,” she observed. You can be kind, but there has to be a certain sense of business with your answer.”

We teach our ladies in the island not to be boastful,” she continued. “But let me just say to the ladies, conceit is talking about yourself when no one asks. An interview is telling everyone the reason why you should win. It’s like a résumé. Please remember that. We need boss ladies.”

World.title: Not stealing Jamaican teachers
World.content:
Teacher recruitment agency Foreign Academic and Cultural Exchange Services allows participating teachers to stay up to five years on the cultural exchange programme before returning to their home country.

A United States teacher recruitment agency is making it known that, unlike its counterparts, it is not in the business of draining the Jamaican education system of its finest educators, even as the island struggles to keep teachers in its classrooms.

Foreign Academic and Cultural Exchange Services (FACES), a J-1 cultural exchange programme based in South Carolina, said instead its mission is to give the educators international exposure, new teaching techniques and technology-driven skills they can implement when they return to their home country after three to five years.

The agency’s position comes at a time when Jamaican schools are grappling with teacher shortages and migration, particularly in specialised subject areas.

Recent data from the Ministry of Education revealed that 1,185 teachers resigned between September 2024 and August 2025. The figures reflect a decline in teacher resignations compared to 1,517 the previous year. The staffing challenge mainly arises from global demand for teachers.

While some programmes create the opportunity for teachers to reside permanently in their host country, FACES Communication Director Alexandra Patrascu said it is not in the business of stealing teachers.

“We’ve heard of this interpretation, and we’ve heard of these types of programmes that, to be honest with you, they’re hurting us as sponsors as well. There are many ways that a teacher can stay here [in the United States] after the five years, but it’s not through our programme. Our cultural exchange programme that we sponsor clearly states that a teacher can stay up to five years, and they need to return for at least two years to their country and then they can come back for five years,” said Patrascu.

“There are other programmes that sponsor more pathways towards being a citizen and being here permanently. Those programmes hurt our programme, because the whole purpose of the cultural exchange is not there anymore if somebody’s coming here to stay. Our programme, our J-1 programme, the goal behind it is to bring back the teachers in Jamaica with the US experience, with more technology experience, and with a global teaching experience. The goal is not to steal teachers from Jamaica. We want, and we demand that our Jamaican teachers return to their country because if they don’t, they’re hurting our programme,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Patrascu said since its establishment in 1987, the agency has recruited more than 2,000 educators from across the globe. Of that number, approximately 60 teachers have been from Jamaica. She said the agency particularly loves to work with Jamaican teachers because of their ability to control a classroom, their knowledge of the curriculum and their positive spirits, but more than anything, they want the educators to go back and apply what they learned in the local education system.

She pointed to a Jamaican Spanish teacher who did just that, as proof that the programme is effective in building the local education system.

“I had this amazing Spanish teacher join our programme that I was training, and she went back to Jamaica, and now she works in her school. I keep in touch with her from now and then, and she keeps on saying, ‘I can’t believe how much I’ve learned from the programme in the United States. I was able to make my classroom so much better when I returned due to the things that I’ve learned in South Carolina.’ That makes my heart very proud,” said Patrascu.

She added that she is grateful to every participant who came on the programme and applied what they learned in their local schools, stressing the need to protect and enrich education systems across the country.

“If they [educators] don’t go back, they hurt us, they hurt the Jamaican population, and they hurt the Jamaican Government. That’s not something that we want,” said Patrascu, urging educators to give back to their country.

World.title: LATTIMORE’S LEGACY
World.content:
Late former national footballer Keith Lattimore

Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts has paid tribute to former national player, coach, and administrator Keith Lattimore, describing him as someone who remained deeply committed to football even in his later years.

Lattimore, who died at age 75 on Saturday, was a national player in the 1970s and went on to make significant contributions to the sport at the club and national levels.

“It’s always sad when you hear of the passing of a sports icon. I remember Lattimore well; in fact, the last time I saw him it was in the Spanish Town area, and we had a brief conversation and he told me that he’s trying to resuscitate a football club in a community where he lives, and even though he was getting on in years he still had the love, the passion, and the commitment to ensuring that young men get an opportunity to play football,” said Ricketts.

“So I am just deeply saddened at the passing of someone whom I would have known well and someone who would significantly have contributed to the sport of football, not just at the club level, but certainly at the national level,” Ricketts said.

“May his soul rest in peace as we sincerely offer our condolences to his family members and close friends,” he said.

Lattimore was one of the prominent footballers of his generation, alongside his brother Arthur Lattimore. He played for Liguanea FC, YMCA, FC Nascimento, and Electro Cap in St Thomas.

A talented striker, Lattimore was also known for his long throws, which fans likened to corners.

He later ventured into coaching and led Portmore Strikers to the Sherwin Williams Women’s Premier League title in 2002. He also played for RJR 720 Kickers, winning the Tourers Masters League.

Lattimore worked as a sports officer at the Institute of Sports (InSports) until his retirement, and was instrumental in the development of the Primary Schools Athletics Championships.

His career spanned playing, coaching, and administration, with his contribution to Jamaican sport extending well beyond the football field.

World.title: Youth Praise to raise funds for community initiatives
World.content:
Gospel artiste Johnmark Wiggan (right) performs at last year’s staging of Youth Praise.

Gospel artistes Prince Saj, Orville Sutherland, Treze-Gaye Smith, Donielle Anderson, and youth ministers from Church of the United Missions (COTUM); Christian Fellowship World Outreach; Union Baptist Church from Pennsylvania, USA; and Waltham Park Road New Testament Church Of God are scheduled to perform at the fourth staging of Youth Praise on October 2.

The event, which seeks to raise funds for the COTUM Youth Ministry, will take place at the Waltham Park New Testament Church of God. According to organisers, it provides a safe and spiritually sound platform for young people to express their faith and talent as well as immerse themselves in worship irrespective of church affiliation.

In an interview with the Jamaica Observer, Youth praise director and youth leader, Kay-Ann Swaby, spoke about the initiative and its growth since its first staging in 2023.

“COTUM Youth Ministry has been impacting many young lives, especially young males who are considered “at-risk” youths. We currently have a 17:4 male-to-female ratio and Youth Praise is our main fund-raiser to fund the youth initiatives and programmes to help impact these youths and help us to reach more young men. Through Youth Praise we offer full sponsorship to youths from different communities to attend Christian Youth Camps we have seen the impact: educational support — community youths now go to school five days per week instead of two or three days, scholarships and grants; social exposure — engaging them in spaces that cultivate good values and purpose-driven activities; sports programmes; youth development workshops. Our goal is to maintain an active presence and an influential voice that overshadows the negative influences in the lives of the youths,” Swaby explained.

She added, “We also use this initiative to share the gospel with the youths through the arts and music because Youth Praise is a youth-targeted event reaching youths from all over.”

Swaby states that the event has grown since its first staging three years ago.

“Our first event was well supported. At that time, it was our first youth concert in probably over two decades. The event was planned and executed in less than six weeks, no social media promotion — just word of mouth and a voice-over recording circulating to a few contacts — and we had over 400 people in attendance. The church was full to capacity, and we even had people standing outside. And now, entering our fourth consecutive staging, Youth Praise has grown on a significantly wider scale — from a local church initiative into a transformative community event. We have youth ministries reaching out to have their young people minister at Youth Praise; we also have gospel artistes requesting to be on the line-up. The trajectory has accelerated impressively,” Swaby disclosed.

“The high point over the period has been the energy each year, which is unmatched,” said Swaby. “Experiencing the youths channelling their energy into purpose and creativity as they honour the Lord with their talent/gift, worship together, and enjoy the presence of God whilst ministering and supporting each other. The realness of the artistes — over the years in the midst of their ministry they have shared their personal stories (testimonies), level and relate with the youths whilst encouraging them to stay with God or give their lives to Jesus Christ.”

DJ Tarik Pryce will provide recorded music prior to the performance of the gospel acts, and radio personality Ava-Gay Black Blair is the host.

Said Swaby, “You can expect to be richly blessed by the youths! Expect a euphoric evening of praise and worship from beginning to end. Be ready for the move of God; Expect prizes and surprises.”

World.title: Former national footballer Keith Lattimore dead at 75
World.content:
Former national player and footballing icon Keith Lattimore has died. He was 75.

Lattimore was one of the legendary football players of his generation, alongside his brother Arthur Lattimore. He played for Liguanea FC and was known for his long throws, as well as being a very talented striker.

Lattimore ventured into coaching and led Portmore Striker to the Sherwin Williams Women’s Premier League crown in 2002. He played for RJR 720 Kickers, winning the Tourers Masters League.

He also worked at the Institute of Sports (INSPORTS) as a sports officer until he retired.

World.title: Cooper’s Pen pledge
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (second left) in dialogue with Cooper’s Pen resident Debbie Lewis (second right) during a tour of the community on Friday. Looking on are (from left) minister of state in the Office of the Prime Minister Senator Abka Fitz-Henley; Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett; and Member of Parliament for Trelawny Northern Tova Hamilton. Photo: Horace Hines

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has given a commitment to “personally oversee” the relocation of residents of Cooper’s Pen whose houses were demolished during a dispute over privately owned land, saying he may have to invoke emergency powers to get the process started by December.

Residents will be provided with a relocation grant to replace belongings damaged during the eviction, but they will have to pay for the land and utilities once they are resettled. Two sites within Trelawny are being contemplated for the subdivision which will house them.

Holness — who on Friday toured the community alongside Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett, Trelawny Northern Member of Parliament Tova Hamilton, and state minister in the Office of the Prime Minister Abka Fitz-Henley — said his intention is to move eligible residents into a properly planned community instead of shifting them from one informal settlement to another.

“My wish is that by December we could start the process of the relocation,” Holness told residents.

He cautioned, however, that the December timeline was not a firm commitment, given the number of factors involved, including the need for contractors and infrastructure works, as well as possible delays caused by weather.

“It means that I may have to use emergency powers to address some of the situation,” he said.

The prime minister also pointed out that of the two sites being contemplated, the one closer to Cooper’s Pen may not be large enough.

“I don’t believe we can accommodate all the legitimate claims that are here,” Holness said, explaining that by legitimate he meant individuals who had been acknowledged as squatters on the land before the court action and orders.

The lots will be surveyed and pegged, there will be roads, water, and electricity, and land titling will also be part of the plan.

But Holness was emphatic that the land would not be free.

Options available to residents, based on their circumstances, include long-term leases, outright purchase, and social housing arrangements for those assessed as unable to afford the cost.

Some residents who contribute to the National Housing Trust (NHT), he noted, could access their contributions to assist with acquiring the property.

For those found to have little or no means, the prime minster said there could be fully or heavily subsidised lots, with some contribution from residents through “sweat equity”.

“Government’s role is to make it affordable,” Holness said, adding that the objective was to put residents on a legitimate path to property ownership rather than perpetuate what he described as a “freeness” mentality.

He also explained the rationale behind the relocation grant.

“The Government couldn’t take up public taxpayers’ money and pay for damage caused by a private action,” he said, adding that the distinction was important to avoid setting a legal precedent that would lock the Government into being held responsible for similar circumstances in the future.

Holness framed the Cooper’s Pen saga as a pivotal moment in the country’s long-running battle with a culture of squatting.

“I see Cooper’s Pen as the watershed. This is the incident that must change Jamaica’s spatial settlement for the better,” he argued.

The prime minister said a social survey is already being conducted to determine who should benefit from the relocation programme. The Ministry of Housing has interviewed about 70 per cent of the occupants, he said, while the survey team is being augmented by the Social Development Commission along with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.

The combined exercise, he said, will provide a clearer picture of the households, families, and vulnerable people in the community and help determine who qualifies for assistance.

Holness also warned that people who had not been living in the community before the demolition should not attempt to move in to take advantage of the Government’s response.

“I want to make it clear that anybody [who is] trying to scam the system, it won’t work!” he said.

“Bear in mind that we don’t have limitless resources, so the more people we have to accommodate, is the less you get,” he told residents.

He also reiterated that his Government does not condone or encourage squatting, adding that he has tasked Minister with Responsibility for Land Titling and Settlements Robert Montague to review the Government’s policies for dealing with squatter settlements and return with a broader proposal on regularisation and relocation.

Holness used the occasion to criticise previous administrations which, he argued, encouraged people to occupy land informally with the expectation that their status would eventually be regularised.

“The answer can’t be to acquire property illegally. The answer must be to create a process through which all Jamaicans — regardless of your colour, your class, your place of birth, your religion, your status in society — you have a fair opportunity to acquire property,” he said, adding that he was determined not to repeat those missteps.

Still, the prime minister struck a sympathetic tone with the displaced residents, saying the Government recognises the difficult circumstances in which they now find themselves.

“I don’t want any of you to feel as if the State has abandoned you. I don’t want you to feel shame, and I don’t want you to see the Government as your enemy,” he said.

“The fact is that you are also a victim of history and a victim of bad government policy… My objective is to make all of you here property owners,” he added.

World.title: Russia plans new ground attack on Kyiv, Ukraine warns
World.content:
Ukrainian flag fluttering as smoke rises from a warehouse following an air attack in the Kyiv. | Vladyslav Musiienko/AFP via Getty Images

Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s office reveals new intelligence about Kremlin plans for an offensive against the capital.

Ukraine has intelligence that Russia is planning new ground offensives against Kyiv and Chernihiv — while Moscow ramps up drone strikes on Ukrainian cities.

Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine’s presidential office, told reporters that Russian military chiefs have been tasked by the Kremlin’s political leaders with planning and preparing for attacks on the two cities, according to intelligence received and verified by Ukraine.

Palisa said there is not yet evidence that Russian troops are gathering to carry out the attacks, and that Ukraine’s priority is to “prevent the creation of conditions for the Russians to be able to launch any offensive actions at all.”

World.title: Trump-shaped ecstasy pills can be fatal, Dutch drug institute warns
World.content:
The tablets are shaped like the U.S. commander-in-chief’s head, researchers say.

An ecstasy pill shaped like the head of U.S. President Donald Trump is potentially lethal and should not be taken “under any circumstances,” a Dutch drug institute has warned.

The pills come in different colors, are shaped like the commander-in-chief’s head and are stamped with the words “Trump” and “NL,” according to a red alert issued by the Trimbos Institute, a drug and addiction research center based in Utrecht, on Friday.

It's currently not possible to know how many of the pills are in circulation, but "multiple" drug-testing locations have received them, Anniek Groothuis, a spokesperson for the institute, told POLITICO. Testers have previously encountered pills shaped like Superman logos or featuring car brands, Groothuis said.

World.title: Germany plans to blame Russia for Leipzig attack as tensions with Putin escalate
World.content:
One of the officials familiar with the matter said that in response to the Leipzig drone incident, it was no longer enough to expel individual Russian diplomats or close the Russian House in Berlin. Tougher measures were needed, such as intensified sanctions or even more extensive arms deliveries to Ukraine. The three officials declined to provide further details on which precise measures Merz plans to announce.

It is unclear to what extent Berlin plans to hold individual Russian actors or the Russian government responsible for the attempted drone attack. Berlin is already preparing for a sharp counter reaction, as the officials said Germany must prepare for punitive measures from Moscow.

The planned move lands amid high tension with Russia, amid a spate of incidents on European soil that top officials have described as "hybrid warfare." On Tuesday, CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise trip to Moscow where he warned the Russian government against escalating tensions with NATO.

But the timing of Merz's expected announcement is also domestically sensitive. On Sunday next week, elections will take place in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, followed by elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin two weeks later. In Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — known for its pro-Russia stance — is leading in the polls.

Merz had already announced Tuesday that there would be severe consequences for the Leipzig incident, though without naming any specific party.

“The drone attack in Leipzig, among other things, shows that we are also facing very real threats,” he said. “The federal government is making the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this.”

World.title: Russia kills dozens as drone hits ammo warehouse near homes in Ukraine
World.content:
The warehouse appears to have been storing ammunition; Zelenskyy referred to a detonation after the drone strikes, and to a police investigation into why ordnance was stored close to residential properties, which is prohibited. Criminal proceedings on charges of negligence have also begun. “Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions,” he said.

Russia is bombarding Kyiv with “virtually nonstop attack from jet-powered drones,” Zelenskyy added. In a separate video address Friday evening, he admitted Ukraine needs to “significantly accelerate” production of interceptors capable of taking down the Iranian-designed, jet-powered Shahed drones.

In response to Russia’s increased attacks, Ukraine plans to launch 1,000 long-range drones into Russia every day, up from a current average of 300. There “must be more” strikes, Zelenskyy said Friday night.

Kyiv’s use of long-range drones — striking deep into Russia, disrupting its economy, logistics and bringing the reality of the war to ordinary Russians previously shielded from it — has in recent months improved Ukraine’s position in the conflict. One Ukrainian commander has described them as “our most important card in this war.”

While noting Kyiv's priority is to strengthen defenses against jet-powered drones, sending more long-range drones into Russia will make it “feel even more responsible for its choice to continue this war,” Zelenskyy said Friday night.

In the same address, he also pointed to signs that Russia’s economy is ailing, including the fact that it is now importing gasoline, an unusual step for one of the world's largest oil exporters.

Zelenskyy also said American representatives briefed Ukraine on the recent unexpected visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, who warned Russian officials not to escalate conflict with America’s NATO allies. Zelenskyy thanked the U.S. for the "necessary tone of the conversation with Russia."

This article has been updated.

World.title: Ein Spaziergang mit Manuela Schwesig
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Strand, Sonne und ein erbitterter Kampf um das politische Überleben. In Rostock-Warnemünde begleitet Gordon Repinski Manuela Schwesig auf einem Spaziergang durch den Wahlkampfendspurt in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Die SPD-Ministerpräsidentin will ihr Land unbedingt gegen den erstarkenden AfD-Herausforderer verteidigen.

Um die Menschen an der Ostsee zu überzeugen, schlägt Schwesig ihren ganz eigenen Weg ein und geht auf maximale Distanz zur Bundespolitik. Sie attackiert den wirtschaftlichen Kurs von CDU-Kanzler Friedrich Merz schonungslos und fordert einen staatlichen Preisdeckel für Sprit. Die arbeitende Mitte dürfe in diesen Zeiten nicht länger die Hauptlast tragen, ist ihr Mantra.

Neben scharfen Angriffen in der Rentendebatte zeigt sich Schwesig beim Spaziergang aber auch von der persönlichen Seite. Sehr offen reflektiert sie ihre überstandene Krebserkrankung und wie dieser Schicksalsschlag ihren politischen Fokus verändert hat.
