World.title: Ousted Ukrainian defense chief Fedorov takes advisory role with Italy
World.content:
Fedorov, who called for wartime elections after being pushed out of government in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s latest reshuffle, also stressed that he is not decamping to Rome. “My main focus remains unchanged,” he wrote, adding he will continue working in Ukraine on projects to strengthen the country’s defense and attract international resources.

Crosetto first offered the position in July, saying he called Fedorov the day after his dismissal and asked: “When would you like to come to Rome to work with me as an adviser?” He praised Fedorov as an innovator who had “completely changed the rules of the game on the battlefield.”

The former minister was dismissed in mid-July after roughly six months at the helm of Ukraine's defense department amid tensions with the country’s military leadership and policy disputes. His removal triggered rare wartime protests.

He has since sharpened his criticism of President Zelenskyy, calling for elections earlier this month despite Russia’s ongoing invasion and warning that Ukrainians “cannot endlessly live” without understanding how major decisions are made.

Zelenskyy has rejected the idea, warning that wartime elections could “destroy” the country.

World.title: Climate and AI to loom large in von der Leyen’s State of the Union
World.content:
During Friday's discussion with the cabinet chiefs, Seibert linked the expected focus on climate to the damage caused by floods and wildfires over the summer, according to the two officials, who were briefed on the gathering. They were granted anonymity to discuss the closed-door talks.

The climate focus comes as von der Leyen’s Commission tries to defend its 2040 emissions-cutting target while responding to mounting pressure from industry and national capitals to limit the economic cost of the green transition.

The discussion also touched on how to present AI’s impact on jobs. Von der Leyen’s team has asked the Commission’s relevant policy units, in particular DG Connect, to provide fresh statistics for the speech on the number of jobs likely to be lost and created as AI adoption spreads, according to one of the officials.

Seibert also raised migration as a likely topic in the address, referring to the crisis in the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta, according to one of the officials. The Commission is expected to revamp the mandate and operations of EU border agency Frontex, a third official said.

The Commission president's speech is expected to include references to social policy around the 10th anniversary of the European Pillar of Social Rights next year, alongside Ukraine and enlargement, according to one of the officials. But the topics have yet to be finalized.

The meeting was the second major opportunity for commissioners to get their priorities name-checked, with their cabinets having already submitted two- to three-page pitches to Seibert. The Commission's policy units, known as the directorates-general, also submitted documents outlining the topics they want von der Leyen to cover.

World.title: What it’s like to live through Kyiv’s constant air raids
World.content:
Kyiv has survived more than 20 air raid alerts since Thursday night. Some were an hour long, while others lasted for up to 10 minutes.

Indeed, every alert, as Russia continues its persistent destruction of millions of books, food warehouses and liquor factories, also means everything has to stop until we hear the words: “Air raid alert is over.” Dozens of trains are delayed, and businesses shut down and wait, losing customers and money.

But “survivors must still go to work,” as we like to joke bitterly. People are still expected to commute, even though Kyiv’s subway has stopped running between the left and right banks of the River Dnipro. Sleep-deprived civilians need to walk for hours, squeeze themselves into buses, or get stuck in traffic on bridges, just to get to work and back home. Transport chaos overground means even more danger for people stuck in large groups all around the city.

But our wartime economy, on which we need to rely more and more due to the slowing of foreign aid, cannot afford to stop.

“The country’s defense spending is constantly growing, and this requires maximum mobilization of domestic resources,” said Hlib Vyshlinsky, the executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy think tank based in Kyiv. “The policy of zero tolerance for the risk to the life and health of civilians under constant missile and drone strikes becomes irrelevant, because the state is still not able to protect them at 100 percent.”

As a Kyivan, I can tell you that this terror sends your mental stability into a spiral.

World.title: Nepal warns of more possible floods as communities grapple with devastation
World.content:
Authorities in Nepal are warning of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River.

 

Flood warning notices were sent to people’s phones throughout Sunday morning, as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst-hit by Wednesday’s catastrophic floods.

In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. People pointed to enormous rocks that had been washed downriver during the earlier floods, as others standing on a suspension bridge over the water were warned off with whistles.

Along the river entire homes, vehicles and farm tractors could be seen jutting from the thick grey-brown sediment that has enveloped entire villages in the worst-hit flood areas. Rice terraces along the riverside had experienced landslides, dropping parts of their field into the river.

The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 750 dead and over 3,000 people missing after the latest updates on Sunday. Nepal’s disaster agency said the death toll had climbed to 734 with 2,498 people missing, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, including over a hundred Nepalis and people from over a dozen countries.

People leave after salvaging their belongings from their damaged homes following flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Si AP Photo

The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told the Associated Press.

But residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they’ve received since the initial floods.

“Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain,” said local resident Govind Shreshta. “It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and a 70-year-old mom. I must carry them, and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”

Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river with less easy access.

“Those that are there are now stuck there. Those who are here are stuck here. It’s going to be very difficult,” said Sattan Singh Tamang, 47, who was working near a bridge when Wednesday’s the floods came.

Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.

Prithivi Highway is a crucial supply route for food, fuel and other goods entering Kathmandu from other parts of the country. While most of the highway is operational, other parts still face repair challenges.

World.title: From doomscrolling to nomophobia: new digital-age conditions reshaping our brains
World.content:
Can you not go five minutes without checking your phone? Do you open Instagram "just for a second" and find that half an hour later you are still there? Do you wake up during the night and the first thing you do is check your notifications? Or do you keep scrolling through bad news even though you know perfectly well it is making you anxious?

 

Welcome to the age of new digital addictions.

Experts stress that the point is not to demonise smartphones, social networks or video games. The digital world is now part of our lives and can bring huge benefits. The problem begins when use becomes hard to control and starts to crowd out sleep, work, study, relationships or physical activity.

And research is starting to put a name to many of these behaviours.

The first real diagnosis: gaming disorder

One distinction is crucial. Not everything that gets called "smartphone addiction" is officially a disease.

The World Health Organization has, however, recognised in the International Classification of Diseases, ICD-11, gaming disorder.

That does not mean that playing a lot is automatically an illness. The disorder is about a loss of control over gaming, a growing priority given to play over other activities and continuing the behaviour despite negative consequences. To reach a diagnosis, there has to be a significant impact on personal, family, social, school or work life, generally for at least 12 months.

And it affects a minority of players, not everyone who spends a few hours in front of a console.

Social media addicts: when endless scrolling is the problem

Here the picture becomes more blurred.

Social media addiction, often referred to in research as problematic social media use or social media use disorder, is not currently an independent ICD-11 diagnosis like gaming disorder.

But the phenomenon has now been widely studied.

The signs are fairly intuitive: wanting to stop and being unable to, spending more time online than planned, feeling a strong need to check social media, neglecting other activities, becoming irritable when you cannot access platforms, or continuing to use them despite the problems they cause.

The American Psychological Association urges people to pay attention to exactly these behaviours, especially among teenagers.

And the figures are striking. According to the latest major Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) survey by the World Health Organization in Europe, carried out among almost 280,000 young people aged 11, 13 and 15 in 44 countries and regions, 11% of adolescents show signs of problematic social media use, compared with 7% in 2018. The share rises to 13% among girls and falls to 9% among boys.

FOMO: the fear of being the only one who does not know

One of social media’s most powerful traps now has an extremely familiar name: FOMO, Fear Of Missing Out.

It is that feeling that makes you think: "What if something has happened in the meantime?".

So we check WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok, the news and chats even when we have no real reason to do so.

FOMO is not a psychiatric diagnosis. It is, however, a psychological phenomenon studied in relation to problematic use of the internet and social media. A study published in 2024 looked precisely at the link between FOMO, problematic social media use and doomscrolling, and found that emotion regulation mechanisms play an important role.

In other words: the more we feel we need digital tools to manage anxiety, boredom or unpleasant emotions, the more we risk being drawn into a vicious circle.

Doomscrolling: why we keep reading bad news

It is probably one of the most characteristic phenomena of the smartphone era.

Doomscrolling is the compulsive consumption of negative news: wars, disasters, crises, accidents, illnesses, scandals. One story leads to another and your finger keeps scrolling.

The paradox is obvious: we look for information to feel better prepared and often end up feeling even more anxious.

Doomscrolling is not an independent medical diagnosis either, but it has become a focus of research into problematic online behaviour. Studies have linked it to FOMO and difficulties in regulating emotions.

And it can turn into another trap: the more worried we are, the more information we seek; the more negative information we consume, the more our worry grows.

Nomophobia: when the phone is gone, the anxiety arrives

"Nomophobia" is a word coined from no mobile phone phobia.

It does not simply mean "I am annoyed that I left my phone at home". It is the term used to describe the discomfort or anxiety linked to the absence of a smartphone, loss of connection, or the inability to access information and one’s digital relationships.

Again, it is worth being careful with words: it is not an official standalone diagnosis.

But it is a studied phenomenon, increasingly entangled with other problematic behaviours. A study published in 2026 analysed nomophobia, social media addiction and FOMO together, identifying the fear of missing information as one of the most important bridges between these phenomena and symptoms of anxiety and depression.

The phone, in short, can become a kind of "safety object": if we have it, everything is fine. If it disappears, even just for a few minutes, something feels wrong.

Phantom vibration: the phone that vibrates even when it does not

Have you ever been certain that your phone was vibrating in your pocket, only to take it out and realise that no notification had arrived?

This is called phantom vibration syndrome, or the phantom vibration syndrome.

It is not a recognised disease, but a studied perceptual phenomenon: the brain can interpret tiny physical stimuli as a phone vibration, especially when we are used to constantly expecting notifications.

It is almost the digital version of "I hear someone calling me" when nobody has called.

And then there is smartphone-induced insomnia

The issue is not only how much time we spend online. It is when we do it.

Scrolling in bed seems harmless: "I will just watch two videos and then sleep". The problem is that those two videos can turn into twenty minutes, an hour or much more.

The APA notes that using technology close to bedtime, and social media in particular, is linked to sleep disturbances in adolescents.

And a longitudinal study published in 2025 found an association between problematic social media use and later depressive and anxious symptoms, with sleep problems apparently playing a partial role in the connection. The authors themselves stress, however, that the relationship is complex and should not automatically be read as cause and effect.

The practical takeaway is easy to grasp: if the phone steals our sleep, the problem is no longer just the time spent in front of the screen.

Social media and the body: the physical impact

The digital revolution is not only about the brain.

Hours spent in front of a screen can mean less movement, more sedentary behaviour, eye strain and musculoskeletal problems linked to maintaining the same posture for long periods.

The so-called tech neck, the "smartphone neck", is now a common expression for the pain and tension associated with the posture of tilting your head towards your device. It is not a new medical diagnosis, but it describes a very concrete problem: we are spending more and more time with our neck bent over a screen.

The WHO, when discussing the effects linked to problematic use of technology and gaming, also highlights sedentary behaviour, musculoskeletal problems, sleep disturbances and eyesight issues.

The brain is not "ill": it is the behaviour that becomes problematic

And this is perhaps the most important distinction.

We should not turn every digital habit into a diagnosis.

Watching TikTok for an hour, playing a video game at the weekend, checking Instagram or reading the news does not necessarily mean being addicted. Quantity alone is not enough.

What really makes the difference is control and the impact on daily life. The question to ask is therefore not just: "How many hours do I spend on my phone?" It is rather: "Can I stop when I want to? And what am I sacrificing to carry on?"

If the phone starts eating into sleep, work, study, relationships, sport or real life, then the warning bell becomes much more serious.

The new frontier: a possible "social media addiction"?

Research is pushing further.

In 2025, a group of researchers proposed criteria for a possible classification of Social Media Use Disorder, identifying loss of control and a deterioration in everyday functioning as central elements. Among the possible criteria, they also discuss a preference for online interactions and FOMO.

But we are still in the realm of research, not facing a new official diagnosis.

And this is exactly where the future battle lies: understanding when a technology designed to capture our attention stops being a useful tool and starts to turn into a behaviour that is hard to control.

Because the real problem may not be the smartphone itself.

It may be the fact that we have built a digital world that is able to tell us, every few seconds: "Hey, look at me. You have missed something".

World.title: Nearly one thousand people swim across Danube in Budapest for first crossing in six years
World.content:
Nearly one thousand people took the plunge in Budapest on Saturday along one of the Danube's usually busiest stretches — between Corvinus University and the University of Technology — for the Generali OWT Danube Swim.

 

It was the first time in six years the event had been held, since organising it requires serious preparation, organiser Balázs Mezős told Euronews.

"This is a very big event: almost 40 paramedics watch over the swimmers, 12 motorboats look after them, and the entire Danube is closed for four hours, so no one can enter or leave. The larger ships have to be cleared from the start and finish areas and moved elsewhere," Mezős explained.

For competitors, it's an extraordinary experience to swim somewhere that would normally be unthinkable, given the boat traffic and safety considerations. Budapest unfolds before them in a completely different way.

"I used to come to university over Liberty Bridge every day," one young woman told Euronews. "I would always look out from the tram, wondering what it would be like to swim across — whether you actually could. It never occurred to me that it was really possible. Then we found out this event existed, and we signed up as soon as registration opened."

According to the organisers, the water is clean, the stretch is safe, and there are no dangerous eddies.

"People are very wary of the Danube," Mezős said. "That basically stems from the fact that they don't swim in it, because usually you're not allowed to. Fortunately, more and more open-water Danube beaches are being built here in Budapest and across the country, so people are slowly getting used to it. You can see that in our swimming races, where the number of participants keeps growing. So I think there's a kind of mistrust that has no real basis. People tend to mention whirlpools first, but there aren't any here — what little current there is wouldn't even be able to pull under a duck. You have to give it a try: the first time or two might feel a bit uncomfortable, or exciting, or even scary, but by the third time it's a real pleasure. Swimming while carried along by a current of about five kilometres an hour is heaven itself."

"A fantastic experience," said a British man living in Budapest, whose wife and two young daughters were waiting for him in front of the University of Technology. "Every Budapest resident should try it once. The start is tough because of the current — you think you're swimming in a straight line, but you're not. But the organisation is excellent; it's a great event."

The Danube Swim is part of the Generali Night Run sports festival, which offers participants a range of distances to run, in the morning or even at night, through some of Budapest's most iconic locations.

World.title: Hungary's bee population at risk, warns national beekeepers' association
World.content:
Prolonged drought and successive heatwaves have wiped out natural sources of nectar and pollen in Hungary, leaving bees facing starvation.

 

The pollen shortage could affect as much as 80% of the country's bee population, warns the National Hungarian Beekeeping Association (OMME). Experts have also alerted the ministry responsible for agriculture and food policy to the crisis.

Pollen is the most important protein source for bee colonies. It's essential for raising young bees and helping them develop properly. Without it, honey yields suffer—and colonies' chances of surviving winter are directly threatened.

For weeks, around 80% of Hungary's bees have had little or no access to natural pollen. The drought has made things worse: even the damp areas and riverbanks that normally still supply food for bees in late summer have dried up this year.

For a hive to survive, worker bees must carry at least a litre of water back to the queen and her larvae to keep them from drying out. The worse the drought gets, the farther bees must fly to find food and water—burning more energy and dying at higher rates as a result.

A lack of nectar can also cause colonies to turn on each other, driving mortality even higher.

Honey bees Michael Reilly/Daily News-Record

OMME says this could lead to significant colony losses by spring 2027. This matters beyond beekeeping, too: honey bees play a key role in pollinating crops, and by extension, in the food supply.

Because of the crisis, OMME has written to Szabolcs Bóna, the minister responsible for agriculture and food policy. Beekeepers are normally required to maintain a set number of colonies, but because of these exceptional losses, many will be unable to meet that requirement through no fault of their own.

OMME is asking the authorities not to automatically penalize beekeepers for expected losses, but instead to take into account the extreme weather and the unprecedented shortage of natural food sources.

The effects of the drought and heat won't end when the season does. How much pollen is available now could decide whether colonies survive the winter, how well they recover next spring, and ultimately, how much honey Hungary produces next year.

World.title: One dead, five injured in shooting at Swiss rave as major police operation unfolds
World.content:
One person was killed and five others injured, some seriously, after shots were fired at an event attended by around 3,500 people in the Swiss town of Aarau in the early hours of Sunday, Aargau cantonal police said in a post on X.

 

Aarau is located around 40 kilometres west of Zurich.

The incident occurred at around 3 am during a rave. Witnesses said they initially mistook the gunshots for fireworks.

Around ten shots can be heard in a video published by the Swiss newspaper "Blick", which was reportedly recorded near the scene.

Police are searching for the person or people responsible. "Possible motives and the exact circumstances of the incident remain unclear," cantonal police said. Authorities have not provided further details about the suspect or suspects.

Police are currently carrying out a large-scale operation, they confirmed to the Swiss news agency Keystone-SDA. Shortly after 7 am, Pascal Wenzel, a spokesperson for Aargau cantonal police, said authorities were dealing with a "special situation".

Police have urged the public to avoid the affected area.

According to Swiss emergency news outlet BRK News, a Swiss military Super Puma helicopter has also been deployed over the wider Aarau area.

Flight data show the aircraft making several movements around the town. It is not yet clear what role the helicopter is playing in the ongoing operation.

Our journalists are currently working on this story. The article will be updated as soon as new information becomes available.

World.title: Lausanne Grand Slam 2026: Switzerland Celebrates a Historic Judo Day
World.content:
Welcome back the ECOLE MONT-OLIVET LAUSANNE GRAND SLAM in Switzerland and the Vaudoise Arena.

 

Before the event Mr Marius Vizer, International Judo Federation president and Sergei Ashchwanden, Swiss Judo Federation president signed a contract to bring the 2028 world championships to Switzerland.

President Vizer then officially opened the grand slam. There were also speeches from: Ms Emilie Moëschler - Director of Sports and Social Cohesion for Lausanne, Ms Christelle Luisier Brodard - President of the Council of State of Vaud, Mr Sergei Aschwanden - President of the Swiss Judo Federation, Mr Demien Antoine - President of the Deaf International Judo Federation.

Additionally, Kazuhiro Mikami Sensei was awarded his 10th dan, the highest rank in judo.

Continuing the unity between the world tour athletes and the adaptive judo disciplines, today … deaf judoka were immersed in the grand slam competition, taking to the tatami alongside their peers.

On the mat, at -63 kg Angelika SZYMANSKA pounced on a failed attack from Manon DEKETER, deploying her trademark arm lock for the win.

Mr Christoph DUBI, IOC Olympic Games Executive Director was on hand to award the medals.

In the -73 kg final, with Swiss World Champion, Nils STUMP watching on, Daniel CARGNIN came back with a huge counter to take the gold medal.

I’m very happy because now it’s important for the points to qualify for the olympic games Daniel Cargnin

He was awarded his medal by President of ASOIF, Mr Ingmar DE VOS.

Miriam BUTKEREIT and Giovanna SCOCCIMARRO of Germany both made it to the final at -70kg with BUTKEREIT judged the victor.

Mr Simon BENHAMOU, CEO of CBH Bank awarded the medals.

Yesterday the school children were here, and always a good crowd, a loud crowd, I love it! Miriam Butkereit

In the final of the -81kg category Abylaikhan ZHUBANAZAR produced a lightning fast foot sweep for yuko to win.

The final day awaits!

World.title: Which cities are the most expensive to buy an apartment in Europe?
World.content:
Housing is a major issue across Europe. The problem is not just availability, but affordability too, with housing being particularly expensive in capital cities, major urban areas and tourist destinations.

 

House prices and rents vary significantly across Europe. So, which countries and cities are the most expensive for buying a house or flat in 2026? How much does a square metre cost? And how much is needed to buy an apartment in a city centre?

The "Mapping the World’s Prices 2026" report, published by Deutsche Bank Research Institute, compares the price per square metre of buying an apartment in the city centre across 69 cities, 28 of them in Europe.

Switzerland is the most expensive country to buy a house

Two Swiss cities rank at the top, making Switzerland the most expensive country to buy real estate in city centres. The price per square metre for an apartment is €22,910 in Zurich and €19,439 in Geneva.

For an 80-square-metre apartment, that would mean a price of around €1,833,000 in Zurich and €1,555,000 in Geneva.

London ranks third at €17,241 (£14,782) per square metre. So, an apartment of this size would cost around €1,379,000, or £1,183,000.

London is 35% more expensive than Paris

While Paris comes next, real estate in the French capital is comparatively cheaper than in London. The price per square metre is €12,771. Buying an apartment in London city centre is around 35% more expensive than in Paris.

Vienna completes the top five, with a price of €12,483 per square metre.

Only two cities in the top five are from Europe’s largest economies: London in the UK and Paris in France.

The most expensive city in Germany is Munich at €11,435 per square metre.

Luxembourg (€11,011), Copenhagen (€10,191), Stockholm (€10,037) and Oslo (€9,785) are also in the top 10. The price falls below the €10,000 mark in the Norwegian capital.

Three Nordic cities are in the top 10 while Helsinki ranks 13th at €8,431 per square metre.

Milan and Amsterdam are just above the Finnish capital at €9,378 and €9,273 per square metre respectively.

Prague is pricier than Madrid and Berlin

Prague is more expensive than the Spanish and German capitals. The price per square metre to buy an apartment in the city centre is €8,352.

This compares with €7,831 in Madrid and €7,613 in Berlin. Rome follows at €7,328 per square metre.

It is still above 7,000 levels in Dublin (€7,185) and Frankfurt (€7,162)while it is over 6,000 in Lisbon (€6,636) and Barcelona (€6,485).

Cheapest cities: Istanbul and Athens

Istanbul is the cheapest European city on the list at €2,646 per square metre, followed by the capital of neighbouring Greece, Athens, at €3,442.

Brussels, the EU capital, is also among the cheapest cities, ranking third from the bottom. The price per square metre to buy an apartment there is €4,380.

Birmingham in the UK (€4,671) is also below the €5,000 mark, while Budapest (€5,243), Warsaw (€5,443) and Edinburgh (€5,708) are above this level.

The simple average across the 28 cities is €9,090 per square metre.

Based on this, the cost of an 80-square-metre apartment exceeds €1 million in only four cities. Zurich is actually close to €2 million, while Geneva is above €1.5 million.

The average price for an 80-square-metre apartment across the list would be around €727,000.

Hong Kong is the most expensive, Cairo the cheapest

Among all 69 cities in the report, Hong Kong is the most expensive, at €23,790 per square metre, followed by Zurich (€22,910) and Seoul (€21,897).

The cheapest cities are Cairo (€784) and Johannesburg (€913), both below the €1,000 mark.

The figures in the report are based on data from Numbeo and Deutsche Bank. They were converted into euros using the ECB’s average exchange rates for the first half of 2026.

World.title: Iceland's EU referendum edges closer to 'no'
World.content:
Results from five of six constituencies showed that 52.5% of Icelanders don't want to reopen accession talks with the European Union.

Partial results from Iceland's referendum on resuming European Union membership talks showed a slim lead for the "no" camp on Sunday morning.

With final results counted from five of six constituencies, 52.5% of ​voters opposed the government's ​proposal to resume EU negotiations, while 47.5% backed the plan, Iceland's public broadcaster RUV reported.

Some 270,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote. There was no information yet about voter turnout.

Election officials warned that a more reliable result might not be available until midday on Sunday.

Iceland debates joining EU amid Trump's Greenland interest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iceland has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming the bloc's 28th member. Talks were suspended 13 years ago by the euroskeptic government at the time.

Iceland's current left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a vote next year but brought it forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.

This article will be updated as votes continue to be counted in Iceland.

World.title: Nepal issues fresh flood warning as 3,000 still missing
World.content:
Rescuers are trying to reach dozens of hydropower workers trapped in flooded tunnels, but have been hampered by further rainfall.

The combined death toll from the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet rose to 750 on Sunday, with more than 3,000 people still missing, authorities said.

A fresh flood alert was issued after river levels rose again, while Tibetan authorities warned of a new barrier lake forming behind landslide debris.

Several scientists believe a glacier collapse in the Himalayas may have triggered Wednesday's disaster, sending huge volumes of water down a river valley.

Nepal flood survivors still searching for some 3,000 missing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What's the latest on the floods?

Nepal's disaster authority put the number killed on its side of the border at 734, while Chinese state media confirmed 16 dead in Tibet, an autonomous region of China.

Chinese authorities said the dead included over a hundred Nepalis and people from more than a dozen countries.

The Nepalese disaster agency issued a warning for fresh floods on Sunday and told residents around the Bhotekoshi River to remain on high alert as water levels rose.

Flood warning notices were sent to residents' phones, advising them to move to higher ground.

On the Tibet side, Chinese state media said monitoring drones on Saturday night had picked up a new lake forming from a barrier created by a landslide near the Gyirong border port.

Rescue teams near the Gyirong border port were moved because of the risk of the barrier bursting.

Nepal's disaster agency has issued a warning for fresh floods Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Hydropower workers still trapped in tunnels

Meanwhile, Nepalese rescuers are trying to reach more than 100 hydropower workers believed trapped and still alive in tunnels swamped by flood debris.

Rescue teams are focusing on several hydropower projects on the Trishuli River, where more than 900 workers went missing during the floods.

At one of the sites on Saturday night, army teams used drills to break into the upper part of a mud-swamped tunnel to pump oxygen and deliver a camera inside.

Nepal's prime minister's office said that teams faced "continuous rainfall and difficult conditions" but had worked nonstop overnight, "making tireless efforts to search for and rescue those who may be trapped."

Several thousand people remain missing, four days after the floods hit Image: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo/picture alliance

Rescue effort bolstered by neighbors

Specialized teams from India and China have joined the rescue effort, along with Nepal's mountain rescue squad, which helps climbers on the world's highest peaks, including Everest.

Nepalese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said the country needed assistance in such areas as tunnel rescue, DNA testing and identifying the victims.

The US State Department wrote on X that it would provide $3.6 million (€3.1 million) in "life-saving humanitarian assistance" to Nepal, including up to three months of emergency food aid for up to 10,000 flood-affected households.

The ⁠Red Cross estimates that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster.

World.title: Swiss police report 1 dead, 5 injured  in Aarau shooting
World.content:
The shooting happened outside a rave in the northern Swiss town of Aarau. Police said they were still searching for the perpetrators.

One person has died ​after a ​shooting ​at ‌a rave ​in Aarau, Switzerland, ​police said Sunday.

Five other people were wounded in the incident, some of them seriously, the police added.

A "manhunt" for the "unknown perpetrators" is underway, the police said in a statement on X, adding that the motive and the exact circumstances of the incident were still unclear.

A large contingent of the Aargau Cantonal Police has been deployed and a probe into the incident has begun, the police said.

Police presence has also been stepped up beyond Aarau as a precaution, they added.

Police officers patrolling a street in downtown Aarau Image: Michael Buholzer/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

The Cantonal police earlier said that a ‌major ​operation was ongoing following the shooting and had asked people to stay away from the area.

They have also appealed to people to share any videos or images of the incident.

What else do we know about the shooting?

According to Swiss newspaper Blick, the shots were fired before 3:00 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) during the annual Aarauer Rave.

The newspaper quoted police spokeswoman Vanessa Rumpold as saying that the shooting occurred at the Schachen race course where the techno party was being held.

Aarau has about 22,300 residents and is located about 40 kilometers (25 miles) west of Zurich.

Police blocked off streets near the horse racing track where the rave was taking place Image: Michael Buholzer/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

World.title: Germany news: Merkel tells voters to 'stand up' for democracy
World.content:
Skip next section Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'

08/30/2026 August 30, 2026 Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called on her compatriots to "stand up" for democracy ahead of next weekend's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

The far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is leading polls raising questions about what kind of government will be formed.

Despite this, the majority of Germans are not AfD voters, Merkel said at a political event in Berlin on Saturday night.

"I believe that now, once again — something we haven't had to do for many decades — we must really fight for this democracy, simply stand up for it, be a little brave, stand by our word and say that this is a wonderful way to live," she said.

Merkel said the AfD had, to some extent, managed to "dominate all our discussions from morning to night" about politics in Saxony-Anhalt. This meant that many voters no longer knew the policies of the other parties, she said.

But while the AfD has long polled strongest in the eastern states, Merkel — who herself hails from the former East Germany — said the rise of the AfD was not limited to those areas.

"It has become a pan-German phenomenon," she said.

World.title: Norway’s new King Haakon remembers ‘dear father’ Harald in first speech as sovereign
World.content:
New monarch Haakon VIII paid an emotional tribute to his late father, Harald V, in his first address to the nation. Vowing to follow his own path, Haakon pledged to uphold Norway’s democracy, unity and inclusive values.

King Haakon VIII of Norway paid tribute to his late father, King Harald V, calling him "such a wonderful papa" in his first address to the nation as monarch.

"Above all, you were a person who remained committed to your values and dedicated to your duties," Haakon said Saturday in a televised speech. "We greatly mourn his loss. At the same time, it gives us consolation and strength to know that there are so many who are grieving with us."

Norway's King Harald died at 89, after more than three decades on the throne, during which time he became known as a reformer and a popular monarch. In a televised speech from the palace, Haakon praised his father as a "warm and devoted family man."

Haakon became emotional while speaking about his widowed mother, Queen Sonja. He noted that his parents would have celebrated their 58th wedding anniversary on Saturday.

Norway's King Harald V dies at 89 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Earlier on Saturday, Haakon met at the palace with leaders of the Church of Norway, parliament and the Supreme Court. He also received Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who viewed the late king’s casket after it was brought to the palace from Oslo University Hospital on Friday evening.

Flags flew at half-mast Saturday as mourners continued to gather at the palace, laying flowers alongside tributes left the previous day by more than 20,000 people.

Haakon stresses he will do things 'his own way'

Haakon said he would follow his own path, as his father did before him, while reaffirming the principles of Norway’s constitutional monarchy. He is due to swear an oath in parliament on Tuesday to uphold the country’s constitution and laws.

"We believe in our system of self-governance — and in democracy. We believe in a society built on the rule of law, where every individual has equal worth," he said.

Haakon automatically became king following his father’s death. Norway does not hold coronations, which were abolished by parliament in 1908.

But, like his father and grandfather before him, Haakon could opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906.

The Norwegian prime minister told Reuters news agency that Haakon shared many of his father’s qualities, particularly his "ability to create an atmosphere of togetherness."

Crown Princess Sonja and Crown Prince Harald, future King and Queen of Norway, with newly born Crown Prince Haakon in Oslo, Norway. [FILE: July 26, 1973] Image: TT/IMAGO

Mourning and challenges for the royal family

A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet set for Harald’s funeral. Churches across Norway will hold memorial services Sunday, including one in Asker, south of Oslo, which the royal family was scheduled to attend.

Harald was widely regarded as a symbol of an open and tolerant Norway and praised for leading a modern, modest monarchy.

The king had been hospitalized in Oslo since August 17 with hemolytic anemia, a condition that causes the rapid destruction of red blood cells and can lead to fatigue and shortness of breath. His health had deteriorated in recent years, forcing him to reduce his official duties.

Haakon's wife, Mette-Marit, is under scrutiny for her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. [FILE: 17 June, 2026] Image: PPE/IMAGO

The royal family has also faced a series of challenges. Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, has come under scrutiny over her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

In June, her son from a previous relationship was sentenced to four years in prison for two rapes, a sentence he is appealing.

Mette-Marit, 53, who has a serious lung disease, underwent a lung transplant in July.

World.title: Turkish, Somali forces free vessel seized by pirates in Somalia
World.content:
Turkish and Somali forces have freed the MV LUTUF after pirates hijacked the vessel off the coast of Somalia. The 10-day operation killed 14 alleged pirates and destroyed four boats used by the attackers.

Turkey’s navy and Somali armed forces have freed a hijacked vessel in Somali waters and killed 14 alleged pirates following a battle that lasted several days, Somalia’s government said on Saturday.

"During the 10-day operation, four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed," said a Somali Defense Ministry statement. "The sustained military pressure finally forced the remaining pirates to abandon the ship."

The MV LUTUF, a Cameroon-flagged vessel, was hijacked on August 17 off the coast of the Nugaal region of Puntland state. The joint Turkey-Somalia operation was carried out as part of a defense cooperation agreement between the two countries.

The ministry did not provide details about any casualties or the well-being of the crew aboard the vessel but said, "The forces subsequently secured the MV LATUF, which has now safely resumed its journey."

According to AFP news agency sources, at least eight members of the crew were on board, including one Turkish national.

Resurgence of piracy along Somalia’s coast

The Horn of Africa has seen a resurgence in piracy since April, according to figures from the International Maritime Organization, with at least 15 attacks off the coast of Somalia this year.

At least five cargo ships were held hostage, the most recent of which was seized on August 20 off Yemen.

Maritime police patrol to ward off piracy off the coast in Puntland, Somalia [FILE: January 29, 2024] Image: Abuukar Mohamed Muhidin/Anadolu/picture alliance

These attacks are the highest since 2013. Piracy was rampant off the coast of Somaliain the 2000s. It peaked in 2011 before being curbed by international naval deployments and new protection measures for commercial shipping.

The resurgence of piracy in the Horn of Africa is adding to mounting challenges for international shipping in the Middle East, where vessels are already navigating around the contested Strait of Hormuz and seeking to avoid Houthi attacks in the Red Sea.

In recent years, pirate attacks have also increased along the West African coast, adding another layer of risk for commercial shipping.

World.title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinian homes in West Bank
World.content:
Masked Israeli settlers launched their first major attack since initiating a siege in the village of Qusra earlier this month. Saturday's attacks were met with rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, pelting them with rocks and trapping residents in their homes.

The incident was the first major attack by Israeli settlers since they began a siege in the villages of Qusra and neighboring Jalud earlier this month.

On Saturday, settlers descended on Qusra and began pelting Palestinians with rocks. When dozens of residents sought to barricade themselves in a home, settlers followed them in, according to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).

"The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside the house," said an IDF statement.

Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who is the IDF protecting in such situations?

Although the IDF said settler vehicles had been impounded and authorities were gathering evidence, Palestinian media said the IDF protected the settlers during the melee.

A number of Palestinians said they were injured after being pepper sprayed by settlers, and reported that other Israeli settlers had tried to burn nearby fields owned by Palestinians.

One Palestinian said the IDF had fired tear gas into the home that he was in and held several people inside while at the same time letting Israeli settlers go free.

Other Palestinians said IDF officers had handcuffed, blindfolded and beaten residents trapped inside before letting them go.

Local Palestinians told international news teams that they had been trapped in their homes for hours waiting for help from the IDF.

The IDF did not comment on the use of tear gas nor accusations of handcuffs and beatings.

Saturday attacks elicit rare criticism from Netanyahu

Saturday's attacks took place just yards away from three other Qusra homes that radical Jewish settlers targeted in a siege that began three weeks ago.

Despite a massive Israeli military presence that local Palestinians say has kept them imprisoned in their houses, residents report near-daily settler encroachments.

Rights groups say settler aggression is part of an — illegal — effort to seize land from residents in the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians hope to one day found their own independent state. The Israeli government has rejected accusations of illegality. Various Israeli political figures have justified the settlements for security reasons or argued there are biblical grounds for the creation of the settlements.

The IDF has said it will continue "to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area."

Although settlers have been emboldened by the stance of Israel's far-right government — which has encouraged settlement building despite broad international opposition — the Saturday attack managed to elicit rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

On Saturday, Netanyahu released a statement on X saying, "I strongly condemn the criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Qusra and Jalud by a handful of rioters who are violating the law, causing a grave injustice to the law-abiding Jewish community, interfering with the IDF in carrying out its missions, and harming Israel's standing in the world."

Increasing Israeli settler violence has even garnered criticism from US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who recently denounced radical settlers in the West Bank as "Israeli terrorists," adding that those behind the siege of Qusra could face US sanctions.

World.title: Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27
World.content:
Dozens of people were killed when a minibus carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck in central Zimbabwe. The crash near the town of Chivhu is the latest deadly road accident in the African country.

At least 27 people were killed in a minibus crash in central Zimbabwe after the vehicle carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck, police said Saturday. Seven people were injured.

Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said members of a popular Indigenous African Christian denomination, known for wearing white robes, were traveling to a conference on Friday when their minibus collided with a truck on a major highway near the town of Chivhu, about 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital, Harare.

The foreign-registered haulage truck was overtaking another vehicle when it collided with the minibus. Both vehicles were carrying an "unspecified" number of passengers, Nyathi said in a statement.

Footage shared on social media by public broadcaster ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell.

Zimbabwe faces road safety crisis

Authorities say 94% of road accidents occur due to human error. Many Zimbabweans rely on privately operated minibus taxis, known locally as kombis, for everyday transportation. The vehicles are often criticized for carrying more passengers than allowed.

Zimbabwe’s roads are also riddled with potholes after years of underfunding and neglect, while driving standards can be poor.

In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in southern Zimbabwe. Earlier that month, a woman and her five children were killed when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa.

Rescue personnel work at the site of a bus accident on a major highway near Harare [FILE: January 18, 2015] Image: Xinhua/imago images



Road crashes kill about 300,000 people across Africa each year, accounting for roughly a quarter of the global road death toll, according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The continent has the world’s highest road fatality rate, the commission says.

This is despite Africa’s 1.5 billion people accounting for only about 3% of the world’s vehicle fleet.

World.title: Asombrosas experiencias en San Cristóbal de La Laguna: practicar el salto del pastor, comer en una cueva o viajar en el tiempo en Bajamar
World.content:
La primera capital de la isla de Tenerife es ciudad patrimonio de la Unesco, uno de los Pueblos Gastronómicos de España y la puerta del selvático y abrupto macizo de Anaga. Además, en verano hace fresco

En la Península hay pocas localidades donde no haga un calor preocupante en verano. Y en Canarias, que están 1.400 kilómetros más al sur, menos aún. Eso es lo que piensan muchos viajeros al hacer la maleta, y cuando llegan a San Cristóbal de La Laguna descubren tiritando que deberían haber leído algo más de historia y geografía tinerfeñas, que la primera capital de la isla se fundó en 1496 a buena altura, a 550 metros sobre el mar, en un valle del noreste rodeado de montañas, ideal para defenderse de los guanches alzados, pero también para quedarse pajarito, porque los alisios amontonan nubes y humedad que da gusto. Es la eterna panza de burro, les advierten a los turistas los muy pacientes y abrigados laguneros, ya demasiado tarde.

Así que lo primero extraordinario que hay que hacer si se viaja allí en verano es incluir algo de ropa de abrigo en el equipaje. Algo para arriba y para los pies, porque la laguna que dio nombre a la ciudad sigue estando ahí, enterrada bajo las calles en damero que sirvieron de modelo para trazar muchas urbes de América. Cómo era la laguna de La Laguna —valga la redundancia— puede verse en el plano que dibujó en 1588 el ingeniero italiano Leonardo Torriani y que está reproducido en el suelo de la plaza de la Junta Suprema. Aquí traen los guías a los muchos ingleses que suben al atardecer desde la soleada costa sur de Tenerife y visitan esta alta y nublada ciudad maldiciendo la hora en que decidieron venir en chanclas y manga corta.

Más información Las mejores terrazas de los cafés históricos de Viena

Un ciclista por la calle San Agustín, en el centro histórico de La Laguna. Andrés Campos

Tan importante como hacer bien la maleta, es dar en el clavo con la compañía aérea, que sea económica pero formal. Por unos 45 euros se puede volar en agosto con Iberia Express de la Península al aeropuerto de Tenerife Norte, que está a 10 minutos de La Laguna, y hacerlo con absoluta puntualidad: en 2025 fue la aerolínea de Europa más cumplidora en esto por tercer año consecutivo. Si se coge el vuelo de las 6.35, se estará desayunando a las 9.00 un canelé de Burdeos o cualquiera de las dulces maravillas que obra Pablo Fernández del Castillo en Makika, en el casco histórico de La Laguna.

Desayunar frutas ecológicas

Tampoco se desayuna mal en el bufé del céntrico y señorial hotel Laguna Nivaria, sobre todo si se explora su sección de frutas ecológicas: plátanos, papayas, mangos, aguacates, acerolas, piñas… Todo esto lo cosechan en La Vizcaína, una finca certificada de 50.000 metros cuadrados que hay en Valle de Guerra, a 15 kilómetros al noroeste de La Laguna. Si tenemos mucho interés, se puede visitar solicitándolo en el mismo alojamiento. Allí descubriremos frutas insólitas en España —como los canisteles mesoamericanos que, en el árbol, parecen limones, pero saben a dulce de leche y tienen una textura harinosa, como de yema de huevo duro— y también animales de granja autóctonos, como el cochino negro canario o la oveja pelibuey.

Visitantes observando los papayos en la finca ecológica la Vizcaína. Andrés Campos

De paso, podemos parar a curiosear y desayunar (¡otra vez!) en Frutas y Verduras Nito, un mercado con cafetería del vecino municipio de Tegueste propiedad de Sergio Rodríguez, Nito, un agricultor que vende sin intermediaros lo que cultiva y que arrasa en Instagram —tiene 161.000 seguidores— con sus reels francos y combativos.

Moverse como una torre de ajedrez por el tablero urbano

Después de desayunar, los forasteros en Canarias suelen bajar a la playa o a la piscina. En La Laguna no hay playa —en el municipio, sí, como luego veremos— y pocos hoteles tienen piscina descubierta, por motivos obvios. Además, aquí lo que apetece es entrar en calor y, para ello, nada como moverse adelante y atrás, a izquierda y derecha, cual torre de ajedrez, por el tablero de San Cristóbal de La Laguna, primer ejemplo de ciudad colonial no amurallada trazada en cuadrícula, y patrimonio mundial de la Unesco desde 1999.

Si tomamos como casilla de partida la plaza del Adelantado, donde se alza desde el siglo XVI la mansión que hoy ocupa el Laguna Nivaria, saldremos por la calle Obispo Rey Redondo y nos plantaremos enseguida delante de la Casa de los Capitanes Generales, palacio de toba volcánica roja y amplio patio donde entre 1705 y 1723 vivieron seis mandamases de Canarias. Admiraremos luego los dragos de la plaza de los Remedios, frente a la catedral, que son talluditos, pero unos jovenzuelos de 60 años comparados con otros varias veces centenarios de la ciudad. Y subiremos 99 escalones para otear La Laguna desde lo alto del campanario de la iglesia de la Concepción.

El antiguo convento de San Agustín, en La Laguna (Tenerife). Andrés Campos

Al pie del campanario, en el patio de la Casa Museo Cayetano López Felipe, hay una terraza perfecta para un descanso. Bajando después por la calle San Agustín, veremos el mapa de Torriani, el formidable claustro renacentista del antiguo convento de San Agustín y la no menos imponente Casa Lercaro, sede del Museo de Historia y Antropología de Tenerife. Los forofos de la historia se arrimarán finalmente al convento de Santa Catalina de Siena para recordar a la monja milagrosa Sor María de Jesús, La Siervita, y a la parroquia de Santo Domingo de Guzmán, donde yace bajo una losa decorada con una calavera pirata su devoto amigo Amaro Pargo (1678-1747), el corsario más famoso de España, un lagunero que ha inspirado leyendas, novelas e incluso un juego para buscar un tesoro suyo oculto en la ciudad siguiendo las pistas con el móvil.

La tumba del corsario Amaro Pargo, en la parroquia de Santo Domingo de Guzmán. Andrés Campos

Quienes prefieran la ruidosa multitud, concluirán el recorrido urbano paseando con un montón de vecinos y con cien palmeras canarias seculares a cada lado por el llamado Camino Largo, la Avenida de la Universidad, o acercándose al mercado municipal para cotillear en los puestos de papas —Tenerife cuenta con ¡18 variedades— y en las pescaderías donde las viejas, los chernes, los pejeperros y las morenas compiten por ver quién es el pez más feo y colorido.

Viajar 50 años atrás en el tiempo, a Bajamar

En los años sesenta y primeros de los setenta del siglo XX, antes de que se inaugurara el aeropuerto de Tenerife Sur y el litoral meridional de la isla se masificara, uno de los mayores reclamos turísticos de la misma era Bajamar, a 15 kilómetros al norte de la ciudad de La Laguna. Como en el resto del municipio y del norte de Tenerife, aquí no lucía mucho el sol. Tampoco había playas excelentes en esta empinada y abrupta orilla: solo una pequeña protegida por una escollera y otra de arena negra volcánica y cantos rodados donde rompían, y rompen, olas de susto. Por ello, el turismo en Tenerife tomó otros derroteros más soleados y Bajamar se fue quedando traspapelada, con el hotel Neptuno —el mejor de los años dorados— en ruinas, y con una fecha escrita debajo, “diciembre de 1971”, cuando Camilo Sesto inauguró la discoteca Tívoli, muy cerca del anterior.

La asociación Cervantear invita a viajar al Bajamar de hace medio siglo con guías locales, recordando las paellas multitudinarias que aquí se hacían —hubo una en 1973 para 10.000 personas— y la riada de 1977 que convirtió este rincón de la costa lagunera en una escombrera, en un lugar que ya no levantaría cabeza. Invitan porque la ruta es gratis. Tres lugares que hay que visitar, con guías o sin ellos, son la cancha de fútbol donde el hijo más famoso de Bajamar, Pedri, dio sus primeros pases; el mural en homenaje al cantante Quevedo que alegra las ruinas del hotel Neptuno y las piscinas naturales de dimensiones olímpicas que hay junto al faro, al borde del océano, y en las que, a falta de buenas playas, uno se puede bañar como hace medio siglo, con permiso de las olas, que son tremendas.

Bañistas en las piscinas naturales de Bajamar. Andrés Campos

Caminar hasta un observatorio guanche y practicar el salto del pastor

Un poco más al norte, donde la costa urbanizada y/o urbanizable se acaba y empiezan los acantilados y barrancos del macizo de Anaga, se encuentra Punta del Hidalgo, que, al igual que Bajamar, tiene un aire demodé, de lugar de vacaciones de los setenta metido en una bola de cristal.

El plan extraordinario aquí es seguir el sendero litoral que lleva en menos de una hora hasta la ermita de San Juanito, pasando al pie de un altísimo y futurista faro blanco. Junto a la ermita, en la rasa intermareal basáltica, hay un yacimiento de cazoletas y canales guanches. Era un observatorio donde los aborígenes del achimenceyato de Addar veían cómo el sol naciente asomaba una vez al año a través de la cima hendida del cercano Roque de los Dos Hermanos —Aramuygo, para ellos— y sabían que era el solsticio de invierno. Así lo cuentan los profesores laguneros José Farrujia y Miguel Ángel Martín en su libro Cuando el cielo nos habló. Y así lo creen muchas personas que se acercan el 21 de diciembre a este punto para ver amanecer.

Un senderista en la laurisilva del macizo de Anaga, cerca de Cruz del Carmen. Andrés Campos

Cualquier otro día, lo que se ve en los altos roques de Punta del Hidalgo es a gente que practica el salto del pastor canario, deporte que consiste en descender por las escarpadísimas laderas apoyándose en una larga lanza o astia de madera con un picudo regatón de hierro. Al llegar abajo, los saltadores invitan amablemente a los curiosos a iniciarse dando unos pequeños brincos en la orilla rocosa, delante de la ermita. Solo unos saltitos. Más no, porque es peligroso y hay que estar federado. En Tenerife hay 161 apasionados de esto federados. Y hay demostraciones y cursos de los que se informa en la web saltodelpastorcanario.org.

Comer pescado del día

En Cofradía de La Punta, en Punta del Hidalgo, se cena viendo los barcos arribar al puertito con lo que llevará la parrillada. Abundan en el municipio de La Laguna los restaurantes como este, donde hacen bien lo de cerca y lo de siempre, y también los que le dan una vuelta imaginativa, sin pasarse. Por eso La Laguna forma parte de la Red de Pueblos Gastronómicos de España. ¿Sugerencias? Tomen nota.

En el centro ajedrezado de la ciudad, merece la pena reservar en El Guadyl, en Bejeque y en Sorimba. El primer restaurante, moderno y desenfadado, está siempre a tope, y el almogrote y las cervezas artesanas Chutney no deben faltar en la mesa. En el segundo, el venezolano de raíces lusas Adrián Oliveira elabora lo canario con técnicas japonesas. Usa carbón Binchotan, el más puro y caro del mundo. Y el tercero es ideal para cenar: todo lo sirven en platos de cerámica artística y atienden con susurros.

Fuera del casco histórico, pero a solo 10 minutos de paseo, se encuentra Mallar, un restaurante que engaña, porque parece un tosco mesón y es un no parar de platillos deliciosos: taco de vieira, lomo de salmón fileteado con aceite de sésamo y picadillo, chorizo picante de El Hierro con huevo frito... El joven chef Rubén Pérez también engaña: tiene más experiencia de la que aparenta. Por último, en un promontorio sobre la cala del Roncador, en la costa norte, está Agrocardón, con mucho comedor al aire libre rodeado de huertos y frutales y con animales por doquier: cabras, burros, caballos, ponis, gallinas, pavos reales… En la zona chill-out, los bípedos implumes liban cócteles y las mariposas monarca, el néctar de las asclepias.

A la Reserva de Anaga en guagua

Cuesta creer que, a solo seis kilómetros de la ciudad histórica de La Laguna, una urbe trazada a escuadra y cartabón, bastante llana y sin apenas nada verde a la vista, se encuentre la Reserva de la Biosfera de Anaga, un territorio primitivo, montañoso y selvático a más no poder que alberga la mayor extensión de laurisilva que hay en Tenerife y un número de endemismos sin igual en Europa. Es como si el Renacimiento y y la era Terciaria —cuando se formaron la ciudad y la laurisilva­— fueran dos páginas seguidas de un mismo libro.

Si vamos a Anaga en coche, pararemos de camino en Las Mercedes para conocer el venerable molino de gofio La Fuerza de La Voluntad, que lleva en marcha desde el 2 de febrero de 1942. Si subimos en guagua —en la número 275, desde el intercambiador de La Laguna—, llegaremos directamente, en una media hora, a Cruz del Carmen, donde está el Centro de Visitantes y arrancan dos senderos sencillos, perfectos para empezar a explorar a esta jungla primigenia: el de los Sentidos y el el de Hija Cambada. Para ver bien Anaga, necesitaríamos un mes. Habrá que volver.

Comer en La Cueva y bajar 500 escalones para catar vinos

Javier González, en su Bodega 500 Escalones. Andrés Campos

Aunque poca, en Anaga vive gente: hay unas 2.500 personas repartidas por 30 aldeas y caseríos, seis de los cuales pertenecen al municipio de La Laguna. En uno de ellos, Chinamada, se siguen usando casas-cueva, como en tiempos de los guanches, y se debe comer en el restaurante La Cueva (922 69 00 76), que está excavado en la roca volcánica. Hay escaldón, papas, ropa vieja, más papas, carne de cabra, carne con papas, queso frito de cabra… Todo muy sencillo, muy guanche, muy rico. Aquí no hay sumiller, ni vinos extraordinarios. Para esto último, hay que ir a la Bodega 500 Escalones, que, como su nombre avisa, está medio millar de peldaños más abajo que el caserío Los Batanes, en el fondo de un barranco aparentemente inhóspito. No hay carretera. Hay un viejo guinche, un montacargas suspendido de un cable en el que los enoturistas podrían bajar y subir cómodamente antes y después de alucinar visitando los viñedos que alguien plantó allá abajo y que recuperó en 1999 Félix González, el padre de Javier, que es el enólogo y la cara visible y sonriente de esta increíble bodega. Pero no está preparado para que lo usen personas. Lástima. Toca bajar por la escalera labrada en la toba volcánica, catar un par de vinos y subir los 500 escalones con varias botellas a cuestas. Se habla mucho de la viticultura heroica y poco del enoturismo heroico.

World.title: Por el Rouletenburg de Dostoievski: un viaje a Baden-Baden, Wiesbaden y Bad Homburg
World.content:
El escritor ruso desplegó pasión, literatura y su adicción a la ruleta en estas tres ciudades de Alemania que le sirvieron de inspiración para ‘El jugador’

Roulettenburg es la ciudad ficticia de juego y aguas termales que Fiódor Dostoievski creó para El jugador (1866) con su memoria de las ciudades de Baden-Baden, Wiesbaden y Bad Homburg, en Alemania. Anna Dostoievskaia, su joven esposa y taquígrafa de la novela, taquigrafió en agosto de 1867 cómo fue el regreso del genio a Baden-Baden, donde empeñó incluso su anillo de bodas (el de ella) para seguir jugando. Sudaba, temblaba, perdía casi todo otra vez soñando con el dinero que traería la ruleta. Pero se recuperó con la genialidad de ella, que se convertiría en su editora y librera, y en quien logró consolidar su obra globalmente.

En el centro de Baden-Baden, al suroeste del país y una de las tres ciudades que inspiran el lugar donde transcurre El jugador, está el paseo Lichtentaler, con decenas de tipos de rosas, dalias, castaños, azaleas, ginkos y robles junto al Museo Frieder Burda de arte contemporáneo. Más o menos al final de los más de dos kilómetros junto al río Oos, a los pies de la Selva Negra, el viajero observa un edificio neoclásico con columnas y la maestría de las pinturas mural: es el Trinkhalle. El edificio se construyó en la primera mitad del siglo XIX y Jakob Götzenberger pintó los murales que representan mitos autóctonos y adornan su fachada. Llama la atención el de la sirena enamorada —¡pobre!— de un cazador al que fue enriqueciendo con joyas sacadas de un palacio submarino. Pero él quería siempre más joyas; hasta exigir a su amada que robara la corona de oro del rey de las profundidades. Tras morir a manos del rey, la sangre de la sirena tiñó el agua. El cazador, arrepentido, deambuló por siempre. Jamás pudo perdonarse haber sacrificado a su gran amor.

Más información Las mejores terrazas de los cafés históricos de Viena

Estatua de Fiódor Dostoievski, del artista Nikolai Karlychanow, en un parque de la ciudad alemana de Bad Homburg. Joerg Hackemann ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Los viajeros que buscan las huellas del escritor ruso en Baden-Baden descubren que en el verano de 1867 Anna y su genial esposo debieron ver los frescos cada tarde y reparar, de entre todos, en el de la sirena del lago. Dostoievski siempre pedía dinero, joyas, ropa lujosa para empeñar. Él temblaba a veces. Ella lloró al conocer las pérdidas. Esta era la ruta de su paseo vespertino, cuando él salía del casino. El lugar no ha cambiado mucho desde entonces. Hotelitos y restaurantes limitan con el paseo. Estamos en la zona joya del Estado de Baden-Wurtemberg, en una ciudad de cerca de 60.000 habitantes donde se citaban en verano los aristócratas y burgueses en el siglo XIX que durante el invierno se iban a París. Aunque en agosto la ciudad, que en el estío se llena de música, sufre temperaturas inusuales y tormentas eléctricas.

Exterior del Museo Frieder Burda de arte contemporáneo, en Baden-Baden. Peter Schickert ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Anna Dostoievskaia taquigrafió en su diario la cara más inusual del genio y el lugar, la del jugador y su trampa. Harto de deudas, Dostoievski firmó un contrato mortal con su editor: entregaría en tiempo récord El jugador o perdería los derechos de todas sus obras. Y ella llegó a su vida con el reto de taquigrafiar la obra en 26 días. Él, viudo y 25 años mayor, le pidió que se casaran. En el verano de 1867, Anna estaba embarazada y escribía en su diario la odisea paralela a El jugador. Taquigrafió: “Sus jardines son perfectos, sus fuentes cantan, pero cada rincón huele a dinero perdido”. También: “Las calles están llenas de rusos que pasean con sonrisas falsas ocultando que por la noche han empeñado sus abrigos”. Además: “Me desesperaba que Fedja siguiera convencido de que podía ganar miles”. Ese agosto también anotaba: “Llevamos cuatro días comiendo sin pagar (…) no nos quedará más remedio que empeñar mi vestido morado, el único que queda para empeñar”. “Fedja se abalanzó sobre mí (…) y confesó llorando que lo había perdido todo…”, dejó escrito el 21 de agosto de 1867.

La pareja vivía en dos habitaciones en una casa humilde de la calle BäderstraBe, junto al balneario de Caracalla —piscinas abajo, arriba zona nudista con aguas de contraste, baño turco y un restaurante sencillo para comer—. En la calle adoquinada y en la casa que se alza donde ambos vivieron hoy el genio permanece con un busto, libro e inscripción en la fachada en su honor. Nada aquí recuerda que ese tiempo no fue fácil.

Baden-Baden es joya de la Unesco y hoy, como debió ocurrir siempre, tiene su propio plan de sostenibilidad en, por ejemplo, transporte y aguas termales. Según la actriz Marlene Dietrich, tiene también el casino más bello del mundo. El lujoso casino, en el edificio Kurhaus, está decorado imitando el estilo del palacio de Versalles. Frente a las ruletas, los y las crupiers piden que se haga juego, cortan el aire con la palma de la mano y hacen girar la rueda. “He visto de todo aquí”, dice un crupier de ascendencia española. “Es un buen lugar. Hay gente que pierde. O gana. Es bonito el sitio y la ciudad. ¿Qué es lo que siempre sale? No podría decirte”. Un jugador, frente a él, apunta en un rústico cuaderno dónde pone cada ficha. Parece probar un método de juego, comprobar una ley. Dostoievski también creyó haber encontrado la fórmula para ganar. Taquigrafiaba en su diario Anna: “Él regresó a casa. Entonces teníamos 55 taleros. Se los di. (…) Nos quedamos con cuatro taleros porque el quinto estaba reservado para el almuerzo”.

Interior del casino Baden-Baden. JLGuti ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Él se había enganchado a la ruleta en Wiesbaden, capital del Estado federal de Hesse —y también inspiración para Roulettenburg—. Wiesbaden, junto al Rin, es tan tranquila, ordenada y armónica que, pese a sus casi 300.000 habitantes, el viajero siente el lugar como hogar.

Una de las calles en el centro histórico de Baden-Baden. carla65 ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Rodeado de jardines, recuerda mucho a Baden-Baden, incluso por sus termas, las aguas que manan de fuentes en la calle, el juego y su atracción. “Creía tener el método para ganar. Tenía poco más de 20 años. Trabajaba. Me arreglaba. Iba al casino. Apostaba. Mi método de juego no podía fallar, pero en poco tiempo perdí todo. Así descubrí que dentro de mí había un jugador. Corté con las apuestas y dejé de ir al casino, pero el jugador sigue ahí”, dice Thomas, de pie junto a la Kurhaus de Wisbaden. Él tiene 59 años, nació en Wisbaden y el juego y el dinero forman parte de su ADN. Y también forma parte de su memoria la paz que hay a los pies de los montes Taunus. En 1865, Dostoievski comenzó aquí Crimen y castigo, y tramó El jugador. “Todo en la ciudad es una trampa. Las aguas te curan el cuerpo y matan el alma”, escribió en El jugador. “El parque era magnífico, con castaños centenarios y fuentes que cantaban. Pero yo no veía nada de eso, solo veía el casino, que me llamaba como un abismo”. Su esposa, que, según escribió en sus memorias, taquigrafiaba 200 palabras por minuto cuando conoció al escritor, pronto tomó el timón administrativo de la familia. A orillas del Rin, en Wiesbaden, él la escribía: “Lo he vuelto a perder todo. (…). Envía dinero para ir”.

Interior del Kurhaus de la ciudad de Wiesbaden. ZImages / Alamy / CORDON PRESS

En verano, hoy la Luisenplatz de Wiesbaden se llena de terrazas con comida de todos los continentes junto a la catedral. En invierno aquí huele al vino caliente del mercado de Navidad. El busto de Dostoievski está en la Nizzaplätzchen, en el Kurpark, pero no describen sus gestos la relación casi mística con la ruleta, ni su obsesión. Todo el foco estaba en el juego —“De las maravillas de la naturaleza solo he visto el Rin con sus orillas. Eso sí es una maravilla”, escribiría—. También en Bad Homburg, ciudad balneario que los reyes prusianos y emperadores alemanes utilizaron como residencia de verano habitual en el siglo XIX, atrayendo a la alta sociedad europea.

El Kaiser-Wilhelms-Bad, un histórico edificio balneario en la ciudad de Bad Homburg. Luise Berg-Ehlers ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

En esta ciudad alemana, la Torre Blanca despunta en el horizonte y se siente el vivificante aire de los Taunus. A partir del siglo XX esta ciudad de poco más de 50.000 habitantes se convirtió en la predilecta de los más adinerados de Fráncfort, en especial tras la devastación de la guerra. La ciudad, que nació sobre más de veinte manantiales, este año ha eliminado de los festejos estivales los fuegos artificiales, las hogueras y cualquier tipo de fogatas. Aquí Dostoievski acabó de construir su Roulettenburg.

La torre blanca del castillo de Bad Homburg. Sina Ettmer ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

El genio pareció encontrar la cura tras jugar tres días seguidos y perder: “Anya, ángel de mi guarda. Me ha ocurrido algo grande: me he librado de la abominable ilusión que me ha atormentado durante casi 10 años. (…) soñaba con ganar dinero. Soñaba con ello en serio, con pasión. ¡Pero ahora se acabó! Esta fue verdaderamente la última vez. (…) ahora dedicaré mi mente a cosas de provecho (…) Y así mi trabajo será mejor y más rentable, (…) sigamos juntos nuestro camino, ¡y me encargaré de que seas feliz!”. Era 1971. Pocos meses después, la joven Anna editaba y enviaba los libros de su marido al extranjero. Convertida en editora y librera, cumplió el sueño de él de atraer dinero.

World.title: Italia quiere poner orden en el caos de sus 12.000 playas privadas: más transparencia y nuevas tasas
World.content:
Entre el 33% y el 42% de los arenales del país son de pago. El Gobierno de Meloni, presionado por Bruselas, abrirá a concurso su gestión

Italia presume de sus 8.000 kilómetros de costa, pero disfrutar de ellos no siempre es gratis. Mientras que en otras partes ir a la playa significa buscar un hueco en la arena, en Italia la experiencia suele ser muy distinta. Encontrar un espacio donde plantar la sombrilla sin pagar puede convertirse en toda una aventura. En amplios tramos del litoral, el acceso al mar está gestionado por empresas privadas, mediante concesiones públicas, que han transformado las playas en un negocio multimillonario. El resultado es una de las estampas más características del verano italiano: bosques interminables de sombrillas perfectamente alineadas, acompañadas de sus respectivas tumbonas, esperando a ser alquiladas por precios que pueden superar los 35 euros al día.

Este modelo, muy arraigado en el país y marcado por una gestión plagada de irregularidades, afronta una reforma que lleva años aplazándose a pesar de la presión de Bruselas para poner orden. Las playas gestionadas por concesionarios privados no han dejado de ganar terreno. Según la asociación ecologista italiana Legambiente, ocupan ya más del 42% de los arenales del país. El Ministerio de Infraestructuras rebaja esa cifra al 33%, una diferencia que se explica por el criterio utilizado para el cálculo: el Gobierno utiliza para sus cuentas toda la línea costera italiana y no únicamente las zonas aptas para el baño.

Desde hace décadas, las empresas, casi siempre familiares —las concesiones suelen heredarse—, pagan cánones relativamente bajos al Estado por explotar espacios públicos, mientras los precios para los usuarios han aumentado de forma exponencial. Las concesionarias gestionan los servicios como los baños, las duchas, los vestuarios, los aparcamientos, además del alquiler de sombrillas y tumbonas. También controlan los chiringuitos y cafeterías y se encargan de las labores de salvamento. Mientras que las zonas públicas suelen estar descuidadas, a menudo sucias, y desprovistas de servicios públicos.

Se trata de un asunto sensible que divide a la opinión pública italiana. Para unos, las playas de pago garantizan orden, limpieza y comodidad; para otros, representan la privatización de un bien público que debería ser accesible para todos. La principal crítica al sistema es la enorme diferencia entre lo que pagan las concesionarias por explotar las playas y los beneficios que obtienen. El Estado recauda entre 80 y 100 millones de euros al año por las concesiones, mientras que el sector, marcado por la opacidad, mueve más de 2.000 millones de euros anuales, según distintas estimaciones. El propio Tribunal de Cuentas italiano ha advertido de que los cánones abonados por los empresarios no suelen ser proporcionales a los ingresos que obtienen.

Uno de los aspectos más controvertidos del modelo italiano es que las concesiones se han renovado durante años casi por inercia. Sin concursos abiertos ni una competencia efectiva y sin controles ni transparencia, los mismos operadores han conservado la explotación de amplios tramos del litoral público durante generaciones, consolidando un sistema difícil de encontrar en otros países europeos.

Un paso adelante

Bruselas lleva años reclamando cambios. La Comisión considera que Italia incumple la directiva Bolkestein de 2009, que obliga a garantizar la libre competencia en la adjudicación de este tipo de concesiones, y ha presionado repetidamente a Roma. Tras décadas de aplazamientos y enfrentamientos, el Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni ha abordado la cuestión. La reforma aprobada prevé que para el 30 de septiembre de 2027 salgan a concurso público todas las playas de pago, unas 12.000 repartidas por todo el país. Además, las concesiones tendrán una duración limitada, de entre cinco y 20 años, y habrá compensaciones económicas para los actuales titulares por las inversiones y obras que hayan realizado.

La perspectiva de abrir el mercado ha despertado, sin embargo, inquietud entre muchos empresarios del sector, que temen que los concursos favorezcan la entrada de grandes grupos turísticos o fondos de inversión capaces de desplazar a los negocios familiares que tradicionalmente han dominado las costas italianas.
