The experts say violence was committed by both sides during the war. In their view, Georgian society still has a taboo around discussing abuses committed by its own armed forces during the Abkhaz war, although acknowledging them is necessary to understand the causes of the tragedy. Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation launched in Turkiye: The experts believe ending Abkhazia’s isolation is in the region’s long-term interests and does not contradict Georgia’s interests, despite Tbilisi’s continued efforts to create obstacles.

Full text of the discussion

Inal Khashig: Hello! On the air is “Chegemskaya Pravda.”

The past week was very event-filled. Strictly speaking, that is what we will be discussing. Many events occurred there, both in foreign and domestic policy. And today, our regular political expert, Astamur Tania, is visiting us. Astamur, good day!

Astamur Tania: Good day!

Inal Khashig: Yes, the problem with gasoline, with fuel, which has gripped Abkhazia and not only Abkhazia – Russia is reeling from a gasoline shortage as well. And today I refueled at 110 rubles per liter.

Astamur Tania: You can be congratulated.

Inal Khashig: Yes, two or three weeks ago this would have seemed, probably, like something unnatural.

Astamur Tania: Maybe you’ll save the gasoline and sell it in a week for 150.

Inal Khashig: Yes, but that’s how it turned out. I refueled and I’m happy. It turns out one doesn’t need much for happiness. And in this context, of course, there is a lot of all kinds of talk regarding this shortage. A certain portion of the shortage was compensated through deliveries from Georgia.

This is no humanitarian aid; it is pure business, but nevertheless, a heap of all kinds of talk. By the way, I took a look with my own eyes at who said what officially. The Abkhaz government acknowledged the shortage and said that it would not obstruct it. In Georgia, the authorities said that the Georgian government has nothing to do with it; it is pure business. Nevertheless, in Georgia itself…

Astamur Tania: They also said that they would not obstruct it.

Inal Khashig: They won’t obstruct it, yes.

A portion of our society is chronically opposed to any contacts with Georgia in this regard. On the other hand, as for me… Well, you know, not all contacts are the same. When your entire economy is at a standstill due to a lack of gasoline at the height of the resort season, and you have the opportunity to buy, to acquire this gasoline in Georgia, then it seems to me that here one needs to set what is more important—certain conventionalities, or the fact that a lack of gasoline primarily hits the security of the country. It seems to me that this is the most important thing.

On the other hand, in Georgia itself, there is also a scandal. That is, there are also people unhappy there with the fact that gasoline is being sold to Abkhazia. And there it is being presented under the sauce that this gasoline goes directly to Russian military bases. That is, such nonsense as well, but which many willingly believe. Nevertheless, such is the situation. And based on what is happening with oil refineries in Russia, the end of this crisis is not visible in the near term at all.

How do you generally view this entire situation with this fuel, with all these deliveries from Georgia, and so on?

Astamur Tania: Over many years, you and I have spoken with enviable regularity about the need to search for and expand contacts in areas representing mutual interest. In particular, we spoke about the development of border trade, about the legalization of trade relations. So it would be strange if I were now to say that I am against these deliveries.

If we speak about the political component of our relations, despite this, we have quite fruitful relations in the field of energy. And why hide it, there are very many Georgian agricultural products on our market. It can be said that an expansion of the product range has occurred.

Despite the fact that both Abkhaz and Georgian representatives of their respective authorities state that they are not obstructing it and that it is linked to humanitarian and other issues, even here it was openly acknowledged that this gasoline comes from Georgia. They even came up with the term “gasoline from alternative sources.” It makes it seem as though we border Russia to the west and alternative sources to the east. A political science term for local application could already be coined: “Abkhaz-Alternative negotiations took place…”

Joking aside, I think this is ultimately a positive step. When you and I discussed this, we were aiming precisely at the point that a de-escalation of our relations is necessary. There is a lot of propaganda and hate speech involved in all of this, yet steps like these help build a climate of trust—that much cannot be denied.

It is another matter entirely whether this will remain a one-off occurrence or project into something broader, leading to significant decisions in other areas. Time will tell.

Naturally, we see that the reaction on the Abkhaz side is also mixed. However, our main political figures refrained from using this situation to issue statements condemning the Abkhazian leadership. We know that voices within opposition circles have also repeatedly stressed the need for a negotiation process with Georgia. In that sense, a certain consensus exists. The situation in Georgia, of course, is quite different, as internal political tensions there are much sharper.

Inal Khashig: They’re jailing people there.

Astamur Tania: Yes. In general, if we look back—even if we trace things back to the origins of the armed conflict—I believe domestic political circumstances were among the main drivers that triggered it.

The illegitimate State Council regime in power at the time held onto authority almost purely through force. In suppressing the supporters of the ousted president, Gamsakhurdia, they conducted bloody raids into Western Georgia. Their position was extremely precarious, so they shifted the center of escalation to Abkhazia to address their internal political objectives.

They ultimately lost control over Abkhazia, but it must be acknowledged that Shevardnadze’s regime managed to retain power back then. That was the price.

Today, the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict continues to be used primarily for domestic political ends.

We saw how former president Saakashvili, currently imprisoned, suddenly re-energized. It appears this entire wave was initiated by him. He provoked it, drawing on his substantial base of supporters, effectively giving the green light to inflame the crisis surrounding gasoline deliveries to Abkhazia.

I view this entire affair as a maneuver in an internal political struggle.

How much restraint and patience the current authorities will display remains to be seen. As for the opposition spectrum, it is naturally heterogeneous.

Even if we imagine a scenario where a power shift takes place in Georgia, it would be naive to expect liberals to take charge. Judging by the prevailing tone in the media space, there is a serious threat that populist-chauvinists could come to power—figures with whom it would be far more difficult for us, and indeed for Georgian society, to deal. That risk is by no means zero.

The real concern is that we risk once again becoming a tool for aggressive domestic political propaganda, and we must keep that in mind.

There is another aspect that directly concerns us: we must diversify all risks related to fuel supplies and secure multiple sources. If the Georgian side were to become the sole supplier of fuel, that position would quickly turn into a lever of economic coercion.

Our approach must remain highly flexible and rely on diverse sources—from Georgia, from Russia, and from other avenues we have yet to explore.

Inal Khashig: As before. There was Romania, Bulgaria.

Astamur Tania: Yes. All these possibilities need to be explored.

In general, we need to get used to the idea that, unfortunately, the stable period—stable in an economic sense, in terms of deliveries, financial inflows, and so on—is, in my opinion, behind us. Our authorities and political circles must be prepared for extraordinary steps and new, unexpected challenges.

We simply need to understand that we are living in such a time, and it is not getting any better.

In this sense, it seems to me that these emerging contacts with the Georgian side still need to be brought into the realm of political detente as well. I believe there is someone to talk to in Georgia.

The tragedy is simply that Georgian legislation on occupied territories prohibits Georgia itself from conducting negotiations with Abkhazia. As a result, our relations are reduced to exchanging mutual claims in the public sphere.

Even regarding this decision on gasoline—localized as it is—if such a situation had occurred during the existence of the Coordination Council prior to 2008, I don’t think it would have caused such upheavals. The two sides would have sat down, agreed, signed a protocol, and affixed the signatures of international representatives, as the UN and others did. It would have been a bilateral agreement, and no questions would have arisen from either side.

Therefore, I say once again: we need to think about how to revive a full-fledged negotiation format where two sides exist. Otherwise, we will encounter these issues continuously and will have to solve them manually.

Inal Khashig: The topic of Georgia has been quite prominent in recent days. I don’t know whether it is connected to another anniversary of the start of the war, the events of August 8, or something else, but nevertheless, while this discussion around the conflict isn’t the primary headline in Georgia, it remains on everyone’s lips.

Former State Minister of Georgia Gia Baramidze gave an interview to a Georgian YouTube channel. In it, he stated that during the war he participated on the Georgian side of the commission for the exchange of prisoners, refugees, and the search for missing persons—working alongside Paata Zakareishvili. Beslan Kobakhia represented our side. To clarify his role back then: he stated that during the war, the Georgians could not execute prisoner exchanges with the Abkhazians because they had no leverage or prisoner pool left, as they were actually executing Abkhazian captives.

Naturally, a scandal erupted in Georgia, leading to a very telling reaction from the Georgian authorities: they opened a criminal case against Baramidze under the charge of high treason—not under slander, mind you, but high treason.

Astamur Tania: Because he was an official who possessed relevant information. And he presented this information, which was classified, in an open format. All of this is being hidden.

Inal Khashig: But on the other hand, this means that they do acknowledge it after all. I see another opportunity here. The war and what happened during it—how it started, how it developed, how it ended, and so on—constantly becomes a tool tailored to the political climate within Georgian society, serving both domestic political agendas and external audiences.

If you remember, it originally started as a Georgian-Abkhaz conflict. Now, however, they deny that it is a Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, choosing instead to view it strictly as a conflict with Russia, with the Abkhaz framed as mere bystanders.

This admission might actually serve as a starting point for them to confront the root causes of the war internally and finally acknowledge what they ultimately did.

If we look at the facts, I can name a dozen Abkhaz right now who were taken prisoner and executed. For example, in August, at the very beginning of the war, Oleg Ashba was captured and shot. The same happened to the Akirtava brothers, Sasha Mirzoyan, Amichba, and many others who were taken prisoner and ostentatiously executed right at the funerals of Georgian soldiers. These facts are well-attested. On our side, thank God, all of this is fully documented: there is the White Book, and the Prosecutor General’s Office formally recorded these cases at the time.

If people in Georgian society truly want to understand what happened and how, it costs nothing to present these documents. The names, surnames, dates of capture, and execution details are all fully recorded. I think this could serve as a genuine starting point in searching for a resolution to the conflict. Obviously, the overall issue is vast, but concrete steps are necessary. If they want to understand why the war started and how it unfolded, this is where they ought to begin—especially now that there is a public admission from a former high-ranking Georgian official who directly handled missing persons and prisoner exchanges. Let them investigate it; I believe it is vital.

There is another interview currently sparking active debate in Georgian society—an interview with Nika Gvaramia, the former Prosecutor General and an opposition leader who recently served time and is now free. By the way, he is originally from Sukhumi. He pointed out that Georgian society spends far too much time clinging to memories, dwelling on what Abkhazia used to be, grieving its loss, and so on. He argues that they need to abandon this mindset and focus instead on the future—discussing what lies ahead rather than constantly digging through the past.

I think this is a very important message. How he visualizes it in practice and how it will unfold remains another question. Nonetheless, he asserts that the Abkhaz must be shown progress toward the European Union, demonstrating that they would feel secure and comfortable within it.

I believe any real initial steps must begin with trust, right? If trust is the goal, then we inevitably return to that ill-fated Law on Occupied Territories that restricts us in every way. That law would likely need to be repealed if you want to achieve results on the other side…

Astamur Tania: Well, at the same time, he sharply criticized the idea of fuel deliveries to the territory of Abkhazia.

Inal Khashig: There is no cohesive approach.

Astamur Tania: In my view, all of this belongs mostly to domestic political discourse. Abkhazia is simply being used there to heighten emotional intensity. That applies to Gvaramia’s statement, and I would emphasize once more that no one should draw far-reaching conclusions based on a single remark. We need to watch how public sentiment evolves.

As for Baramidze’s statements, there is nothing new for us here. Parties in any armed conflict live within a standard narrative—at least one generated for public consumption and propaganda—where only noble knights like Ivanhoe or Wilfred of Ivanhoe fought on your side, while the other side was made up of savages. In reality, to chart a path toward understanding this problem—despite all the complexities of our pre-war political relations with the Georgians (which, by the way, were barely evident at the everyday level, but certainly present politically due to differing national projects)—the primary responsibility always rests with the side that made the moral choice to resort to violence.

If a side made that moral choice, one must expect that military abuses of the kind Baramidze described would stem primarily from them. They did not dispatch regular units into Abkhazia without a track record; these were people whose hands were already stained with blood. They had just brutally suppressed the Zviadists in Samegrelo, gaining extensive experience in illegal detentions, arrests, and crackdowns. They were well-practiced in these methods, and naturally, such behavior came seamlessly to them.

For the residents of Abkhazia, it was an absolute shock—not only for the Abkhaz, but for local Georgians as well. They could not believe their own countrymen were capable of such actions, given the notorious criminal background of the leaders driving the entire process and the figures actively carrying it out.

Of course, as a conflict expands and intensifies, violations inevitably occur on all sides. It would be naive to imagine that the Abkhaz are the kind of people to turn the other cheek in such a situation; it is a completely different reality, and that must be understood.

Crimes were committed on both sides, but the fundamental responsibility for initiating the process rests with the party that started it.

As for their methods… why stick our heads in the sand? Those methods are well known, not just from what happened in Abkhazia, but from what took place within Georgia proper.

It is clear that due to current domestic political issues in Georgia, they prefer to sweep this topic under the rug. I see virtually no public discussion about what transpired in Western Georgia on the eve of the Georgian-Abkhazian conflict. A taboo has been placed on that topic for obvious reasons—nobody wants to reopen those raw wounds when society already faces so many problems. Nevertheless, it must be taken into account.

Sooner or later, history always resurfaces in its darker manifestations if we attempt to study it in a sanitized form. We must know this history in its entirety. As for that… I suppose that is everything I wanted to say on the matter. Yes.

We are operating against a very heavy historical backdrop, yet there are occasional glimmers showing that people are attempting to look at the problem from a different angle. This is even happening within government circles.

Take, for example, the statements made by Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze. We certainly do not expect him to tell us how wonderful we are or that they intend to recognize Abkhazia’s independence, but he did mention the restoration of confidence-building measures. That is a very important step. Occasionally, articles appear offering a relatively objective look at the history of our relations since ancient times. Furthermore, some Georgian writers are even addressing the notorious pseudo-scientific theory of Ingorokva, which has poisoned the minds of multiple generations. Granted, such pieces are rare amid the vast sea of opposing literature, but they do appear.

In that sense, there are small glimmers of hope that genuine realization will come.

We also need to draw conclusions regarding our own policies—for instance, concerning the Gali district. That is something we will inevitably need to address.

However, given the current lack of trust, any step forward is easily misinterpreted as granting unfair advantages to the other side. For that reason, I do not believe in grand, immediate solutions, nor do I think it is productive to debate overarching political questions right now. Instead, targeted measures—focusing on transport, communication, humanitarian concerns, and the movement of people and goods across the border—are precisely what would help establish the foundational conditions needed for genuine dialogue.

Inal Khashig: Let’s move on to another topic: the de-isolation of Abkhazia. In Turkey, a campaign to de-isolate Abkhazia is gaining momentum. On the one hand, it includes the recognition of Abkhaz passports as valid travel documents; on the other, it seeks to restore direct communication—specifically maritime links—between Turkey and Abkhazia that existed immediately after the war. For a time, those connections operated, people could travel, and passenger boats ran. Although that was later cut off, a campaign to revive it is unfolding now.

At first, this was an initiative driven by private individuals within the Abkhazian and Adyghe civil sector. It then expanded to the point where eight political parties represented in the Turkish parliament formed a united front, declaring that Abkhazia must be de-isolated. Initially, our Confederation of Abkhaz Communities in Turkey (Abkhazfed) reacted with a certain degree of possessiveness, arguing that the movement had no right to take the lead and that Abkhazfed should have authored the idea. It was a completely unnecessary friction. However, after Abkhazian society here voiced strong support and our Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement, a course correction took place. Representatives from both the initiative group and Abkhazfed met and reached a consensus that a consolidated movement for de-isolation is essential.

How do you view this prospect overall? On the one hand, these eight political parties belong to the opposition, spanning a varied spectrum from left to right. How viable is this initiative, and to what extent might it simply be an element of internal Turkish political maneuvering to capture votes—specifically from the Abkhaz and Adyghe diaspora, who by various estimates number up to four million—ahead of upcoming parliamentary and early presidential elections?

In your view, is this driven purely by domestic politics, or is there a real opportunity here to translate this into a broader movement originating from the civil sector and picked up by the opposition? Could Ankara actually take concrete steps such as de-isolating Abkhazia, recognizing Abkhaz passports, and reopening maritime transport?

Astamur Tania: Naturally, I supported this initiative—as did you and many others. It would be foolish not to support it. Indeed, many on our side did.

At the same time, we must recognize that over the last few decades, there has been an obvious degradation in our expert and public outreach across all fronts, including the Turkish direction.

I carefully read what Elchin Adzinba wrote. Fortunately, we have experts of such high caliber who understand the inner workings of Turkish politics. We must take his insights into account in our work, as there are bound to be hidden undercurrents. But in politics, nothing is ever entirely positive or entirely negative; it is a constant struggle. He called for expanding the circle of people with whom we engage because decisions on such a significant issue—whether made behind the scenes or officially voiced—are ultimately crafted in government corridors. This strategy ensures the effort does not look like a mere pawn in Turkey’s internal political competition. He specifically warned about this, and we must keep it in mind.

Returning to the reaction of our own society: it often resembles a sparkler. Something reactive happens, everyone flares up instantly, and then all at once it goes out, gets forgotten, and passes. In six months, no one will even remember it. That is the tragedy.

We still have public organizations and specialized institutions that operate on state funding. Previously, we periodically held conferences, including on legal issues, where our situation was discussed from the perspective of international law—specifically how our rights are restricted regarding freedom of movement, education, and other matters.

In international politics, only that which exists in the information space actually exists. If we say nothing ourselves—well, thank God Turkish Abkhazians stepped up to raise this topic. But the initial momentum ought to stem from here, as they do not face direct isolation problems themselves; they hold passports that allow free movement worldwide. Yet no initiative originated from our side.

As a proposal, we could hold a scientific conference—one with real public resonance. Rather than merely recounting history, it should analyze how this tightening of constraints came about, which norms of international law it violates, and what consequences it brings. Even if we set aside the Georgian side’s internal political confrontation, the de-isolation of Abkhazia does not contradict their interests either.

Obstacles are always created from that side. For instance, after the armed conflict, we conducted negotiations and signed documents on the non-use of force, peacekeeping forces, and refugee return procedures. Then they claimed it did not suit them because the return was too slow. Now they make empty claims about 300,000 refugees, even though that many people never lived in Abkhazia to begin with. Meanwhile, we returned about 50,000 refugees to the Gal district—which apparently was still not enough for their narrative.

Later, we held negotiations on confederate relations and union structures—using various terminologies from 1997 to 1998, up until the May events. Domestic political circumstances intervened again. In the end, who won? Neither the refugees nor Georgian society. The exact same logic applies to this issue.

Honestly, I would consider it rational if the Georgian side did not obstruct Abkhazia’s de-isolation, as it could easily be included in a package of measures to build mutual trust.

As for Ankara, everyone understands that if the Georgian side stated it had no objections, the matter would be resolved much more easily. Otherwise, it is difficult to predict how long it will take or whether it will yield concrete results.

However, the fact that both our society and our diaspora are actively engaged around this vital issue is a result in itself. Regardless of whether our passports are ultimately recognized in Turkey, it demonstrates that society is thinking about its prospects and modeling its future. It shows a living society.

And this is not our only challenge; we have plenty of other problems. Sometimes one recalls how dynamic things were in the 1990s and early 2000s—the proactive responses, the strong stances taken by different individuals and organizations. Now, it feels like a stagnant swamp, with only the occasional outburst. You cannot achieve results in such a state. We must work on all fronts and in all directions. Some efforts will succeed, others won’t—but it can be said with certainty that if you do nothing, nothing will happen.

Life recently forced us to deal with pressing issues like fuel supplies. We will face many more such challenges, and we will have to manage them. If you claim to be an independent state, you have to act like one. Independence is not just a collection of legislative acts and political declarations; it requires active work to fill those structures with real substance. It is a creative process.

If a nation lacks that creative drive, it begins to fade and dull. Unfortunately, we are observing this trend. You and I spoke about the Abkhaz language earlier—it is good that there is activity, though whether it will yield results remains to be seen. But above all, society must show signs of life. Nobody will look out for us if we don’t stand up for ourselves. That is what I wanted to say.

Inal Khashig: In any case, during our turbulent times—and not only in turbulent times, but in any period, whether peaceful or turbulent—there must be clear plans for the future. Moreover, there should be multiple options across all directions, including a Plan A, Plan B, and Plan C, along with continuous modeling of potential scenarios.

I am basing this once again on the recent gasoline crisis, when under Aslan Bzhania, a sudden decision was made to hand the entire fuel market over to a single pair of hands. One ought to have considered the consequences beforehand and anticipated how all of this would play out—not just focusing on how beautiful and well-maintained our gas stations would look, but realizing that the primary problem arises when there is no gasoline at those stations in the first place. That situation highlights a lack of deep analysis and the absence of a pragmatic, truly calculated strategy.

Astamur Tania: Well, you understand that we aren’t experts in all fields of government, right?

Inal Khashig: No, of course not.

Astamur Tania: On gasoline, I’m definitely not an expert, nor on these monopolies. One simply needs to involve the expert community where we do not understand. Give public resonance to the problem. I see many things being done, but they lack competent public coverage.

Inal Khashig: Astamur, say you have money, right? No level-headed businessman will tell you that all your money needs to be placed in one specific bank. He spreads it across different banks.

What I’m getting at is that when we have no oil of our own—oil might be lying around somewhere, but there is neither refining, nor extraction, nothing—and we buy this gasoline… When you buy this gasoline, there must be different sources.

Astamur Tania: Now you and I are going in circles. I agree with you, which is why we spoke about diversification.

Inal Khashig: On that note, we will actually conclude our conversation: with the fact that Astamur agrees.

Astamur Tania: To each his own sore point. As for me, I don’t drive.

Inal Khashig: I drive. It somehow turned out that not only I, but probably the majority of Abkhazian drivers go to sleep in the evening with the thought of where to refuel tomorrow, where to find this gasoline. And in the morning they wake up with the same thought. And I think that for the state, this should be the very last problem in reality—when for its citizens, their main thought consists of how to get gasoline. In short, so that we don’t have such problems, I will wrap up. Astamur, thank you very much.

Astamur Tania: Thank you. All the best.

Inal Khashig: Let there be light. Goodbye.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: Georgian minister quits politics shortly after ex-PM’s accusations
World.content:
Georgian minister quits politics

Georgia’s Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze is stepping down from his post and leaving politics. He announced the decision at a briefing at the government administration, saying he wanted to devote more time to his family.

Until April 2026, Mamuka Mdinaradze served as head of the State Security Service. On 21 April, he was appointed deputy prime minister and state minister for the coordination of law enforcement agencies. On 29 July, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would take up the post of state minister for regional policy. The new position was due to be created in September, and until then Mdinaradze was appointed regional development minister.

Mdinaradze said his 10 years in politics had been marked by hard work, service to his country and cooperation with the team of the ruling Georgian Dream party. At the briefing, he thanked party members and leaders, including its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili.

Mdinaradze said he had been considering leaving politics for the past several weeks and had made the decision on his own initiative before discussing it with Irakli Kobakhidze and Bidzina Ivanishvili. He said they initially disagreed with his decision, but he ultimately managed to convince both that it would be better for him.

Mdinaradze explained his decision to leave politics by saying he wanted to spend more time with his family. According to him, his children, aged nine and 13, had grown up with him largely absent.

The former minister stressed that his decision had not been prompted by any political or personal crisis. He also said there was no need for him to remain involved in regional development, as the ruling team had other leaders capable of overseeing the area.

Mdinaradze did not rule out returning to politics one day, but said he would do so only if necessary.

“I will return only if the team really needs me and there is no other option,” he said.

Mamuka Mdinaradze

As for his future plans, Mdinaradze said he might try his hand in the private sector, including business, although he does not yet have any specific plans.

“Believe it or not, I haven’t thought about it. Perhaps I’ll try my hand in business,” Mdinaradze said.

Reflecting on his 10-year political career, Mdinaradze said its intensity and the level of responsibility had not been easy for him, and that he now wanted to focus on the part of his life that he had put on the back burner for years.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s announcement that he was leaving politics came after his name was mentioned in connection with serious allegations made by former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili. Garibashvili, who is currently serving a prison sentence, alleged that he had been pressured “on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders”, with Mdinaradze acting as an intermediary, to confess to a corruption offence in order to prevent him from returning to politics in the future.

On 24 August, Garibashvili was charged with a new corruption offence. The charge carries a prison sentence of 11 to 15 years.

According to investigators, key testimony in the case was provided by former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze, who has also been convicted of a corruption offence. According to his testimony, of the 1.5m lari (around $555,000)received as a bribe from businessman Zurab Tukvadze, who won a tender for the Gori Military Hospital, Burchuladze personally handed 750,000 lari (around $277,000) in cash to Irakli Garibashvili in several instalments.

Garibashvili denies the allegations. He says the demand that he admit guilt was politically motivated and intended to limit his ability to return to politics in the future. It was in this context that he mentioned Mamuka Mdinaradze as an intermediary and alleged that the demand had been made on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders.

Mdinaradze did not address the allegations against him when explaining his decision to step down.

World.title: ‘No to occupation and de facto annexation’: Anti-annexation platform launched in Georgia
World.content:
Anti-annexation platform launched in Georgia

A new public association, the Anti-Annexation Platform, has been established in Georgia.

Its founders say the group will be non-partisan and apolitical, with its main goal being to oppose Russia‘s occupation and de facto annexation of Georgian territories through legal and peaceful means.

At the platform’s launch at the Tbilisi Marriott hotel, a declaration entitled “No to occupation and de facto annexation – yes to justice, peace and Georgia’s territorial integrity” was adopted.

According to the declaration, the platform brings together Georgian citizens who regard the country’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, the principles of international law, freedom and human dignity as core values.

The founders say that Russia’s occupation in any form, the de facto annexation of the Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions, support for separatism and forced demographic changes in the occupied territories constitute violations of international law and fundamental human rights.

The declaration also states that the organisation is ready to cooperate with members of any political party, regardless of their political affiliation.

Among the platform’s main objectives are supporting Georgia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty and promoting a legal assessment of Russia’s continuing occupation and de facto annexation.

The group plans to work to protect the rights of internally displaced people and refugees from the occupied territories, prepare legal research and analytical papers, and raise public awareness of developments in the occupied regions.

The platform also intends to cooperate with international partners, think tanks and diplomatic missions. Its activities will include organising conferences, discussions and educational events, as well as helping to protect the rights of people affected by the occupation and de facto annexation.

The platform supports targeted international sanctions against the leaders of the de facto regimes in the occupied regions and individuals involved in the annexation process. The declaration also calls for efforts to initiate international criminal proceedings.

The document stresses that the group’s activities will not be limited to the political agenda.

“We believe that the struggle against occupation and de facto annexation by the Russian Federation is not only a political issue. It is a struggle for justice, human dignity, historical truth and the security of future generations,” the declaration says.

According to its founders, the platform is based on the peaceful and legal resolution of conflicts, respect for international law and the protection of human rights.

“Russia’s de facto or de jure annexation will never become a legal reality, and borders changed by force will never acquire moral or legal legitimacy,” the declaration says.

World.title: Iran’s Supreme Leader сalls on Muslim countries to unite
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 30. Iran is calling on the leaders of Muslim countries, particularly the leaders of the states of West Asia and the countries located around the Persian Gulf, to unite.

Iran’s Supreme Leader, Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, said this today, August 30, in a message marking Unity Week in Iran.

“The solution to the problems of Muslims is unity, friendship and cooperation for the sake of goodness,” he said.

Iran’s Supreme Leader called on the countries of West Asia and the states located around the Persian Gulf to recognize their enemies and confront them.

“The United States and Israel do not want friendship and unity among Muslim countries. The United States and Israel are opposed not only to Iran, but also to the peoples of West Asia and North Africa. It has not even been forgotten that they use disrespectful terms when referring to the leaders of some Muslim countries,” he said.

Khamenei noted that unity among Muslims in the fields of science, security and prosperity, as well as cooperation on various issues, would create conditions for the development of Muslim countries.

Iran’s Supreme Leader called on Iranian citizens not to take actions that could also lead to disagreements and misunderstandings among Iranians themselves.

On February 28, Iran’s former Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, was killed as a result of US and Israeli aerial military strikes against Iran. His son, Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, was appointed to replace Ali Khamenei by a decision of the Assembly of Experts.

World.title: One Nation could revive NSW trade posts scrapped in 'jobs for the boys' saga
World.content:
One Nation NSW leader Mike Newman has said he would consider bringing back overseas trade commissioners if elected next year.

Mr Newman, 54, the party's candidate for Cessnock, was the state's senior trade and investment commissioner in Tokyo from 2022 to 2024.

The Minns government scrapped the roles when it came to power following a "jobs for the boys" scandal involving former deputy premier John Barilaro's appointment to the New York position.

Mr Newman (left) was NSW's senior trade and investment commissioner in Tokyo from 2022 to 2024. (ABC News)

The veteran investment banker, a critic of the state's "bloated" bureaucracy, told the ABC it was a mistake to get rid of the trade posts.

"I commend the Minns government, to be honest, for living up to an election promise. I'll give them that," Mr Newman said.

"But I think what they did was capture what was a scandal and turn it into perhaps a poorer decision.

"If I'd still been the senior trade and investment commissioner during Minns's term to date, he would have been harangued by me constantly to have gone into Japan, Korea, India.

"You can't be the hermit kingdom."

'Too many public servants'

During his announcement as leader on Friday, Mr Newman pledged cuts to the state's public service, which he said was the largest in the southern hemisphere.

"There is so much money and waste that is inside the public service," he said on Friday.

"Having worked inside, I saw firsthand how your money is being misallocated and misspent."

'Like Florida and Texas': One Nation's plans for NSW Former NSW investment commissioner Mike Newman will lead the party to the 2027 state election.

But in an interview with the ABC on Saturday, Mr Newman said the trade commissioners were valuable, and he would seek to reinstate the roles.

"If One Nation has the opportunity to lead, I would definitely look at doing something similar to that, but as I said I want to bring experienced people from the private sector," Mr Newman said.

The trade commissioners were paid a salary of about $487,000 plus allowances, according to a parliamentary committee report in 2023.

The committee reported that the six posts cost taxpayers $12.7 million in 2021-22.

Asked whether bringing back the jobs would increase the size of the bureaucracy, Mr Newman said he wanted to hire people that want to serve their state.

"When I talk about the bloated bureaucracy, I'm saying there are too many public servants, especially amongst those in the senior executive class, who basically see this as a self-serving situation.

" Put it this way, I could have done five times as much business [as trade commissioner] on one-fifth the number of staff. "

Mr Newman says he has seen firsthand how "money is being misallocated and misspent" in the public sector. (ABC News: Bridget Murphy)

Tomorrow, Premier Chris Minns begins a four-day visit to India to "attract investment", his first overseas trip as the state's leader, and one Mr Newman said he should have made much earlier.

On Saturday, Mr Minns said he was "pretty impressed" by Mr Newman's candour.

"He seems like he's going to say what's at the top of his head. I think it's going to be very difficult for Pauline [Hanson] to muzzle him," Mr Minns said.

"I think he's going to say whatever he wants to say. I think that's a good part of politics, I welcome him to the debate."

World.title: Rider dies after 'critical incident' during motorcycle racing event
World.content:
A rider has died after a "critical incident" at a motorcycling racing event south-east of Adelaide.

SA Police said emergency services were called to a private racetrack at a motorsport event at Elwomple following reports of a crash just before 11AM on Sunday.

"Sadly one person has died and a report will be prepared for the coroner," a police spokesperson said.

In a statement, Motorcycling South Australia and The Bend said a "critical incident occurred" during a motorcycle racing event.

The Bend is a motorsport park about 100 kilometres south-east of Adelaide.

"The rider was treated by paramedics and died at the scene," the statement said.

The statement also thanked officials, paramedics and first responders.

"We extend our deepest condolences to the rider's family, friends and the wider motorsport community.

"We ask that the privacy of the rider's family, friends and all those affected be respected at this difficult time."

Motorcycling Australia said it was working with the "relevant authorities" following the incident.

World.title: 'I was a wreck': Popyrin bares his soul before US Open bid
World.content:
Alexei Popyrin hit rock bottom when he feared he wouldn't enjoy even his own wedding next month.

From the giddy high of taking down Novak Djokovic at the 2024 US Open, Popyrin needed a wildcard into this year's New York grand slam after slumping to as low as number 139 in the rankings last month.

He knew then he needed professional help.

The fallen Australian tennis star turned to Oscar Piastri's esteemed mindset coach and credits Emma Murray for helping him find contentment again. To a point.

"It's not easy," Popyrin said in a raw interview ahead of his first-round Open date with former semi-finalist turned 2026 qualifier Grigor Dimitrov.

"A lot of that is what was eating at me, thinking about things, searching for that feeling of being at the career-high rankings, of playing at that level, and it becomes a kind of an unhealthy obsession.

"It becomes a really negative and bad balance between you and tennis and it's what was really not helping me and it was the main culprit in what has been happening over the last few months.

Emma Murray is now working with Alexei Popyrin as he tries to rise in the rankings. (Getty Images: Kym Illman)

"I needed to change that and I needed to change just the whole way I look at tennis as a whole, and it's still a work in progress and it's not going to be a quick fix over one or two weeks."

Popyrin took his first mental-health break after Wimbledon last year before needing another reset following a straight-sets first-round loss at the All England Club six weeks ago to Jiri Lehecka.

"After Wimbledon, I was a wreck," said the former French Open junior champion.

"I used to — well, I still do — every time I lose, I think I don't deserve to have fun. After, I think I don't deserve to be happy.

Popyrin's birthday win Alexei Popyrin has won for the 12th time in 13 matches at the Canadian Masters, giving himself a 27th birthday present by reached the last 32 for the third year in a row.

"I was worried that I wouldn't enjoy my wedding because of my tennis, and when I had that thought for the first time I was like, 'OK, something is really, really wrong and I've really got to take some time and figure things out.'"

The 27-year-old one-time world number 19 has been working with Murray for only a short time, but already the high-performance emotional regulator is making progress.

"I'm trying to not associate my results with how I feel as a person," Popyrin said.

"I'm trying to look at it in a way that it's just a journey that I'm on. Where I am is where I am and what I have to do is just continue trusting the process that I'm on.

"I've stuck with the same team and I haven't changed anything. I believe in the guys. I believe in myself. I believe that everything is just mental for me.

"And if I'm able to make those changes up in my head, then I'm able to not only get to where I am, but I believe I can go further.

"I've got to kind of start from scratch, which is never easy. It's something I have done before, but it's even harder for me to do that because of where I have been and what I have done and what I have achieved.

"But it's important for me if I want to continue playing tennis that I get through this, and the way I get through this is continuing on the trajectory that I have been the last month."

AAP

World.title: Dees deliver Lions' greatest AFLW defeat, Port star's cruel injury blow
World.content:
Melbourne has steamed past an injury-ravaged Brisbane by 56 points to claim a perfect 3-0 start to the AFLW season.

Elsewhere, Port Adelaide lost star forward Indy Tahau to a suspected serious knee injury, overshadowing a thrilling four-point win over GWS in Canberra.

Brisbane grabbed the first goal but the Demons were unstoppable from there, kicking the next 12 and going on to hand the Lions their heaviest AFLW defeat, a 14.5 (89) to 4.9 (33) shellacking at Casey Fields.

Carlton's subtle transition from AFLW darling to contender After a breakout AFLW season last year, Carlton is using some subtle tweaks to take the difficult next step of challenging for the premiership.

Liv Purcell (31 disposals) continued her magnificent form along with Tyla Hanks (24 disposals, eight tackles and a goal), while Kate Hore (24) was prolific, and Tahlia Gillard (11 intercepts) led an impressive defence.

Ryleigh Wotherspoon (three goals, eight tackles), Georgia Gall (two), Mia Austin (two) and Megan Fitzsimon (two) hit the scoreboard.

Lions Marlow Graham (concussion) and Neesa Dooley (collarbone) were both hurt in the first quarter.

Then Belle Dawes (right shoulder) and Ruby Svarc (concussion) were worse for wear after colliding with each other.

Dawes played through pain and finished with 24 disposals and a goal, while Orla O'Dwyer (21) was strong.

Sophie Conway (left knee) and Eleanor Hartill (foot) also played through issues.

Tahau, who previously tore her left ACL, was helped off with a right knee injury late in the third quarter of Port Adelaide's 7.10 (52) to 8.0 (48) victory at Manuka Oval.

It was a tight contest all day and Port led by nine at three-quarter time before Brodee Mowbray goaled twice to put GWS in front.

GWS led until the death, when Port's Matilda Scholz took a terrific intercept mark to create a late attack that ended with Lauren Young marking and kicking the winner with seconds left.

Scholz (30 hit-outs, 24 disposals) was dominant, while Piper Window kicked three goals.

Alyce Parker (21 disposals) was busy for GWS (1-2), who shared the goals around.

Aine McDonagh (left) kicked another three goals in a strong start to the Irishwoman's season, in Hawthorn's win over the Pies. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

At Victoria Park, Hawthorn won their second game of the season, with a 28-point victory over Collingwood.

It was a close game in the opening quarter, with the Hawks leading by eight points at the first change.

They then went on with it, however, kicking 6.3 to 2.7 in the final three terms.

A four-goal-to-one third quarter made the difference, with Jasmine Fleming kicking one of the goals of the day with a brilliant right-foot finish from deep in the pocket.

Aine McDonagh, who last week surpassed Cora Staunton as the most prolific AFLW goal-kicker from Ireland with three goals against Port Adelaide, repeated the dose with another three majors against the Pies to take her career haul to 59.

Ruck Lucy Wales had another big game for Hawthorn, with 23 disposals, 22 hit-outs, nine marks, five tackles and four score involvements.

For the Pies, there were no multiple goal-kickers, with majors to Ruby Schleicher, Ash Centra and Dominique Carbone.

A five-goal final quarter from the Suns was not enough, as Gold Coast fell seven points short against Geelong at Carrara.

The Suns led by two points at quarter time, and four at the long break before a three-goal-to-one third term gave Geelong the break.

Gold Coast came home with 5.1, but the Cats kicked 4.1 to hold on to win 10.4 (64) to 8.9 (57).

Charlie Rowbottom had 39 disposals in a losing cause, while Havana Harris kicked three for the Suns - including the final goal of the game on the siren.

Ava Usher and Alannah Welsh both booted two for the home side.

Geelong's Georgie Prespakis had 33 disposals and eight clearances, while Chloe Scheer kicked three and Ava Murray two for the visitors, who lost Emma Kilpatrick with a dislocated shoulder and Piper Dunlop with a knee injury.

AAP/ABC

World.title: 'Hit by a bus': What 'biohacker' Bryan Johnson thinks will kill him
World.content:
Bryan Johnson just marked another birthday, a potential inconvenience for the man who says he wants to live forever.

Last week, the controversial Silicon Valley mogul turned 49.

But according to his Australian girlfriend, Kate Tolo, that number does not fit with Johnson's physical and mental state.

Loading...

"He annoyingly feels younger than me!" the 30-year-old tells triple j hack.

" I get off the couch and my knees hurt but he is springing up and trying to dunk [a basketball] at the moment. "

Mackay-born Tolo, who has recently joined her boyfriend on his biohacking mission, seeking to become "the world's most measured woman", says she is excited by what is to come.

"In the back of both our minds, female health was always next, and it's such an important and deeply personal issue to me.

"I feel so fortunate."

"Biohacking" refers to the practices of those committed to extreme anti-aging and longevity regimes.

Bryan Johnson recently visited Australia to meet Kate Tolo's family. (X: Bryan Johnson)

American millionaire Bryan Johnson is the movement's poster boy.

Some of his most notable headline-grabbing endeavours include the multi-generational blood plasma swap he engaged in with his teenage son and father, sharing night-time erection tracking data, and more recently claiming that he had cloned himself.

"We are ridiculous people. We are absurd," he tells hack.

"I am a very weird person, and that's OK.

"We love the haters."

Rage baiting vs communication

Johnson's announcement last month that he had cloned himself as a newborn to become his own "blood boy", as well as to "test therapies" and "grow organs for transplantation" was immediately challenged by the internet, scientists and the medical establishment.

"Human cloning is not possible," read the community note underneath Johnson's post on the social media platform X.

What Johnson had actually done was create induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), a method to reprogram adult cells back into a versatile stem cell state — a technology scientists admit is exciting, but does not equate to human cloning.

"I actually listed out in great detail exactly what steps we followed," Johnson tells hack.

Asked whether he "rage baits" — intentionally posting provocative material to boost engagement — Johnson pauses for a second.

"Kate and I have moved the conversation of eight billion humans on planet Earth to discuss the idea of Don't Die," he says.

"So we have a way of communicating things to people that they understand … gets them talking.

"Sometimes we're like, 'are we just over the edge?'

"We're always trying to find that sweet spot because trust and credibility is the number one thing we care about."

'We are artists'

"Don't Die" is the name of the movement started by Johnson, who is still committed to his goal of achieving immortality by 2039.

Earlier this year, he revealed that he had been diagnosed with autoimmune gastritis, a chronic inflammatory condition of the stomach with no cure.

"Points for irony and points for the haters!" he laughs.

" There's a substantial portion of the world that wants me to die. "

While Johnson says it is highly likely he developed the condition long before he started his longevity journey, doctors say that cannot be confirmed conclusively.

Bryan Johnson working out while wearing a VR headset. (Twitter: Bryan Johnson)

Now his focus is on finding a cure.

"The only way we prove ourselves worthy of this mission is if we both get diagnosed with an incurable disease and we have to solve it.

"We're trying to broker a peace between all humans, all countries, AI, and the planet and say, 'can we just be sober for this moment and say none of us want to die, right now?'

"At heart, we are artists … and [Kate and I] just want to play.

"We think it's really a spectacular time to be alive and we're grateful to exist."

The female Bryan Johnson

Kate Tolo's long journey from north Queensland to the centre of Bryan Johnson's biohacking empire in the United States might surprise many, including herself.

She is now listed as the co-founder of Johnson's brands Blueprint, Don't Die, and Immortals, and featured in the Netflix documentary Don't Die: The Man Who Wants to Live Forever.

Australian Kate Tolo is aiming to become the "world's most measured woman" (X: Kate Tolo)

Tolo has now signed up to collect "14 million data points on her menstrual cycle", as part of a protocol that she says involves more than 100 tasks a day and dozens of devices.

"I didn't know how bad the literature was around female health," she tells hack.

"We're measuring my skin, my brain, my microbiome and my gut, my mouth, my stool, my vaginal microbiome, literally everything.

"We're measuring every single day … to translate the lived female experience into numbers so that we can all appreciate and respect it and understand it.

"Let's talk about it. Let's get it out there."

Medical experts weigh in on biohacking

Brooke Nickel, a senior research fellow at the University of Sydney's School of Public Health, is cautious when commenting on the methods used by Johnson and Tolo to boost longevity.

Is Bryan Johnson’s quest to live forever killing us? Scientific discoveries that improve longevity are cause for celebration, but in promoting a rigid lifestyle that is incompatible with socialising, optimisation culture undermines the communal bonds that are central to human flourishing.

"I think there are some genuinely positive things related to the 'biohacking' trends being promoted in terms of prevention and taking an active interest in your health," Dr Nickel says.

"However, much of what is being discussed in these spaces seems to lack robust evidence of benefit and is often accompanied by commercial marketing, particularly when it becomes about 'optimising' or 'hacking' aging.

"So I am sceptical and think we should be careful not to confuse good public health practices with vested interests."

Johnson and Tolo dismiss suggestions that they are trying to make money by capitalising on society's fears around aging and dying, by selling supplements and serums under their brands.

"I think if the goal was for Kate and I to make money, we would not start this business," Johnson says.

"We are genuinely trying to do this to help.

"We don't expect people to believe that."

'I love Australia'

Away from all the headlines, marketing and controversy are ordinary facets of Bryan and Kate's relationship.

He recently visited Australia to meet Kate's family and attend her brother's wedding, which Kate says was one of her favourite moments in life.

"They loved him!" she says.

"He really just, like, integrated with the family."

Loading Instagram content

While Johnson admits the jet lag took its toll (he claimed it increased his biological age by 13 years), he says the long trip was worth it.

"Kate's family is lovely, and I love Australia.

"I did the math, trying to calculate what it would cost to move Australia closer to Los Angeles!"

Asked whether after all of his longevity and biohacking efforts he is worried he will die in a freak accident, Johnson laughs.

"I think I'll probably be taken out by a bus or similar," he says.

" I give everyone full permission to laugh and celebrate it and share with all their friends and family and tell everybody they told them so. "

Tolo's response is more serious.

"If the chances are that we fail, it doesn't stop us from trying anyway.

"We're enjoying our lives, we love this mission, and it's exciting for us to wake up every day and do it."

World.title: More than 30 years on from Lockerbie bombing, first US trial faces delay
World.content:
As the wreckage from Pan Am Flight 103 was being collected from across a small Scottish town, one phrase kept being repeated: "We do not know what happened."

Timeline of the Lockerbie bombing View a chronology of key events in the Lockerbie bombing case.

The plane fell from more than 9 kilometres in the air, crashing into the town of Lockerbie and leaving lives, homes and communities in ruins.

The plane, flying from London to New York on December 21, 1988, simply vanished from radar screens. One moment there, gone the next.

As it was falling, the sky lit up, according to local John Glasgow.

"We tried to get near the plane but it was completely on fire," Mr Glasgow told the Daily News in 1988.

"There were no bodies about. I don't think there would be any chance … It went up in a fireball."

After the Lockerbie bombing, families of victims received $US2.7 billion ($3.7 billion) in compensation from the Libyan government. (Reuters: Greg Bos)

Fragments of a circuit board and timer were later found by investigators, and they established a bomb was placed inside a radio in a piece of luggage on the plane.

Authorities confirmed all 259 people on board were killed, along with 11 people on the ground in Lockerbie.

Before the September 11 attacks of 2001, it was the deadliest terror attack in US history, with 190 Americans killed, and remains the deadliest in the United Kingdom.

The Lockerbie victims also included people from 21 different countries.

The Scottish town of Lockerbie in the aftermath of the bombing of Pan Am flight 103 in December 1988. (File)

US and Scottish investigators have accused a total of three Libyan intelligence operatives since 1991.

One has been acquitted, another convicted, and the third now faces trial in the US, which comes more than two decades since the ruling in the first Lockerbie case.

The trial was scheduled to begin in late August but has been delayed after new evidence emerged.

A hearing has now been set for September.

Interview led to clandestine extradition

In 2020, Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi, a former explosives expert for Libya's intelligence service, became the latest person charged with the Lockerbie bombing.

A 2012 interview Al-Marimi gave to Libyan law enforcement became a crucial piece of evidence for US and Scottish authorities when they obtained a copy in 2017.

"At long last, this man responsible for killing Americans and many others will be subject to justice for his crimes," former US attorney general William Barr said in 2020.

A moment of hope for Lockerbie victims' families Before September 11, it was America's worst terrorist attack — now the alleged bombmaker faces trial

According to US officials, Al-Marimi admitted to building the bomb, working with others to carry out the attack and that it was ordered by Libyan intelligence.

Two years following the charges, Al-Marimi was taken into US custody.

"The families of those killed in the Lockerbie bombing have been told that the suspect Abu Agila Mohammad Masud Kheir Al-Marimi is in US custody," a spokesperson for Scotland's Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service said.

Al-Marimi admitted to building the bomb that took down Pan Am 103 in an 2012 interview, according to US official (AP: Alexandria Sheriff's Office)

US officials did not say how he was detained, but in late 2022 local Libyan media reported he had been kidnapped by armed men from his residence in the country's capital Tripoli.

Who were the other accused terrorists?

Before Al-Marimi, two other Libyan intelligence operatives were charged with conspiracy, murder and the destruction of Pan Am 103 in 1991.

Abdel Baset Ali al-Megrahi was also the head of security for Libyan Arab Airlines, and Lamen Khalifa Fhimah was the LAA station manager at Luqa Airport in Malta.

The evidence that linked them to the attack came from a small fragment inside a piece of a shirt, according to the FBI.

Abdel Baset Ali al-Megrahi remains the only person convicted of the Lockerbie bombing after he was sentenced to life in prison in 2001. (Manoocher Deghati: AFP)

The pair faced trial in 2000 by a panel of Scottish judges, in a purpose-built courtroom on a former US military base in the Netherlands called Camp Ziest.

In 2001, Fhimah was acquitted of the charges, while al-Megrahi was sentenced to life in prison.

He was later released on compassionate grounds in 2009, and died three years later.

In 2002 the Libyan Government offered to pay $US2.7 billion in compensation to victims of the Lockerbie bombing, but tied the payments to lifting US and UN sanctions on the country.

First US Lockerbie trial faces delay

Al-Marimi is set to become the first person accused of the Lockerbie bombing to be tried in a US courtroom.

Loading...

Jury selection for the trial was scheduled for August 25, but it has now been postponed following a judge's ruling after the emergence of new evidence.

But the nature of the evidence was not specified.

US District Judge Dabney Friedrich said the delay was because the defence needed time to "determine how best to defend" this case.

The judge had previously ruled to allow evidence of Al-Marimi's confession, which the defence said was disputed and given under duress.

The prosecution allege the Lockerbie bombing was carried out by Al-Marimi and others under the orders of former Libyan leader Moammar Gaddafi.

They also allege he brought a suitcase containing a bomb which was transported from an airport in Malta, and given to his co-conspirators for a flight to Frankfurt in Germany.

According to authorities, the suitcase then travelled from Frankfurt to London, and then it was loaded inside Pan Am flight 103.

Al-Marimi worked within the Libyan intelligence service between 1973 and 2011, according to the prosecution.

The man now in his mid-70s is facing two counts of destruction of an aircraft resulting in death, and if convicted, faces a maximum penalty of life in prison.

Former FBI special agent Dick Marquise, who led the Lockerbie case, said Al-Marimi was known at the time of the initial investigation.

"It went dormant because the Libyan government disavowed any knowledge of who he might be," Mr Marquise told ABC Radio National.

The judge has scheduled a hearing to discuss the status of the case on September 1.

ABC/AP

World.title: After a bruising defeat, Labor, Liberals look to lessons from One Nation
World.content:
The Labor and Liberal parties are beginning to lick their wounds after suffering a bruising defeat in a by-election in Perth's south as One Nation continues celebrating the result as a major shift in the political landscape.

WA Premier Roger Cook promised Labor would listen to the result, taking it as "a reminder that Western Australians are doing it tough".

"It's a reminder of how important it is we meet Western Australians where they are, and have the conversations to ensure that our community values are reflected in everything that we do," Mr Cook told reporters.

One Nation's Luke Herdegen has claimed the Secret Harbour by-election with a massive swing against Labor in an area it has held for decades.

One Nation supporters were celebrating the historic victory on Saturday evening. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The poll was forced by the retirement of the seat's long-serving MP, Paul Papalia, to care for a sick family member.

The campaign was fought on a range of issues, spanning how often red bins are collected through to the popularity of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and One Nation's national leader, Pauline Hanson.

Federal One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce said the win showed Ms Hanson deserved credit for changing the nature of politics.

Barnaby Joyce and Pauline Hanson. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

"We're going to continue to make sure that we improve so that we gain the respect of the people of Western Australia, the people of Victoria … people of New South Wales and the people of Australia."

PM warns of 'hard-right populists'

Speaking at Labor's state conference in Brisbane, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese did not directly address the loss but warned of "hard-right populists … peddling politics that is dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest".

"Parties like One Nation have no serious answers to problems which are there; their own divisions and disagreements are now showing through," he told party faithful.

Anthony Albanese doesn't directly address the loss but has warned of "hard-right populists". (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"The best way to defeat this coalition of chaos is to give Australians real hope for the better future for their country, for their families and, of course, for themselves, to stay positive, to be the party with the ideas that will make people's lives better."

Labor is understood to have spent about $400,000 on the campaign, including flooding social media with content and sending more than 200,000 pieces of mail.

Labor frontbencher Tanya Plibersek also suggested that messaging was a key part of the problem.

Tanya Plibersek says her party and the Liberals should learn lessons from the by-election results. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

"However, it is important that all of us have a good look at the results here and think about what more we need to do," Ms Plibersek told Insiders.

Hastie warns Zempilas against waving 'white flag' Prominent WA federal Liberal MP Andrew Hastie intensifies his criticism of state opposition leader Basil Zempilas's strategy for Saturday's Secret Harbour by-election.

Outgoing federal Liberal MP Jono Duniam said the result was "not a good outcome for my party, and it's one that we need to look hard at and rectify".

The Tasmanian senator said he shared the feelings of his colleague Andrew Hastie, who earlier in the week criticised State Liberal leader Basil Zempilas for saying a Labor loss would be a win for his party, regardless of the actual winner.

"We shouldn't be talking about being open-minded to work with particular other parties or anything like that," Mr Duniam told News 24, formerly known as Sky News.

" We should be asking people to vote for us. "

Mr Zempilas again rejected the idea his party had run a weak campaign, saying "One Nation would not have won" without the Liberal voters directing their preferences to the minor party.

"The game has changed," he said. "And if the game has changed, that means the way you win the game has also changed.

Basil Zempilas has denied that his party ran a weak campaign in Secret Harbour. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"And as I say, my job as WA Liberal leader is to put the WA Liberal team in the best position for electoral success."

On Sunday afternoon, Mr Hastie emailed his supporters asking for donations to hit a target of $186,000 in September, fearing Labor could win his own seat of Canning due to divided support.

"But I'm not interested in making excuses. I'm only interested in winning and delivering the changes you and I believe Australia needs," he wrote.

Defeat conceded

Labor's candidate, Georgia Tree, formally conceded defeat on Sunday morning, issuing a statement saying it had been an "honour to fight for my community" and highlighting promises made by the party during the campaign.

Georgia Tree has formally conceded defeat on Sunday morning. (ABC News: Ashleigh Davis)

"Make no mistake — all of this will be delivered by the Cook Labor government because of WA Labor and because of our campaign and our fight for Secret Harbour," she wrote.

"Congratulations to Luke Herdegen. It is a great honour to represent your community in Parliament and it is a massive responsibility."

Secret Harbour fast facts: The beachside outer suburban seat south of Perth is very safe Labor territory, with the party holding it with a 11.5% swing.

It's been vacant since the July resignation of Labor's Paul Papalia, who had held the seat and its predecessors since 2007. 16 candidates have nominated for election.

Secret Harbour is home to many young, working families and ranks fourth out of WA's 59 electorates for residents who nominate British or Australian as their ancestry.

One Nation claims win in Secret Harbour by-election One Nation has scored a historic win in Western Australia, securing its first lower house seat in the state.

Mr Herdegen said the result was a loss for Labor but not for Ms Tree personally and urged "anyone who's a supporter of me, show Georgia some love".

"This is One Nation heartland now," he said, pointing to nearby seats like Roger Cook's electorate of Kwinana now being under threat.

"People have had enough. They definitely felt neglected in the outer-southern suburbs.

"They certainly sent a message to Canberra as well and Anthony Albanese that they're unhappy."

The gym owner — who said he is in the process of selling those businesses — said he had already spoken to his federal leader last night.

Rod Caddies (left) and Luke Herdegen outside retired minister Paul Papalia's office. (ABC News: Blake Kagi)

"She was really excited and understands it sends a big message," Mr Herdegen said.

State One Nation leader Rod Caddies said the result should not be seen as a one-off.

"The truth is we know they threw everything at this but the kitchen sink, the people of Secret Harbour had the full undivided attention of this government and they still failed," Mr Caddies said.

"They won't be able to duplicate this in a general election."

The first issue to tackle, Mr Herdegen said, was returning weekly bin collections to the area, after they were cut back to fortnightly with the rollout of FOGO bins.

World.title: How will Trump's oil deal with Venezuela work?
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says his government has struck "the biggest oil deal in history", granting the US access to Venezuela's vast oil reserves.

Venezuela's Acting President, Delcy Rodríguez, says the deal will help to revive the country, and that it retains ownership over its resources.

The South American nation has the world's largest proven oil reserves, but produces far below its potential after years of underinvestment, mismanagement and sanctions.

Here's what we know about the deal.

Announced on social media

Mr Trump announced the deal on Truth Social on Friday night, local time.

Here's some of that post:

"The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY! "At my direction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working closely with Highly Respected Interim President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, and, through a partnership with private business, have secured majority US control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer. "This Historic Transaction MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves, greatly increases our Oil Supply, and will substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future, while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity."

Venezuela's leader praises deal

Ms Rodríguez spoke about the deal in a televised national address on Saturday night, local time.

"This 25-year bilateral project envisages the development of 17 strategic oilfields with a production target of more than 1.5 million barrels per day," she said.

"That figure relates solely to the bilateral agreement between Venezuela and the United States."

Delcy Rodríguez says the deal with the US will revive her country. (AP: Pavel Golovkin)

Ms Rodríguez said the agreement could generate about $US209 billion ($291 billion) in revenue for Venezuela, based on a benchmark oil price of $65 per barrel, though she acknowledged crude prices could fluctuate.

She said roughly $US19 from each barrel produced and sold under the arrangement would flow directly to Venezuela.

She said the "historic" deal would help revive the country's economy and boost government revenues, stressing it would preserve Venezuela's sovereignty over its natural resources,

"One thing must be absolutely clear: Venezuela retains ownership and sovereignty over its resources."

Ms Rodríguez was named the interim leader of Venezuela after the US military captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, in a middle-of-the-night raid in January, and brought him to New York to face federal drug trafficking charges.

Ms Rodríguez had been vice-president to Mr Maduro before his capture.

What are the terms?

The US government and an unnamed private operator in Venezuela formed a new company that was given the rights to untapped oil fields for 100 years, the Associated Press reports.

The deal gives the US 55 per cent effective output of the new private company, including an ownership stake and rights to buy oil at cost.

American purchases of the oil will go towards the US strategic oil reserves along with the military, according to a US official who was not authorised to discuss the matter publicly and spoke to the Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.

The company would be the second-largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco, according to the official.

Will it cut fuel prices in the US?

Probably not any time soon.

Experts have repeatedly warned that Venezuela's dilapidated oil infrastructure will take years and billions of dollars to repair.

They say a substantial boost in production is not expected to happen quickly.

"[The deal could be] helpful in the long run, but it's not going to do anything to change the price of gasoline at the retail station for Labor Day weekend," said Amy Myers Jaffe, director of the Energy, Climate Justice and Sustainability Lab at New York University.

Neither side made clear who would pay for infrastructure investments and at what cost.

The average price of petrol in the US stood about $US4.08 a gallon on Saturday, according to AAA.

The average price was $US3.20 at the same time last year.

Kevin Book, managing director at ClearView Energy Partners, said the oil industry was awaiting clarity on the deal's details.

Venezuela has room to increase its oil production, he said — in the past it produced more than 2.5 million barrels a day above current levels — but investments of this scale do not happen quickly.

"It's going to take time — many years — to deploy that much capital and produce the kind of incremental results that history suggests possible," Mr Book said.

Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves. (Reuters: Carlos Garcia Rawlins)

What questions remain?

Many important details remain unclear, including who will cover necessary investments, the identity of the private operator and how America's stake in the company breaks down.

The US will get 55 per cent of the company's effective output, but it was not clear what portion of that comes from an ownership stake and how much comes from the right to buy oil at cost.

It also is unclear how the industry will react.

Persuading big American oil companies to return to the region could prove a challenge given the political uncertainty and damaged infrastructure.

Chevron, the only US oil company actively producing in Venezuela, declined to comment.

Separately from Mr Trump's announcement, Chevron already had been in talks to expand investment in the country.

Exxon Mobil also declined to comment.

David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said that on the face of it, the deal could double US oil reserves and reduce dependence on crude oil from Canada and Mexico.

He cautioned that there were logistical hurdles though, and said the value of Venezuela's reserves may have been exaggerated under former president Hugo Chávez.

Even with legal and security guarantees, it is not clear that US oil companies "would be eager to invest,'' he said, noting that "there simply might be more enticing commercial opportunities on offer elsewhere".

How will Venezuelans react?

Some in Venezuela considered it a betrayal of what their government has stated repeatedly for decades: Venezuelan resources are for Venezuela, and leaders would not allow the US government access to those resources.

At a market in eastern Caracas on Saturday, Douglas Borjas said he was upset about the announcement.

"I think they're doing it to cling to power," he said of Venezuela's leaders.

"It's like, 'I'm giving you a vast amount of petroleum as long as you leave me alone here in power'.

"The Venezuelan people deserve better. Venezuela has resources that can be exploited, but for the benefit of the people, not for the benefit of the corrupt elite."

Harvard University professor Ricardo Hausmann, a former Venezuelan planning minister, called it a "shameful deal".

"Venezuelans will not respect this illegitimate deal and no major US oil company will take it seriously because they know it will not last," Hausmann said on social media.

He said Ms Rodríguez had "no legitimacy or constitutional power to commit Venezuela to any such deal".

ABC with Wires
