World.title: Great Idea ready to reboot disrupted career at Taree
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Great Idea ready to reboot disrupted career at Taree neil evans August 30, 2026 — 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A talented seven-year-old whose frustrating career has virtually been put on hold for the past year can kick-start a new horizon at Monday’s Taree meeting. Great Idea, a gelded son of dual Cox Plate winner So You Think, has only raced twice since capping an exciting campaign from the middle of last year, winning three from four in an eight-week spread. Great Idea’s trainer Nacim Dilmi. Getty Images That was all when he was stabled with Ben Blay at Muswellbrook, charging home on wet tracks to win his maiden and Benchmark 58 at Tamworth, before rocketing home from the back to claim a Class 2 at Tuncurry in early September. But just when he was ready to tackle bigger races, Great idea was forced into the paddock and didn’t re-emerge until late February, failing in a tougher Class 4 Country Championship Preview.



Four weeks later, he finished well down the track in a Class 3 at Muswellbrook before again being spelled, then transferred into the Nacim Dilmi yard at Wyong. He’s been fitted with two easy trials over the past five weeks, the latest doing his best work late at Gosford from a clear last. Finally, after seemingly more gear changes than races, Great Idea returns to battle in a Class 3 Handicap over 1400m at Taree, quoted around $9.50 in early betting. It will be a stern test for the gelding that sits well behind rival Wyong mare Purple Rose, which opened a $3.90 favourite, and hard-fit Grafton mare Satin And Cash around $4.50. Great Idea has still only had eight starts and had seen the inside of three different stables even before debuting as a five-year-old in early 2025.



Originally in the Bjorn Baker yard at Warwick Farm, he went to Sara Ryan at Wyong, and then the Blay camp before an encouraging debut at Tamworth where he ran home late at huge odds. Related Article Horse racing Tips and race-by-race guide for Taree on Monday Now he heads to the Mid North Coast to reboot his career for a fourth trainer, with one aspect still on his side. While setbacks and false starts are temporary, naturally ability is permanent, and owners Domeland will be banking on that heading into spring. Trainer Dilmi will also be hoping Taree kick-starts a big week, with Wyong’s feature dual Listed Cup meeting on this Friday.



He also saddles up capable four-year-old Bellevue in a very winnable BM 58 Handicap over a mile, as well as resuming smart four-year-old River Jordan in a Maiden Plate over 1300m. Supplied by Racing NSW

World.title: Why this Perth author’s fifth book was her most difficult to write yet
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeLiterature Why this Perth author’s fifth book was her most difficult to write yet Cameron Myles August 30, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Family history and a dark revelation shape West Australian author Tess Woods’ fifth book – and that was just in the writing process. Woods takes readers back to her Egyptian roots and to the foot of the famous pyramids in The Cairo Bridal Shop, which weaves three the storylines of three sisters together to tell a thrilling story of strength, love, family and tradition. West Australian author Tess Woods has released her fifth book, The Cairo Bridal Shop. Penguin Random House It is perhaps the most personal book from Woods, whose last outing – The Venice Hotel – earned critical acclaim. “My nanna, who passed away during the COVID lockdowns, she was a bridal dressmaker,” Woods said.



“She made my bridal gown, and we were incredibly close. “There was only 45 years between my nanna and I … and I truly grieved her death when she died, and I wasn’t able to be with her because of the COVID lockdowns keeping me here in WA. “And I wanted to honour her in some way, so I had had in my mind that I wanted to write a book connecting ancient Egyptian history. “And then, when my grandma passed away, and I wasn’t able to be at her funeral, I wanted to write a book to honour her. “And that’s when I thought of that vehicle of using bridal dresses as a way to connect the past and the present, and have the brides that come into the shop and try on the dresses, take on the lives of the ancient pharaoh queens, and bring them into a modern-day Egyptian setting.”



The concept had been bouncing around for a while, but took form in 2020. Related Article City life With a beloved children’s author on the bill, this Perth festival isn’t afraid to sort fact from fiction Woods’ research threw up more surprises, as she dove into Egyptian history and the 2011 revolution to paint the picture of life of women in the Middle East. By her own admission, “it’s taken me five novels to find the guts to tell the story”. “It was really a difficult balance to get of wanting to show the country that I’m so proud to have been born in, and our hospitality, and warmth, and our traditions, and our culture, and our rich history,” she said.



“All of that I wanted to showcase and make Egypt the jewel that it is, but also at the same time, being realistic about the misogyny and the patriarchy and the corruption of the government, the lack of freedom of speech, and how difficult it is for women with unequal human rights.” Even researching Gamal Abdel Nasser, the second president of Egypt who is regarded fondly for his legacy of bringing the country out of the shadow of British influence, threw curveballs Woods’ way. “When I was researching his story, I came upon the way that he treated the peasant farmers who were out in the rural areas of Egypt, and it was absolutely shocking,” she said. “It really changed … the story I started out telling was not the story that I ended up telling.” Woods admits The Cairo Bridal Shop was her “most difficult book to write”.



But she hopes the message readers will take away involves looking beyond the cliches of the Middle East. “We aren’t subjugated women,” she said. “We just happen to live under patriarchal state laws, but on a personal level, Egyptian women are some of the bravest, most feisty, funny, full of personality [women], so I hope that all of that comes out in the book, and we see Middle Eastern women for who they truly are.” The Cairo Bridal Shop will be released on September 1.

World.title: He survived being hit by a tram. Now he plans to run a marathon
World.content:
NationalVictoriaRunning He survived being hit by a tram. Now he plans to run a marathon Carolyn Webb August 30, 2026 — 5:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Minutes after Ben Turner was hit by a tram, all indications were that he had died. Ambulance officers who arrived at the scene that Friday night, in South Melbourne, in 2005, found that the 29-year-old’s heart had stopped and he wasn’t breathing. Loading Paramedic Mick Stephenson says Turner was lying face-down between the tram tracks in Kings Way, his face smashed, and with one leg flung over his head. Stephenson says Turner’s chances of successful resuscitation were next to none.



“If your heart stops and you stop breathing, from trauma, you rarely survive,” Stephenson says. “He was in a terrible state.” But Stephenson and his partner, John Taplin, refused to give up. Their cool, deft work, beside eight lanes of traffic on Kings Way, saved Turner’s life. Lucky to be alive: Ben Turner shows where he was hit by a tram on Kings Way, South Melbourne, in 2005. Jason South They cut into Turner’s chest and inserted a tube to release air from the lung lining. It relieved the pressure that had stopped the heart. They re-inflated the lung and his heart started beating. Turner regained consciousness in The Alfred hospital in Prahran, three weeks later.



In 2026, the words “grateful” and “lucky” remain with Turner, given he survived a punctured lung, a head injury, 10 broken ribs, a broken leg, and fractured vertebrae. He has made, says Stephenson, a remarkable recovery. Thank you: Ben Turner, centre, with the paramedics who saved his life, Mick Stephenson, left, and John Taplin, pictured in 2006. In October, Turner will run the Melbourne Marathon, to pay tribute to the people who saved him. He says he feels grateful every day.



“Just being here, being able to breathe and run. Being able to be a full participant in life, with my kids, my wife and work, being able to do any of these things, they’re all privileges that we all take for granted. I’m very lucky.” A newspaper report on Ben Turner being hit by a tram. The Sunday Age, February 6, 2005 Turner today has five titanium plates inside his face, and a rod inside his left leg. He has a crooked little finger and a small scar on his face. Turner remembers nothing about the accident. Friends told him he was at a South Melbourne pub. At about midnight he headed towards his St Kilda Road apartment.



News reports said he was talking on his phone when he was hit by the tram. After four weeks in hospital, Turner moved to the Epworth rehabilitation centre in Richmond. Turner remembers feeling amazed that other people could walk up stairs, because he felt so weak. Staunch support: Ben Turner with then-girlfriend, now wife Anabela Correia, as Turner leaves rehabilitation in April 2005. An attitude of “one step at a time” helped, as did girlfriend Anabela Correia, “who wouldn’t let me wallow”. The couple married in 2007 and have two children, Max, 16, and Audrey, 12.



Turner, a technology director in Cloud, Data & AI, started running in 2010 and now trains for about 60km per week. In 2023, he ran a 44-kilometre race on the Great Ocean Road. On October 11, Turner will run the Melbourne Marathon, to raise money for Ambulance Victoria and The Alfred Foundation but also to recognise and assure emergency service and rehabilitation workers that they make a difference. Stephenson, who is now Turner’s friend, says Turner “made a miraculous recovery, compared to where we thought he was”. “Every time I see him, I marvel at how well he is, how well he’s done,” he said.



“To think a bloke lying on the tram tracks, for all intents and purposes dead, is 20-odd years later running a marathon, it’s a pretty impressive story. Good luck to him. He’s a fighter, there’s no doubt about it.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mixed emotions for Ivan Cleary as son Jett stars on debut to put Warriors on top
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Mixed emotions for Ivan Cleary as son Jett stars on debut to put Warriors on top Christian Nicolussi August 30, 2026 — 4:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Ivan Cleary would have sat in a corporate box at Go Media Stadium with mixed emotions on Sunday afternoon. His 21-year-old son, Jett, had just made his NRL debut for the New Zealand Warriors and more than held his own. Loading His kicking game was excellent, he survived plenty of early pressure from the Newcastle Knights and finished with four try assists, including stepping off his left foot and throwing the final pass for Jacob Laban’s first half try. Jett’s famous older brother Nathan, who also made the trek to New Zealand, was caught by the TV cameras having a giggle when the playmaker was upended by the Knights late and a melee erupted.



While Jett will never forget the sunny – then rainy – afternoon when he helped the Warriors to a 46-32 win over the Knights, the result also meant Ivan and Nathan’s Penrith dropped to second on the ladder. The Panthers head into the final round trailing the Warriors by just one on points differential. Thanks, Jett. The Cleary family congratulate Jett at full-time. Getty Images The Warriors will host Manly while the Panthers complete their regular season against Wests Tigers. Either way, both teams are now assured of a home qualifying final. Warriors coach Andrew Webster is firming to be crowned Dally M coach of the year for guiding the Warriors to a potential minor premiership, not to mention building a squad with such excellent depth.



Jett will return home to Penrith to be coached by Ivan next year before the coach walks away from the Panthers to spend time with family, travel and potentially mentor representative sides. Jett was only given his start on Sunday following injuries to halves Luke Metcalf (hamstring), Te Maire Martin (hamstring) and Chanel Harris-Tavita (hamstring tightness). The Warriors have been protective of Jett, who has attracted plenty of interest due to his surname. Loading The Warriors were delighted for him at full-time. “I thought he looked like he belonged,” co-captain Mitch Barnett said. “He defended really well. [Knights winger Greg] Marzhew is not easy to handle. Even their back-rower [Francis Manuleleua] has been causing havoc on his edge. Jett held his gloves up. He’ll only get better each time he takes the field.”



Knights captain Kalyn Ponga said: “I think he went well, he played his role; he’ll be proud and his family will be proud. When you’re sitting at home in years to come and you look back at your debut, it’s a win, so he’ll be happy.” Cleary may play again next week now Webster has the opportunity to rest a few of his main men knowing it will not impact the club’s chances of hosting a final in week one of the play-offs. Webster was giving little away. The Knights will also play finals, but the loss to the Warriors proved costly. Representative prop Jacob Saifiti was sent off in the 12th minute and may not play again this year after a high shot on Luke Laulilii. Laulilii switched to the Warriors mid-season from Wests Tigers, but his first game for his new club ended early after he suffered a category-one head knock. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Does the NRL really have room to bring back a midweek cup? PVL thinks so Neil Breen National sports editor



The Knights have the bye next week, so any ban for Saifiti would take effect once the finals begin. Coach Justin Holbrook joked and hoped the “sin bin” was a sufficient punishment. Manuleleua also failed to make it to half-time because of a shoulder injury. The Knights raced to a 16-0 lead, and even though the home side stormed back and kicked clear early in the second half, the visitors refused to surrender and were brave. Marzhew’s second-half try was entertaining after he kicked ahead for himself, only for the ball to ricochet off the head of Taine Tuaupiki and Ali Leiataua’s leg before slamming back in to the winger’s chest for a four-pointer.

World.title: Secret Harbour shellacking a warning for Labor, Coalition
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Secret Harbour shellacking a warning for Labor, Coalition James Massola August 30, 2026 — 4:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last week, on his 45th visit to Western Australia, Anthony Albanese promised his government would never alter the outrageously generous GST deal that hands extra cash to Australia’s richest state. West Australians (barely) thanked him for the guarantee, and then on Saturday handed Labor a thrashing in a byelection for the state seat of Secret Harbour. Newly elected One Nation state MP Luke Herdegen. Colin Murty While some may argue that One Nation’s thumping win in Secret Harbour means little for federal politics, that would be a mistake. Albanese did not visit Secret Harbour, claiming last week that he didn’t campaign in state byelections – never mind that he opened a Medicare urgent care clinic in the WA state seat of Rockingham during a 2023 byelection – and will probably play down the federal implications of this result.



WA Labor has been in power at a state level for nearly a decade, which made it harder for the party to hang on, and it’s true that state and federal issues don’t overlap perfectly. One Nation Leader Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce attend the Farmers Fightback rally at Marnoo in western Victoria. Facebook But the fact that the winning candidate, Luke Herdegen, campaigned without any substantial policies and a pitch that amounted to “if you’re fed up, vote for me” – as my colleagues Hamish Hastie and Michael Philipps noted – has to be a concern. Speaking after the win, the first time Labor had been beaten by One Nation in a head-to-head contest, Herdegen declared “there are no safe Labor seats in this state or in this country anymore”. The swing against Labor was savage, with Herdegen defeating Labor’s Georgia Tree 57-43 in the two-party preferred vote.



Meanwhile, on the other side of the country in western Victoria, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce were attending a wild One Nation rally that included props such as a coffin with a giant nail in it and inscribed with the words “Net Zero”. One Nation’s meteoric rise in the polls, which began quietly last September before accelerating rapidly from December, has been fuelled by people who are fed up with the old two-party system and are struggling with high interest rates, inflation and rent, and other cost-of-living concerns. Albanese is acutely aware of that. And it’s very much the case that cost-of-living concerns cut across state and federal politics. Anthony Albanese is adamant that Labor must defeat One Nation, declaring “we owe it to history”. Perhaps most telling was that on Sunday morning, Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers both took aim at Hanson during speeches at the Queensland Labor Party’s state conference.



“This is a crucial time for our movement because across the world, hard-right populists are on the march, peddling politics that is dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest,” the prime minister told party members. “They’ll say anything and do anything, bend any facts, peddle misinformation and disinformation, turn Australian against Australian.” Those are not the words of a Labor prime minister who thinks there are no federal implications from the Secret Harbour result, or who is unconcerned about the rise of One Nation. But the result is also a blow to the Coalition. While Secret Harbour, in its various iterations and under different names, has been solidly Labor since the 1980s at the state level, the seat sits in the federal seat of Canning, which is held by Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie. The Liberals stood a candidate in this contest, too, but he finished a distant third.



Related Article ALP ‘Dangerous, divisive, dishonest’: Albanese, Chalmers take aim at One Nation Hastie is already facing blowback for testifying against his former SAS colleague, Ben Roberts-Smith, in court while Hanson has taken up the mantle of one of Robert-Smith’s chief defenders. This result will, at a minimum, have Hastie pondering his own political mortality. Secret Harbour is older, whiter and more British than the average federal seat, and the anger with the Albanese government on the ground is palpable, as my colleague Paul Sakkal reported. It’s a state version of the sort of outer-suburban seat that Peter Dutton and Scott Morrison before him have tried to win over at the past two federal elections in the outer suburbs of Australia’s major cities and mostly failed to claim, though Hastie was one of few Liberals to increase their margin at the 2025 federal election.



Editor's pick Updated

Floods ‘Blessed’ to be Australian: Survivor of Nepalese floods speaks out So the fact that voters have skipped past the Liberals and cast their vote for One Nation is a blow to the opposition. The Secret Harbour result confirms One Nation’s rise is far from done. And that’s a problem for both major parties. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Britain just shelved a key defence goal. That’s not good for Australia
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeUK Britain just shelved a key defence goal. That’s not good for Australia David Crowe August 30, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: When the British government imploded in June, one key factor was a public dispute between ministers about how much the country could afford to spend on defence. The goal was so pivotal for the defence secretary at the time, John Healey, that he quit the cabinet in protest when the prime minister, Keir Starmer, would not agree to lift the outlay to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030. John Healey’s resignation as defence secretary was a factor in the downfall of former prime minister Keir Starmer. Getty Images Healey set off a detonation that made the leader look doomed. Starmer resigned 11 days later. Now, that same target is haunting the government led by Prime Minister Andy Burnham. And it is causing trouble for Healey, who was one of the big winners in the new ministry when he was promoted to chancellor of the exchequer.



His decision is to go soft on the hard target. Healey is going to shelve the 3 per cent goal, according to reporting in The Financial Times and other media. Rather than doing what he thought was so important only six weeks ago, he is sending the matter to a review over the next year. This exposes Healey to accusations of hypocrisy or weakness, of course, and it is a reminder of the self-serving positioning by ministers in the dying weeks of the Starmer government. But it also highlights a more important truth: changing a few leaders does not solve Britain’s budget mess. And it is a reminder of the risks for Australia when so many defence projects, including AUKUS, depend on the British defence industry. Now you see me: Healey (third from left) and former British foreign secretary Yvette Cooper (left) host Penny Wong and Richard Marles in London in June. Bloomberg On the surface, leaders from Britain and Australia try to show that everything is fine. Healey hosted Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Richard Marles in London in June to display a steady friendship. But Healey quit the next day, so the visit merely highlighted the instability at the top of this relationship.



Australia is already dealing with erratic allies in Washington. It could do without the same in London. Things are settling down under Burnham. The UK’s new defence secretary, Wes Streeting, is a friend of Australia – he visited in 2023. At a personal level, the alliance between the UK and Australia is in good hands. The next logical step is for Marles and Streeting to set up a meeting. Related Article Defence Australia urged to spend billions on top-shelf US missile interceptors But there’s a problem. Britain is already spending beyond its means and is in no position to commit to an even bigger increase in its defence outlays. This does not directly endanger AUKUS, but it highlights how stretched national security is in one of Australia’s most important allies. Britain’s defence budget is forecast to reach £62.0 billion (about $117 billion) this financial year, rising to £79.1 billion in 2029-30, according to the House of Commons Library. The spending is on track to reach 2.7 per cent of GDP by 2030. Going further, however, looks simply too hard.



Burnham and Healey have been mugged by reality. One estimate suggests they would need to find an additional £10 billion per year to reach 3 per cent. They obviously cannot find the money. This is not a problem of their own making. The previous Conservative government allowed defence spending to stagnate and budget deficits to deepen over 14 years in power. It would take years to turn this around if Britain’s leaders could ever agree on how to do so. The UK’s public sector net debt just passed £3 trillion, according to market estimates based on official numbers from the Office for Budget Responsibility. This is the net figure after accounting for public assets. It is 94 per cent of GDP. Burnham visited Kyiv last week pledging renewed British support for Ukraine. Henry Nicholls/Pool AFP via AP And it is not getting any better as the years pass. The government’s overall borrowing – the difference between total public sector spending and income – was £56.7 billion in the year to the end of June. The debt will grow. The bond markets are watching and will punish the government if it cannot restrain its spending.





The challenges were laid bare when Iran attacked Cyprus in March during the first wave of drone strikes around the region. The Royal Navy struggled to send a warship to respond swiftly, with several ships unavailable and destroyer HMS Dragon only setting sail one week after the attack. The pressure will only increase as long as Russia remains a threat to Europe. The Russian attacks on Ukraine are highlighting the shortage of Patriot interceptors and other systems to counter Russian missiles. The Russian strike on a Kyiv ammunition depot, killing 37, was the latest sign of this. Britain, along with its major allies in Europe, is now trying to make up for lost time by developing new hypersonic missiles and missile defence systems. (Some of these will be tested at Woomera in South Australia.) It also has to spend on protections against Russian hybrid warfare, such as cyberattacks. None of this comes cheap. The broader context is the withdrawal of American support under President Donald Trump, who wants Britain and other NATO allies to spend more on their own security. Healey thought he had the answer to this in June when his job was to spend the money. It is harder now that his job is to find the money.



Burnham, meanwhile, is enjoying a honeymoon in the opinion polls, as most leaders do after taking office with high hopes. This changes when leaders start making hard decisions. Burnham has spent his first weeks setting ambitious and worthy goals, such as tackling homelessness, but he has yet to do anything that risks offending the Labour base. The hard decisions are yet to come. One of them will be how to pay for more defence spending. Australia has a stake in what Burnham and Healey decide. World.title: Great Idea ready to reboot disrupted career at Taree
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Great Idea ready to reboot disrupted career at Taree neil evans August 30, 2026 — 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A talented seven-year-old whose frustrating career has virtually been put on hold for the past year can kick-start a new horizon at Monday’s Taree meeting. Great Idea, a gelded son of dual Cox Plate winner So You Think, has only raced twice since capping an exciting campaign from the middle of last year, winning three from four in an eight-week spread. Great Idea’s trainer Nacim Dilmi. Getty Images That was all when he was stabled with Ben Blay at Muswellbrook, charging home on wet tracks to win his maiden and Benchmark 58 at Tamworth, before rocketing home from the back to claim a Class 2 at Tuncurry in early September. But just when he was ready to tackle bigger races, Great idea was forced into the paddock and didn’t re-emerge until late February, failing in a tougher Class 4 Country Championship Preview.



Four weeks later, he finished well down the track in a Class 3 at Muswellbrook before again being spelled, then transferred into the Nacim Dilmi yard at Wyong. He’s been fitted with two easy trials over the past five weeks, the latest doing his best work late at Gosford from a clear last. Finally, after seemingly more gear changes than races, Great Idea returns to battle in a Class 3 Handicap over 1400m at Taree, quoted around $9.50 in early betting. It will be a stern test for the gelding that sits well behind rival Wyong mare Purple Rose, which opened a $3.90 favourite, and hard-fit Grafton mare Satin And Cash around $4.50. Great Idea has still only had eight starts and had seen the inside of three different stables even before debuting as a five-year-old in early 2025.



Originally in the Bjorn Baker yard at Warwick Farm, he went to Sara Ryan at Wyong, and then the Blay camp before an encouraging debut at Tamworth where he ran home late at huge odds. Related Article Horse racing Tips and race-by-race guide for Taree on Monday Now he heads to the Mid North Coast to reboot his career for a fourth trainer, with one aspect still on his side. While setbacks and false starts are temporary, naturally ability is permanent, and owners Domeland will be banking on that heading into spring. Trainer Dilmi will also be hoping Taree kick-starts a big week, with Wyong’s feature dual Listed Cup meeting on this Friday.



He also saddles up capable four-year-old Bellevue in a very winnable BM 58 Handicap over a mile, as well as resuming smart four-year-old River Jordan in a Maiden Plate over 1300m. Supplied by Racing NSW

World.title: Why this Perth author’s fifth book was her most difficult to write yet
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeLiterature Why this Perth author’s fifth book was her most difficult to write yet Cameron Myles August 30, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Family history and a dark revelation shape West Australian author Tess Woods’ fifth book – and that was just in the writing process. Woods takes readers back to her Egyptian roots and to the foot of the famous pyramids in The Cairo Bridal Shop, which weaves three the storylines of three sisters together to tell a thrilling story of strength, love, family and tradition. West Australian author Tess Woods has released her fifth book, The Cairo Bridal Shop. Penguin Random House It is perhaps the most personal book from Woods, whose last outing – The Venice Hotel – earned critical acclaim. “My nanna, who passed away during the COVID lockdowns, she was a bridal dressmaker,” Woods said.



“She made my bridal gown, and we were incredibly close. “There was only 45 years between my nanna and I … and I truly grieved her death when she died, and I wasn’t able to be with her because of the COVID lockdowns keeping me here in WA. “And I wanted to honour her in some way, so I had had in my mind that I wanted to write a book connecting ancient Egyptian history. “And then, when my grandma passed away, and I wasn’t able to be at her funeral, I wanted to write a book to honour her. “And that’s when I thought of that vehicle of using bridal dresses as a way to connect the past and the present, and have the brides that come into the shop and try on the dresses, take on the lives of the ancient pharaoh queens, and bring them into a modern-day Egyptian setting.”



The concept had been bouncing around for a while, but took form in 2020. Related Article City life With a beloved children’s author on the bill, this Perth festival isn’t afraid to sort fact from fiction Woods’ research threw up more surprises, as she dove into Egyptian history and the 2011 revolution to paint the picture of life of women in the Middle East. By her own admission, “it’s taken me five novels to find the guts to tell the story”. “It was really a difficult balance to get of wanting to show the country that I’m so proud to have been born in, and our hospitality, and warmth, and our traditions, and our culture, and our rich history,” she said.



“All of that I wanted to showcase and make Egypt the jewel that it is, but also at the same time, being realistic about the misogyny and the patriarchy and the corruption of the government, the lack of freedom of speech, and how difficult it is for women with unequal human rights.” Even researching Gamal Abdel Nasser, the second president of Egypt who is regarded fondly for his legacy of bringing the country out of the shadow of British influence, threw curveballs Woods’ way. “When I was researching his story, I came upon the way that he treated the peasant farmers who were out in the rural areas of Egypt, and it was absolutely shocking,” she said. “It really changed … the story I started out telling was not the story that I ended up telling.” Woods admits The Cairo Bridal Shop was her “most difficult book to write”.



But she hopes the message readers will take away involves looking beyond the cliches of the Middle East. “We aren’t subjugated women,” she said. “We just happen to live under patriarchal state laws, but on a personal level, Egyptian women are some of the bravest, most feisty, funny, full of personality [women], so I hope that all of that comes out in the book, and we see Middle Eastern women for who they truly are.” The Cairo Bridal Shop will be released on September 1.

World.title: He survived being hit by a tram. Now he plans to run a marathon
World.content:
NationalVictoriaRunning He survived being hit by a tram. Now he plans to run a marathon Carolyn Webb August 30, 2026 — 5:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Minutes after Ben Turner was hit by a tram, all indications were that he had died. Ambulance officers who arrived at the scene that Friday night, in South Melbourne, in 2005, found that the 29-year-old’s heart had stopped and he wasn’t breathing. Loading Paramedic Mick Stephenson says Turner was lying face-down between the tram tracks in Kings Way, his face smashed, and with one leg flung over his head. Stephenson says Turner’s chances of successful resuscitation were next to none.



“If your heart stops and you stop breathing, from trauma, you rarely survive,” Stephenson says. “He was in a terrible state.” But Stephenson and his partner, John Taplin, refused to give up. Their cool, deft work, beside eight lanes of traffic on Kings Way, saved Turner’s life. Lucky to be alive: Ben Turner shows where he was hit by a tram on Kings Way, South Melbourne, in 2005. Jason South They cut into Turner’s chest and inserted a tube to release air from the lung lining. It relieved the pressure that had stopped the heart. They re-inflated the lung and his heart started beating. Turner regained consciousness in The Alfred hospital in Prahran, three weeks later.



In 2026, the words “grateful” and “lucky” remain with Turner, given he survived a punctured lung, a head injury, 10 broken ribs, a broken leg, and fractured vertebrae. He has made, says Stephenson, a remarkable recovery. Thank you: Ben Turner, centre, with the paramedics who saved his life, Mick Stephenson, left, and John Taplin, pictured in 2006. In October, Turner will run the Melbourne Marathon, to pay tribute to the people who saved him. He says he feels grateful every day.



“Just being here, being able to breathe and run. Being able to be a full participant in life, with my kids, my wife and work, being able to do any of these things, they’re all privileges that we all take for granted. I’m very lucky.” A newspaper report on Ben Turner being hit by a tram. The Sunday Age, February 6, 2005 Turner today has five titanium plates inside his face, and a rod inside his left leg. He has a crooked little finger and a small scar on his face. Turner remembers nothing about the accident. Friends told him he was at a South Melbourne pub. At about midnight he headed towards his St Kilda Road apartment.



News reports said he was talking on his phone when he was hit by the tram. After four weeks in hospital, Turner moved to the Epworth rehabilitation centre in Richmond. Turner remembers feeling amazed that other people could walk up stairs, because he felt so weak. Staunch support: Ben Turner with then-girlfriend, now wife Anabela Correia, as Turner leaves rehabilitation in April 2005. An attitude of “one step at a time” helped, as did girlfriend Anabela Correia, “who wouldn’t let me wallow”. The couple married in 2007 and have two children, Max, 16, and Audrey, 12.



Turner, a technology director in Cloud, Data & AI, started running in 2010 and now trains for about 60km per week. In 2023, he ran a 44-kilometre race on the Great Ocean Road. On October 11, Turner will run the Melbourne Marathon, to raise money for Ambulance Victoria and The Alfred Foundation but also to recognise and assure emergency service and rehabilitation workers that they make a difference. Stephenson, who is now Turner’s friend, says Turner “made a miraculous recovery, compared to where we thought he was”. “Every time I see him, I marvel at how well he is, how well he’s done,” he said.



“To think a bloke lying on the tram tracks, for all intents and purposes dead, is 20-odd years later running a marathon, it’s a pretty impressive story. Good luck to him. He’s a fighter, there’s no doubt about it.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mixed emotions for Ivan Cleary as son Jett stars on debut to put Warriors on top
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Mixed emotions for Ivan Cleary as son Jett stars on debut to put Warriors on top Christian Nicolussi August 30, 2026 — 4:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Ivan Cleary would have sat in a corporate box at Go Media Stadium with mixed emotions on Sunday afternoon. His 21-year-old son, Jett, had just made his NRL debut for the New Zealand Warriors and more than held his own. Loading His kicking game was excellent, he survived plenty of early pressure from the Newcastle Knights and finished with four try assists, including stepping off his left foot and throwing the final pass for Jacob Laban’s first half try. Jett’s famous older brother Nathan, who also made the trek to New Zealand, was caught by the TV cameras having a giggle when the playmaker was upended by the Knights late and a melee erupted.



While Jett will never forget the sunny – then rainy – afternoon when he helped the Warriors to a 46-32 win over the Knights, the result also meant Ivan and Nathan’s Penrith dropped to second on the ladder. The Panthers head into the final round trailing the Warriors by just one on points differential. Thanks, Jett. The Cleary family congratulate Jett at full-time. Getty Images The Warriors will host Manly while the Panthers complete their regular season against Wests Tigers. Either way, both teams are now assured of a home qualifying final. Warriors coach Andrew Webster is firming to be crowned Dally M coach of the year for guiding the Warriors to a potential minor premiership, not to mention building a squad with such excellent depth.



Jett will return home to Penrith to be coached by Ivan next year before the coach walks away from the Panthers to spend time with family, travel and potentially mentor representative sides. Jett was only given his start on Sunday following injuries to halves Luke Metcalf (hamstring), Te Maire Martin (hamstring) and Chanel Harris-Tavita (hamstring tightness). The Warriors have been protective of Jett, who has attracted plenty of interest due to his surname. Loading The Warriors were delighted for him at full-time. “I thought he looked like he belonged,” co-captain Mitch Barnett said. “He defended really well. [Knights winger Greg] Marzhew is not easy to handle. Even their back-rower [Francis Manuleleua] has been causing havoc on his edge. Jett held his gloves up. He’ll only get better each time he takes the field.”



Knights captain Kalyn Ponga said: “I think he went well, he played his role; he’ll be proud and his family will be proud. When you’re sitting at home in years to come and you look back at your debut, it’s a win, so he’ll be happy.” Cleary may play again next week now Webster has the opportunity to rest a few of his main men knowing it will not impact the club’s chances of hosting a final in week one of the play-offs. Webster was giving little away. The Knights will also play finals, but the loss to the Warriors proved costly. Representative prop Jacob Saifiti was sent off in the 12th minute and may not play again this year after a high shot on Luke Laulilii. Laulilii switched to the Warriors mid-season from Wests Tigers, but his first game for his new club ended early after he suffered a category-one head knock. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Does the NRL really have room to bring back a midweek cup? PVL thinks so Neil Breen National sports editor



The Knights have the bye next week, so any ban for Saifiti would take effect once the finals begin. Coach Justin Holbrook joked and hoped the “sin bin” was a sufficient punishment. Manuleleua also failed to make it to half-time because of a shoulder injury. The Knights raced to a 16-0 lead, and even though the home side stormed back and kicked clear early in the second half, the visitors refused to surrender and were brave. Marzhew’s second-half try was entertaining after he kicked ahead for himself, only for the ball to ricochet off the head of Taine Tuaupiki and Ali Leiataua’s leg before slamming back in to the winger’s chest for a four-pointer.

World.title: Secret Harbour shellacking a warning for Labor, Coalition
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Secret Harbour shellacking a warning for Labor, Coalition James Massola August 30, 2026 — 4:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last week, on his 45th visit to Western Australia, Anthony Albanese promised his government would never alter the outrageously generous GST deal that hands extra cash to Australia’s richest state. West Australians (barely) thanked him for the guarantee, and then on Saturday handed Labor a thrashing in a byelection for the state seat of Secret Harbour. Newly elected One Nation state MP Luke Herdegen. Colin Murty While some may argue that One Nation’s thumping win in Secret Harbour means little for federal politics, that would be a mistake. Albanese did not visit Secret Harbour, claiming last week that he didn’t campaign in state byelections – never mind that he opened a Medicare urgent care clinic in the WA state seat of Rockingham during a 2023 byelection – and will probably play down the federal implications of this result.



WA Labor has been in power at a state level for nearly a decade, which made it harder for the party to hang on, and it’s true that state and federal issues don’t overlap perfectly. One Nation Leader Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce attend the Farmers Fightback rally at Marnoo in western Victoria. Facebook But the fact that the winning candidate, Luke Herdegen, campaigned without any substantial policies and a pitch that amounted to “if you’re fed up, vote for me” – as my colleagues Hamish Hastie and Michael Philipps noted – has to be a concern. Speaking after the win, the first time Labor had been beaten by One Nation in a head-to-head contest, Herdegen declared “there are no safe Labor seats in this state or in this country anymore”. The swing against Labor was savage, with Herdegen defeating Labor’s Georgia Tree 57-43 in the two-party preferred vote.



Meanwhile, on the other side of the country in western Victoria, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce were attending a wild One Nation rally that included props such as a coffin with a giant nail in it and inscribed with the words “Net Zero”. One Nation’s meteoric rise in the polls, which began quietly last September before accelerating rapidly from December, has been fuelled by people who are fed up with the old two-party system and are struggling with high interest rates, inflation and rent, and other cost-of-living concerns. Albanese is acutely aware of that. And it’s very much the case that cost-of-living concerns cut across state and federal politics. Anthony Albanese is adamant that Labor must defeat One Nation, declaring “we owe it to history”. Perhaps most telling was that on Sunday morning, Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers both took aim at Hanson during speeches at the Queensland Labor Party’s state conference.



“This is a crucial time for our movement because across the world, hard-right populists are on the march, peddling politics that is dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest,” the prime minister told party members. “They’ll say anything and do anything, bend any facts, peddle misinformation and disinformation, turn Australian against Australian.” Those are not the words of a Labor prime minister who thinks there are no federal implications from the Secret Harbour result, or who is unconcerned about the rise of One Nation. But the result is also a blow to the Coalition. While Secret Harbour, in its various iterations and under different names, has been solidly Labor since the 1980s at the state level, the seat sits in the federal seat of Canning, which is held by Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie. The Liberals stood a candidate in this contest, too, but he finished a distant third.



Related Article ALP ‘Dangerous, divisive, dishonest’: Albanese, Chalmers take aim at One Nation Hastie is already facing blowback for testifying against his former SAS colleague, Ben Roberts-Smith, in court while Hanson has taken up the mantle of one of Robert-Smith’s chief defenders. This result will, at a minimum, have Hastie pondering his own political mortality. Secret Harbour is older, whiter and more British than the average federal seat, and the anger with the Albanese government on the ground is palpable, as my colleague Paul Sakkal reported. It’s a state version of the sort of outer-suburban seat that Peter Dutton and Scott Morrison before him have tried to win over at the past two federal elections in the outer suburbs of Australia’s major cities and mostly failed to claim, though Hastie was one of few Liberals to increase their margin at the 2025 federal election.



Editor's pick Updated

Floods ‘Blessed’ to be Australian: Survivor of Nepalese floods speaks out So the fact that voters have skipped past the Liberals and cast their vote for One Nation is a blow to the opposition. The Secret Harbour result confirms One Nation’s rise is far from done. And that’s a problem for both major parties. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Britain just shelved a key defence goal. That’s not good for Australia
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeUK Britain just shelved a key defence goal. That’s not good for Australia David Crowe August 30, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: When the British government imploded in June, one key factor was a public dispute between ministers about how much the country could afford to spend on defence. The goal was so pivotal for the defence secretary at the time, John Healey, that he quit the cabinet in protest when the prime minister, Keir Starmer, would not agree to lift the outlay to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030. John Healey’s resignation as defence secretary was a factor in the downfall of former prime minister Keir Starmer. Getty Images Healey set off a detonation that made the leader look doomed. Starmer resigned 11 days later. Now, that same target is haunting the government led by Prime Minister Andy Burnham. And it is causing trouble for Healey, who was one of the big winners in the new ministry when he was promoted to chancellor of the exchequer.



His decision is to go soft on the hard target. Healey is going to shelve the 3 per cent goal, according to reporting in The Financial Times and other media. Rather than doing what he thought was so important only six weeks ago, he is sending the matter to a review over the next year. This exposes Healey to accusations of hypocrisy or weakness, of course, and it is a reminder of the self-serving positioning by ministers in the dying weeks of the Starmer government. But it also highlights a more important truth: changing a few leaders does not solve Britain’s budget mess. And it is a reminder of the risks for Australia when so many defence projects, including AUKUS, depend on the British defence industry. Now you see me: Healey (third from left) and former British foreign secretary Yvette Cooper (left) host Penny Wong and Richard Marles in London in June. Bloomberg On the surface, leaders from Britain and Australia try to show that everything is fine. Healey hosted Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Richard Marles in London in June to display a steady friendship. But Healey quit the next day, so the visit merely highlighted the instability at the top of this relationship.



Australia is already dealing with erratic allies in Washington. It could do without the same in London. Things are settling down under Burnham. The UK’s new defence secretary, Wes Streeting, is a friend of Australia – he visited in 2023. At a personal level, the alliance between the UK and Australia is in good hands. The next logical step is for Marles and Streeting to set up a meeting. Related Article Defence Australia urged to spend billions on top-shelf US missile interceptors But there’s a problem. Britain is already spending beyond its means and is in no position to commit to an even bigger increase in its defence outlays. This does not directly endanger AUKUS, but it highlights how stretched national security is in one of Australia’s most important allies. Britain’s defence budget is forecast to reach £62.0 billion (about $117 billion) this financial year, rising to £79.1 billion in 2029-30, according to the House of Commons Library. The spending is on track to reach 2.7 per cent of GDP by 2030. Going further, however, looks simply too hard.



Burnham and Healey have been mugged by reality. One estimate suggests they would need to find an additional £10 billion per year to reach 3 per cent. They obviously cannot find the money. This is not a problem of their own making. The previous Conservative government allowed defence spending to stagnate and budget deficits to deepen over 14 years in power. It would take years to turn this around if Britain’s leaders could ever agree on how to do so. The UK’s public sector net debt just passed £3 trillion, according to market estimates based on official numbers from the Office for Budget Responsibility. This is the net figure after accounting for public assets. It is 94 per cent of GDP. Burnham visited Kyiv last week pledging renewed British support for Ukraine. Henry Nicholls/Pool AFP via AP And it is not getting any better as the years pass. The government’s overall borrowing – the difference between total public sector spending and income – was £56.7 billion in the year to the end of June. The debt will grow. The bond markets are watching and will punish the government if it cannot restrain its spending.





The challenges were laid bare when Iran attacked Cyprus in March during the first wave of drone strikes around the region. The Royal Navy struggled to send a warship to respond swiftly, with several ships unavailable and destroyer HMS Dragon only setting sail one week after the attack. The pressure will only increase as long as Russia remains a threat to Europe. The Russian attacks on Ukraine are highlighting the shortage of Patriot interceptors and other systems to counter Russian missiles. The Russian strike on a Kyiv ammunition depot, killing 37, was the latest sign of this. Britain, along with its major allies in Europe, is now trying to make up for lost time by developing new hypersonic missiles and missile defence systems. (Some of these will be tested at Woomera in South Australia.) It also has to spend on protections against Russian hybrid warfare, such as cyberattacks. None of this comes cheap. The broader context is the withdrawal of American support under President Donald Trump, who wants Britain and other NATO allies to spend more on their own security. Healey thought he had the answer to this in June when his job was to spend the money. It is harder now that his job is to find the money.



Burnham, meanwhile, is enjoying a honeymoon in the opinion polls, as most leaders do after taking office with high hopes. This changes when leaders start making hard decisions. Burnham has spent his first weeks setting ambitious and worthy goals, such as tackling homelessness, but he has yet to do anything that risks offending the Labour base. The hard decisions are yet to come. One of them will be how to pay for more defence spending. Australia has a stake in what Burnham and Healey decide. World.title: Warriors at top of NRL table after 14-point win over Knights
World.content:
Jacob Laban's try double has powered NZ Warriors to a 46-32 shootout win over Newcastle Knights, regaining the NRL competition lead with one week remaining in the regular season.

Needing to win by 14 points to sneak past Penrith Panthers on countback, the Warriors did exactly that, but the result looked unlikely as they lurched out of the starting blocks to trail 16-0 early.

Newcastle scored three tries in the opening quarter hour, before the home side could find the scoreboard, through second-rower Laban, sporting a new bleached hairdo for the occasion.

The Warriors were forced into late changes to their selected line-up with halves Te Maire Martin and Chanel Harris-Tavita dropping out through injury.

Jett Cleary - youngest son of former Warriors player/coach Ivan and younger sibling of NRL superstar Nathan - was handed his first-grade debut and played a major hand in several of the eight tries scored by his team.

After Laban's opening try, they piled on three more to hooker Wayde Egan, lock Erin Clark and forward Demitric Vaimauga before halftime to lead 22-20 at the break.

They have not lost a game from that advantage this season and were next to score after the restart, through centre Ali Leiataua, as Laban chased another Cleary kick and offloaded in midair to his teammate.

Wing Luke Laulilii also made his Warriors debut, but left the game in the first half, after he copped a high tackle from prop Jacob Saifiti, who was sent off as a result, leaving his team undermanned for the next 67 minutes.

Adam Pompey replaced Laulilii and scored to stretch the Warriors lead to 34-20 10 minutes into the second half.

Back-to-back tries to Knights wing Greg Marzhew threatened to spoil the Warriors party, but wing Alofiana Khan-Pereira restored some order, leaving them needing a converted try to rise atop the ladder.

They got that from Laban in the dying moments, as he cut back against the grain for an offload from Cleary to score near the posts. Fullback Taine Tuaupiki missed the first conversion of the night, but slotted the next seven - many from near touch - including the decisive kick for the 14-point margin.

The Warriors now host Manly Sea Eagles at Go Media Stadium next Saturday with a minor premiership crown very much on the line.
