Tech.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Took a Call From Donald Trump in the Middle of an All-Hands
Tech.content:
President Donald Trump interrupted Nvidia’s all-hands staff meeting on Thursday morning when he called CEO Jensen Huang midway through, three sources who witnessed the interaction tell WIRED.

Nvidia’s all-hands meetings typically involve Huang presenting or answering questions, on stage, to in-person staff at the company’s Santa Clara, California, headquarters, while thousands of remote employees tune in to a virtual livestream. During the meeting on Thursday, Huang received a call on his mobile phone, which he stepped aside to take.

Staffers could clearly hear Trump’s distinctive voice through Huang’s onstage microphone, although they couldn’t make out what he was saying. Less than a minute later, Huang returned to the stage and resumed the company meeting.

A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on the incident. But staffers were abuzz about the president’s inadvertent interruption.

In a post on social media later that day, Trump congratulated Huang on Nvidia’s "incredible" quarterly sales and rosy financial forecast for next year. On Wednesday, Nvidia had reported second-quarter revenue of $96 billion, up 106 percent from the same period last year.

Huang regularly jet-sets to Washington to lobby government officials on behalf of his company’s interests—selling chips and building AI infrastructure—and has been in closed-door meetings with Trump before. But the president’s direct call to Huang came at an interesting moment for Nvidia: Earlier on Thursday, the chip giant announced a new employee-funded political action committee, through which it plans to donate to federal candidates as debate around AI policy grows. Nvidia and the Trump administration haven’t always agreed on how to regulate open AI models and sales of advanced chips to China. Bloomberg Law first reported the news of the Nvidia PAC.

The Information recently reported that Nvidia agreed to acquire the open-source platform company Hugging Face, which makes AI data sets, models, and development tools widely available to software engineers who are building AI. An acquisition could be valued at more than $13 billion, Business Insider reports, which would almost certainly require merger approval from US antitrust regulators.

Tech.title: Milo Yiannopoulos Detained by ICE in Louisiana
Tech.content:
Milo Yiannopoulos, a British national known for his near-constant reinventions as a vizier within far-right American politics for more than a decade, has been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Louisiana, according to the department’s records.

While it’s not clear which detention facility Yiannopoulos is currently being held in, the ICE directory instructs any family or legal representatives to contact the Enforcement and Removal Office in Alexandria, Louisiana, a processing center for the central part of the state, about 200 miles from New Orleans.

In an emailed statement, a spokesperson from the US Department of Homeland Security says that Yiannopoulos legally entered the country through New York City in May 2019. “He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” the statement says. “Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing.” The DHS spokesperson says Yiannopoulos was detained on Thursday, August 27 and that “he will remain in ICE custody pending removal.”

TMZ first broke the news of Yiannopoulos’ detention. He has previously lived and worked in the US, allegedly on an O-1 visa, which is for individuals with extraordinary abilities in the arts, sciences, and other areas, including journalism—but he has never been a US citizen.

Yiannopoulos got his start in US politics at the right-wing website Breitbart, where he worked from 2014 to 2017. He left the job after his remarks about sexual intercourse between adults and young adolescent boys, which he said could be “perfectly consensual,” resulted in a backlash. He has dipped in and out of right-wing circles for years, and in 2022 claimed to have arranged an infamous 2022 dinner with Kanye West, white nationalist Nick Fuentes, and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago “to make Trump’s life miserable.”

Yiannopoulos married his long-term boyfriend in Hawaii in 2017 but in 2021 claimed he had become heterosexual and Roman Catholic, and announced plans to open a gay conversion therapy facility in Florida. He went on to work with Fuentes as well as former US representative Marjorie Taylor Greene.

Yiannopoulos also serves as spokesman for Kanye West, who is scheduled to perform at the Caesars Superdome in New Orleans on Friday night as part of his 2026 tour. The longtime provocateur joined West’s theoretical 2024 presidential campaign in late 2022, but walked away days after the rapper espoused Nazi beliefs and praised Adolf Hitler on conspiracist Alex Jones’ Infowars livestream. The two continually reunited and split over the following years, with Yiannopoulis claiming in a series of X posts in 2024 that West was addicted to nitrous oxide.

Throughout his evolution as a MAGA figure, Yiannopoulos has rarely shied away from highly public battles with enemies and rivals. Among the most outspoken is the Islamophobic conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer, who on Friday pinned a post on X announcing his detention by ICE—and appeared to take partial credit for it.

“I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” Loomer wrote. “Milo is going to be deported back to the UK where he can live among the Muslims he has recently chosen to embrace. Today is a great day for America.”

Last summer, Yiannopoulos endorsed a hardline anti-immigration stance on his own X account. “There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering,” he wrote. “We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.”

Update, Friday August 28 at 5 pm: This story was updated to include a statement sent to WIRED by the US Department of Homeland Security.

Tech.title: Equifax Class Action: Last Change to Claim Part of the $2.2M Settlement
Tech.content:
If you used Equifax’s consumer credit reports service in 2022, you may be eligible to claim part of a $2.2 million settlement payout. The case centered on allegations that Equifax violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act, a federal statute that dictates credit reporting companies must “follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.”

The class action lawsuit, Bradberry v. Equifax Information Services LLC, alleged that Equifax “wrongfully reported duplicates of negative accounts” on certain consumer reports, and that these duplicated debt tradelines are a result of the company having inadequate datakeeping policies and procedures. The lawsuit alleges that Equifax “negligently and recklessly disseminated false and damaging information” regarding the credit of certain customers.

Essentially, the lawsuit alleges that Equifax’s negligent reporting made some customers’ debts appear larger than they actually were, potentially creating situations where affected individuals couldn’t secure loans, credit cards, mortgages and other lines of credit.

The plaintiff, Charmayne Bradberry, filed the suit in the US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia. Bradberry said that she received a report showing the same $305 collection account twice, and that each instance showed separate “opened” and “reported” dates for the debt. She alleges that her credit score dropped severely following this report, which may have prevented her from securing a vital mortgage application.

Bradberry is one of 37,651 customers Equifax identified as having received reports with duplicate debt tradelines.

Equifax has denied any wrongdoing and denied that settlement class members were harmed by its actions, and the court has not ruled in favor of either side. The settlement was agreed upon by both parties, and the court has preliminarily approved the $2.2 million payment, subject to a final approval hearing.

The settlement website is live now. The hearing is scheduled to take place on Oct. 6, during which the court will confirm the settlement sum, allocate funds for attorneys’ fees and create a plan to distribute money to the affected class members.

While some class action lawsuits automatically pay out from the agreed-upon sum, that isn’t the case with Bradberry v. Equifax. Affected individuals need to file a claim and provide valid payment information by Sept. 1 to receive a share of the funds.

If you wish to opt out of or object to the settlement, you must do so by the same Sept. 1 deadline. Failure to do so will mean you remain part of the settlement class and forfeit your right to separately sue Equifax for this incident.

Who can be part of the Equifax settlement?

Not every Equifax customer is automatically eligible to claim part of the settlement. The money is reserved for people who received reports with duplicated collection account information that reflected larger sums of debt than existed in reality.

In order to join, you must meet the following qualifications:

Be a living individual in the US or its territories. Received one of the identified Duplicate Reporting Letters from Equifax between August and September 2022.

The settlement class in this case is extremely well-defined. Equifax identified 37,651 people who received duplicated reports. These individuals are the qualifying settlement class members.

Affected class members need to file a paper claim or log in through the settlement website in order to receive a payout. In order to file a claim online, you need to use the unique settlement member ID number included within the initial communication sent to affected individuals. This communication was sent out via postcard and email.

How much will the Equifax settlement pay out?

The total payment for each claimant is capped at $600, but actual payouts will depend on how many settlement class members file claims and how much money the court sets aside for attorney and administrative fees.

Whether or not settlement class members file a claim, they will receive six months of Equifax Complete credit monitoring services, including credit reports, credit score monitoring and up to $500,000 insurance for identity theft-related expenses.

During the claims process, class members must select a valid payment method for their share of the settlement funds. According to the paper claim form, you can choose to have the money sent to a PayPal, Venmo or Zelle account, a virtual prepaid card or a check.

If you’re eligible to claim a piece of the settlement sum, you must file by Sept. 1. Payments will be distributed after the court’s final approval hearing, assuming there are no appeals.

Tech.title: Apple Might Skip the iPhone 18 This Year. Is the iPhone 17 Still Worth It?
Tech.content:
The iPhone 17 closed the gap between Apple’s entry-level phone and the pricier Pro models last year with long-overdue display upgrades, alongside nifty camera and durability improvements. Apple also made new features like Center Stage (its new selfie camera) and Dual Capture available across the entire lineup, making the iPhone 17 an even better value.

A year later, it has become the most affordable entry-level flagship across brands, thanks to Samsung and Google raising the prices of their entry-level models due to a surge in RAM prices driven by AI and data centers.

August is usually when we suggest to avoid buying a new iPhone and to wait for the next one. But things are looking different in 2026.

As we inch closer to the next-generation iPhone announcement on Sept. 9, the iPhone 17 is holding strong against its Android rivals. And it will have to compete with newer models till March 2027, since the iPhone 18 won’t launch until then alongside the iPhone 18E, according to the rumors.

So what if you need a new iPhone before March or don’t want to pay $1,100 or more for an iPhone 18 Pro? I charged up my iPhone 17 and revisited Apple’s standard model this week to find out if it’s still worth buying.

Display, durability and camera upgrades keep it strong

Reading on the iPhone 17 is a pleasant experience. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The iPhone 17 arrived last year with multiple major upgrades, many of which you’ll appreciate daily.

The screen is finally on par with Apple’s Pro models and every other Android counterpart. It runs at a smooth 120Hz refresh rate, which also adapts to the on-screen content to save battery. I compared it to the iPhone 15 and the smoother visuals were immediately noticeable when scrolling through the home screen. It makes the phone feel faster and more responsive.

The display is also brighter and less reflective than its predecessor. It is immediately noticeable when you’re navigating outdoors or need to do anything on your phone under bright lights. I put it against the new Pixel 11, which is equally bright, but iPhone 17’s smaller bezels make its screen more pleasing to look at.

Apple said its 2025 iPhones were more durable than ever. While I haven’t used the iPhone 17 for a year straight, I have daily driven the iPhone 17 Pro Max without a case for 10 months. (Yes, I’m that guy.) Compared to my 2024 iPhone 16 Pro, the 17 Pro has fared better against scratches and drops thanks to its Ceramic Shield 2 glass, the same found on the iPhone 17.

The auto framing feature, combined with better stabilization, has been a godsend for recording myself using the front camera. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Some might dismiss it as a minor feature, but the 17’s selfie camera is the best upgrade, in my opinion. The new 18-megapixel square sensor is more of a quality-of-life upgrade than just a mere number bump because it lets you shoot landscape selfies without needing to rotate your phone. The viewfinder automatically repositions its framing based on the number of people in the photo.

I love the camera for two reasons. First, it enables Center Stage, which tracks you (even if you’re moving) on video calls (both on FaceTime and third-party apps like WhatsApp). It’s a handy feature for when I need to move around doing chores, but the camera keeps me in the frame and helps me be less annoying for my girlfriend.

Second, the square sensor improves stability in selfie video recording. I live with a condition that causes constant hand tremors, which makes it difficult to record myself on phones. The iPhone 17 has been helpful as I’m less self-conscious and more confident that I’ll get stable footage instead of a blurry video.

As for the two cameras on the back, they are far more capable than its predecessor. The iPhone 17 has two rear cameras: a 48-megapixel wide-angle camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide, which is an upgrade over the 12-megapixel ultrawide camera on the iPhone 16. You’ll get sharp photos, better indoor shots and a smooth video experience. It misses out on a telephoto camera that the 17 Pro has, so there’s no optical zoom, but these are all the cameras most people would ever need.

iOS 26 has its flaws — I can’t wait for iOS 27

iOS 26 (left) displaces the Control Center settings in landscape orientation. The upcoming iOS 27 (right) has fixed this issue. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The iPhone 17 runs iOS 26, which offers more translucent controls, customization options and Apple Intelligence features. However, my experience has been buggy since the beginning. On multiple occasions, I’ve missed calls and alarms because my iPhone automatically lowered its system volume to a minimum. I didn’t put it in Do Not Disturb or Focus modes. Other times, the keyboard starts lagging out of nowhere, and whenever I need to access the Control Center while watching a video in landscape mode, my controls are all over the place.

Some of these issues have already been fixed on the iOS 27 Public Beta, which I’ve been running on my iPhone 17 Pro Max.

For starters, I can set different volume levels for the call ringer, alarms and media. The Control Center is now better optimized for horizontal orientation, keeping my customizations right where I want them. Then there are smart features, like spatial reframing in Photos for using generative AI to “change” the camera’s position when an image was taken. There’s also an all-new Siri mode in the Camera app.

In CNET’s 45-minute endurance test, which includes streaming, scrolling through social media, joining a video call and playing games, Apple’s entry-level iPhone went from full to 98%, which matches the results of the iPhone 17 Pro. It has the second-longest battery life of any phone CNET has tested in the past 12 months, tied with the OnePlus 15 and Motorola Razr (2026); behind the first-place phone is the iPhone 17 Pro Max.

However, subsequent iOS 26 updates along with continued use have had an impact on the battery life of my personal iPhone 17, causing more overnight idle drain. That’s why I’m looking forward to the upcoming iOS 27 update. If the beta is any indication, it should only improve the iPhone 17 experience with smarter features and better stability.

It has fared well, but what about six months from now?

The iPhone 17 has aged well and stacks well against its 2026 Android rivals. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The baseline model stacks well against the competition. The iPhone 17 was launched at $799, which is $100 less than the $899 Samsung Galaxy S26 and the new Google Pixel 11. But with phone prices increasing across the board and new rumors pointing to higher iPhone prices, the iPhone 17’s current price is good if you are looking for a phone upgrade.

Those notable upgrades make it worth the $799 price, which might not remain the same in a few days from now, when Apple announces the iPhone 18 Pro and its first-ever foldable iPhone Ultra.

While the iPhone 18 is tipped to be announced next year, the Pro series could get a price hike, resulting in a wider price gap between the entry-level and top-of-the-line models.

To compensate, Apple could push the ceiling of its base iPhone and make it more expensive, even before the iPhone 18 launches. This is just speculation right now, based on Apple’s recent price hikes. But the base iPhone has remained at $799 ($829 without a carrier discount) since 2020, and after the new pricing on Macs, iPads and several other products, it makes much more sense to raise the barrier to a new entry-level model than ever.

As for those willing to wait for the iPhone 18, it is unlikely to be a major upgrade. Apple is expected to reserve the most prominent changes like a reduced Dynamic Island and newer cameras for its Pro models. Moreover, a recent rumor on Weibo suggests that the iPhone 18 could align more closely with a lower-cost iPhone 18E model. It might not receive a similarly powerful chip as its Pro siblings, for instance. It’s a similar move Google has made with its base Pixel 11 and budget Pixel 10A.

Given the lukewarm rumors regarding the upcoming model and iPhone 17’s current price tag (and the looming price hike), I think last year’s model is still an excellent deal. And for the first time in my career, I’d say if you want a new iPhone before Sept. 9, it is totally fine to get the iPhone 17 now rather than wait and see what the 18 Pro may bring.

Tech.title: This Website Is the Most Reliable Tool for Looking Up Flock Cameras Near You
Tech.content:
Flock Safety’s AI surveillance cameras, drones and listening devices get plenty of attention these days as they continue to expand across the US — but they can still can catch us by surprise. I’ve seen many people and even city councils surprised that local law enforcement or private organizations have signed Flock contracts. That’s a major reason I created a guide on exactly how to recognize a Flock camera, as opposed to other devices. But there’s also another tool I highly recommend using if you’re worried about Flock and don’t know where to start.

Maintained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the Reynolds School of Journalism at the University of Nevada, Reno, this database tracks police surveillance technology deployments across the US using public records, news reports, community submissions and a whole truckload of research.

In South Carolina, officials have been sparring over whether to install 25 new cameras, a dispute that reflects broader questions about cost, oversight, and how much surveillance communities are willing to accept. The city of Los Angeles recently broke its contract with Flock Safety, though Flock’s CEO argues that the suspension should be temporary while the police department revises its rules.

Public opposition has fueled many of these cancellations, reflecting concerns that the system facilitates mass surveillance and can lead to harms such as discriminatory policing and privacy infringements. It’s also led to a concerning rise in police officers getting arrested for using the systems to stalk exes.

To track such surveillance, journalists and researchers are increasingly turning to a free tool called the Atlas of Surveillance, a collaboration between the renowned digital privacy group Electronic Frontier Foundation and the University of Nevada, Reno. The site has become a go‑to source for mapping police technology — which also includes drones, facial-recognition cameras and body cameras — with a searchable database that’s often more dependable than alternatives.

Atlas searches only take seconds to get started. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

With the Atlas of Surveillance tool, you enter a city, county, state, law enforcement agency or vendor in the US and select which technology you’re interested in tracking. You’ll get a list of details based on your search, including links to public records or news articles.

A major advantage of this tool, besides its reliability compared to other apps, is that it covers all kinds of surveillance technology local governments and police have adopted, not just ALPR cameras but drones, databases, bodycams and other tools, by Flock and a variety of competitors such as Axon.

“We frequently run into situations where local councilpeople don’t even know that a certain tool is in use,” said Beryl Lipton, Electronic Frontier Foundation senior investigative researcher. “Learning about a technology we have logged in the Atlas of Surveillance is meant to help people have conversations [about] whether that tool is appropriate for local use, start asking questions, and advocate for standards around how their police can or can’t use this equipment.”

Surveilling surveillance

While other tools for tracking Flock cameras and similar surveillance systems exist, I prefer the EFF’s approach, which uses reliable crowdsourced data from specific volunteers, including University of Nevada students and staff, as well as experienced researchers. These volunteers use a variety of information, including government documents, press releases, news stories and confirmed social media posts, to create lists of exactly which surveillance technologies local police or sheriff departments are using, as well as when they were adopted.

Deflock, another popular crowdsourced app for reporting Flock camera locations, has an open-source design that leaves it vulnerable to false reports from people who only think they’re seeing a surveillance device. Self-reports are also becoming less reliable as surveillance cameras are being hidden in speed signs and cacti.

The Atlas provides sources for its information and includes records dating back years. EFF

I tried the Atlas tool with several location searches, including Albany, Georgia, where five police officers were fired and arrested in July on charges of misusing the city’s Flock system. Sure enough, I could see exactly when Albany began its Flock program, among other details about the technology it uses.

“While we may know that a police department has a tool, we may not know that they don’t have a governing policy or what is in the policy they have, like how long the data is retained,” Lipton told me.

Lipton recommends that users pair the Atlas tool with the EFF’s Street-Level Surveillance hub, which offers deeper documentation, including details on third‑party vendors that collaborate with law enforcement.

The Atlas database isn’t perfect, and the volunteers can do only so much. In my own searches, I found that my home city offered accurate listings for traffic cameras, but didn’t mention the period when it adopted Flock automated license plate readers last year, before removing them after public complaint. I’ve seen similar patterns in other cities with comparable histories, suggesting the database may emphasize active programs or exclude portions of older records.

Resources like the Atlas of Surveillance give residents a clearer view of the technologies their police departments use, information that can otherwise be difficult to obtain. As I’ve covered before, some cities will carefully omit the name “Flock” when announcing new surveillance or monitoring programs, even if they are using the brand’s drones or ALPR cameras.

If you’d like to volunteer for the Atlas of Surveillance, you can select the Collaborate option to submit a datapoint for consideration.

Tech.title: What Meta’s All-New Social Media Guidelines Promise to Change for Teen Users
Tech.content:
The fallout of an $18 billion lawsuit against Meta, announced on Wednesday, is already here. A new announcement from Meta is designed to meet the terms of the settled lawsuit while helping to prevent teen social media addiction.

In its post, Meta outlined a series of changes to both Instagram and Facebook that will apply only to those under 18. Most of the changes were required as part of the lawsuit settlement, notably the creation of daily limits and night mode controls for teens, as well as the adoption of age-assurance measures to help prevent cheating the system. As part of the agreement, Meta has denied any wrongdoing.

There’s been worldwide pushback against teens and children using social media, including the EU restricting access to social apps for kids under 13, and Australia banning apps like Instagram for anyone under 16. But some advocates worry Meta’s changes won’t be enough to fully protect teens.

In an interview with Democracy Now on Thursday, attorney and co-director of the AI Now research institute, Amba Kak, said the changes don’t address the platform’s architecture, which is designed to addict teenagers with features like infinite scroll. “It’s the business model of surveillance advertising, where it is the optimization of engagement and attention at any cost,” Kak said. “And I think if we don’t get at those root cause fixes, we’re going to be stuck playing whack-a-mole.”

A representative from Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Time limits for kids

Chief among the upcoming changes to Instagram and Facebook are time limitations for teens. A new default time limit will set the social media scrolling time to 2 hours a day for those under 18, and it can only be extended by parents.

An additional night mode will block most access to content such as feeds, stories, explore mode and reels between midnight and 6 a.m. and a school mode will mute notifications between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m.

Meta is also adding a feature to give 15-minute warnings to teens if they’ve been on the apps for an extended period of time, as well as 60-minute and 90-minute warnings they’re daily allotment is running down. To further reduce constant scrolling, autoplay for videos and clips will also be turned off by default, but like most features, it can be adjusted by parents.

Protection against toxic content

Meta is also implementing a number of changes intended to reduce toxicity and obsession with social media. By default, teens won’t see likes and reactions on posts, including their own. They’ll also be restricted from seeing certain content, such as cosmetic surgery and “extreme makeup” filters, although it’s not clear how far those limitations will extend (for example, a filter that adds dog ears).

Meta is adding age-appropriate content restrictions, but it remains vague on the details. While using movie ratings and parent feedback to build filters, the company fails to explain how this applies to social media posts or provide examples of blocked content.

In addition, teens will have the option to choose a non-algorithm version of their feeds that won’t be personalized by any Meta recommendations (which I also want for my own account).

Hazy tools for age verification

A new age-assurance strategy is also coming to Instagram and Facebook, but it’s unclear how it will work.

“We’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to under-13s,” Meta said on its blog. “We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may be between the ages of 13 and 17.”

Meta didn’t provide any details on how this tech would work, what it would look for or how it would flag accounts. I also asked about any appeals process for those incorrectly tagged, but Meta didn’t respond to my request.

It’s possible Meta will be using AI scan to profile context, account activity and visual cues to raise red flags, but there’s not much clarity otherwise.

Rolling out changes

The proposed changes were approved by a judge on Thursday, and Meta will roll out the first protections in the coming months, with the rest to follow afterward, although the exact timeline isn’t clear. As required by the agreement, Meta will also establish an independent social media research foundation to share “consented” user data in an effort to support teen well-being.

In its post, Meta said, “The fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day. All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place … we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard.”

Other platforms have not responded to this call-out.

Tech.title: AT&T Sues Charter Over ‘Fiber’ Internet
Tech.content:
AT&T filed a lawsuit against Charter on Friday, alleging that its marketing of “fiber-powered” internet is misleading customers.

The argument centers around an ad campaign from Charter, which sells home internet under the Spectrum brand name.

Fiber is widely considered the gold standard for home internet. It’s the only connection type that delivers symmetrical upload and download speeds, which makes it especially valuable for activities like online gaming or videoconferencing. On Spectrum’s cable plans, typical upload speeds top out at 40Mbps, while download speeds exceed 1,000Mbps. I always advise readers to go with a fiber provider whenever it’s available.

Over the past couple of years, cable internet providers have increasingly tried to capitalize on that fiber cache. It’s technically true that Spectrum provides “fiber-powered” internet. Like all cable ISPs, Spectrum uses fiber-optic cables — thin glass strands that carry data through light signals — for the vast majority of its network. But it switches to copper coaxial cables in most cases to travel the proverbial last mile to your home. Fiber providers like AT&T, on the other hand, run the fiber connection all the way to the jack in your wall.

Many cable companies are in the process of upgrading that last mile to fiber. Spectrum currently reports to the FCC that 2.3% of US households have access to its fiber plans, while 29.9% can get its cable plans.

“We don’t think customers should have to be telecom experts or squint at the fine print to know what they’re buying,” an AT&T representative told me in an email. “When internet is marketed as fiber, customers deserve 100% fiber all the way to their home.”

I spot-checked a handful of addresses on Spectrum’s website in Dallas, where AT&T is filing its lawsuit, and some of them did return fiber plans. According to FCC data, which is self-reported by ISPs, Spectrum covers around 608,000 households in Dallas, while AT&T covers almost 495,000.

This isn’t the first time Charter has been chided for passing itself off as a fiber provider. In March, Spectrum agreed to modify its “fiber-powered” statements after AT&T brought a challenge through the Better Business Bureau’s National Advertising Division.

Spectrum’s advertising describes its service as “fiber-powered” but notes in the fine print that it’s connected via coaxial lines. Spectrum/Screenshot by CNET

As a part of that challenge, Spectrum agreed to “clearly and conspicuously” disclose that its “fiber-powered internet services are not delivered to customers’ homes over a fiber-to-the-home infrastructure.” The fine print on Spectrum’s internet page notes that the connection to the premises is delivered via coaxial lines.

A representative for Charter did not immediately respond to my request for comment.
